Really, is he to be interrupting me in this way?
CHREMES
Do you proceed.
CRITO
He who received him was a relation of mine. There I heard from him that he was a native of Attica. He died there.
CHREMES
5.4.928:
His name?
CRITO
The name, in such a hurry!
PAMPHILUS
Phania.
CHREMES
(starting.)
5.4.929:
Hah! I shall die!
CRITO
I’faith, I really think it was Phania; this I know for certain,
5.4.930:
he said that he was a citizen of Rhamnus.
CHREMES
O Jupiter!
CRITO
Many other persons in Andros have heard the same, Chremes.
CHREMES
(aside.)
5.4.931:
I trust it may turn out as I hope. (To CRITO.) Come now, tell me, what did he then say about her? Did he say she was his own daughter?
CRITO
5.4.932:
No.
CHREMES
Whose then?
CRITO
His brother’s daughter.
CHREMES
5.4.933:
She certainly is mine.
CRITO
What do you say?
SIMO
What is this that you say?
PAMPHILUS
(aside.)
Prick up your ears, Pamphilus.
SIMO
5.4.934:
Why do you suppose so?
CHREMES
That Phania was my brother.
SIMO
I knew him, and I am aware of it.
CHREMES
5.4.935:
He, flying from the wars, and following me to Asia, set out from here. At the same time he was afraid to leave her here behind; since then, this is the first time I have heard what became of him.
PAMPHILUS
(aside.)
5.4.937:
I am scarcely myself, so much has my mind been agitated by fear, hope, joy, and surprise at this so great, so unexpected blessing.
SIMO
5.4.939:
Really, I am glad for many reasons that she has been discovered to be a citizen.
PAMPHILUS
I believe it, father.
CHREMES
5.4.940:
But there yet remains one difficulty with me, which keeps me in suspense.
PAMPHILUS
(aside.)
You deserve to be —, with your scruples, you plague. You are seeking a knot in a bulrush.
CRITO
(to CHREMES.)
5.4.942:
The names don’t agree.
CRITO
Troth, she had another when little.
CHREMES
What was it, Crito? Can you remember it?
CRITO
5.4.943:
I’m trying to recollect it.
PAMPHILUS
(aside.)
Am I to suffer his memory to stand in the way of my happiness, when I myself can provide my own remedy in this matter? I will not suffer it. (Aloud.) Hark you, Chremes, that which you are trying to recollect is Pasibula.
CHREMES
5.4.945:
The very same.
CRITO
That’s it.
PAMPHILUS
5.4.946:
I’ve heard it from herself a thousand times.
SIMO
I suppose, Chremes, that you believe that we all rejoice at this discovery.
CHREMES
5.4.947:
So may the Gods bless me, I do believe it.
PAMPHILUS
5.4.847:
What remains to be done, father?
SIMO
5.4.948:
The event itself has quite brought me to reconcilement.
PAMPHILUS
O kind father! With regard to her as a wife, since I have taken possession of her, Chremes will not offer any opposition.
CHREMES
5.4.949:
The plea is a very good one, unless perchance your father says any thing to the contrary.
PAMPHILUS
5.4.950:
Of course, I agree.
SIMO
Then be it so.
CHREMES
Her portion, Pamphilus, is ten talents.
PAMPHILUS
5.4.951:
I alm satisfied.
CHREMES
I’ll hasten to my daughter. Come now, (beckoning.) along with me, Crito; for I suppose that she will not know me.
(They go into GLYCERIUM’s house.) SIMO
(To PAMPHILUS.)
5.4.952:
Why don’t you order her to be sent for hither, to our house?
PAMPHILUS
5.4.953:
Well thought of; I’ll at once give charge of that to Davus.
SIMO
He can’t do it.
PAMPHILUS
5.4.954:
How so?
SIMO
Because he has another matter that more nearly concerns himself, and of more importance.
PAMPHILUS
What, pray?
SIMO
He is bound.
PAMPHILUS
5.4.955:
Father, he is not rightly bound.
SIMO
But I ordered to that effect.
PAMPHILUS
Prithee, do order him to be set at liberty,
SIMO
5.4.956:
Well, be it so.
PAMPHILUS
But immediately.
SIMO
I’m going in.
PAMPHILUS
O fortunate and happy day!
(SIMO goes into his house.)

5.5.957:
(Enter CHARINUS, at a distance.) CHARINUS
(apart to himself.)
I’m come to see what Pamphilus is about; and look, here he is.
PAMPHILUS
(to himself.)
Some one perhaps might imagine that I don’t believe this to be true; but now it is clear to me that it really is true. I do think that the life of the Gods is everlasting,
5.5.960:
for this reason, because their joys are their own. For immortality has been obtained by me, if no sorrow interrupts this delight. But whom in particular could I wish to be now thrown in my way, for me to relate these things to?
CHARINUS
(apart to himself.)
5.5.963:
What means this rapture?
PAMPHILUS
(to himself.)
I see Davus. There is no one in the world whom I would choose in preference; for I am sure that he of all people will sincerely rejoice in my happiness.

5.6.965:
(Enter DAVUS.) DAVUS
(to himself.)
Where is Pamphilus, I wonder?
PAMPHILUS
Here he is, Davus.
DAVUS
(turning round.)
Who’s that?
PAMPHILUS
’Tis I,
Pamphilus;
5.6.966:
you don’t know what has happened to me.
DAVUS
No really; but I know what has happened to myself.
PAMPHILUS
5.6.967:
And I too.
DAVUS
It has fallen out just like human affairs in general, that you should know the mishap I have met with, before I the good that has befallen you.
PAMPHILUS
5.6.969:
My Glycerium has discovered her parents.
DAVUS
O, well done!
CHARINUS
(apart, in surprise.)
Hah!
PAMPHILUS
5.6.970:
Her father is an intimate friend of ours.
DAVUS
Who?
PAMPHILUS
Chremes.
DAVUS
You do tell good news.
PAMPHILUS
5.6.971:
And there’s no hinderance to my marrying her at once.
CHARINUS
(apart.)
Is he dreaming the same that he has been wishing for when awake?
PAMPHILUS
5.6.972:
Then about the child, Davus.
DAVUS
O, say no more; you are the only person whom the Gods favor.
CHARINUS
(apart.)
5.6.973:
I’m all right if these things are true. I’ll accost them.
(Comes forward.)
PAMPHILUS
5.6.974:
Who is this? Why, Charinus, you meet me at the very nick of time.
CHARINUS
5.6.975:
That’s all right.
PAMPHILUS
Have you heard—?
CHARINUS
Every thing; come, in your good fortune do have some regard for me. Chremes is now at your command; I’m sure that he’ll do every thing you wish.
PAMPHILUS
5.6.977:
I’ll remember you; and because it is tedious for us to wait for him until he comes out, follow me this way; he is now in-doors at the house of Glycerium; do you, Davus, go home; send with all haste to remove her thence. Why are you standing there? Why are you delaying?
DAVUS
5.6.979: I’m going. (PAMPHILUS and CHARINUS go into the house of GLYCERIUM. DAVUS then comes forward and addresses the Audience.) Don’t you wait until they come out from there; she will be betrothed within: if there is any thing else that remains, it will be transacted in-doors.

0.0.1:
THE PROLOGUE
LEST it should be a matter of surprise to any one of you, why the Poet has assigned to an old man a part that belongs to the young, that I will first explain to you; and then, the reason for my coming I will disclose. An entire Play from an entire Greek one,
0.0.5: the Heautontimorumenos, I am to-day about to represent, which from a two-fold plot has been made but one. I have shown that it is new, and what it is: next I would mention who it was that wrote it, and whose in Greek it is, if I did not think that the greater part of you are aware.
0.0.10: Now, for what reason I have learned this part, in a few words I will explain. The Poet intended me to be a Pleader, not the Speaker of a Prologue; your decision he asks, and has appointed me the advocate; if this advocate can avail as much by his oral powers as he has excelled in inventing happily,
0.0.15: who composed this speech which I am about to recite. For as to malevolent rumors spreading abroad that he has mixed together many Greek Plays while writing a few Latin ones, he does not deny that this is the case, and that he does not repent of so doing; and he affirms that he will do so again.
0.0.20: He has the example of good Poets; after which example he thinks it is allowable for him to do what they have done. Then, as to a malevolent old Poet saying that he has suddenly applied himself to dramatic pursuits, relying on the genius of his friends, and not his own natural abilities;
0.0.25: on that your judgment your your opinion, will prevail. Wherefore I do entreat you all, that the suggestions of our antagonists may not avail more than those of our favorers. Do you be favorable; grant the means of prospering to those who afford you the means of being spectators of new Plays;
0.0.30: those, I mean, without faults: that he may not suppose this said in his behalf who lately made the public give way to a slave as he ran along in the street; why should he take a madman’s part? About his faults he will say more when he brings out some other new ones, unless he puts an end to his caviling.
0.0.35: Attend with favorable feelings; grant me the opportunity that I may be allowed to act a quiet Play in silence; that the servant everlastingly running about, the angry old man, the gluttonous parasite, the impudent sharper, and the greedy procurer, may not have always to be performed by me
0.0.40: with the utmost expense of voice, and the greatest exertion. For my sake come to the conclusion that this request is fair, that so some portion of my labor may be abridged. For nowadays, those who write new Plays do not spare an aged man. If there is any piece requiring exertion, they come running to me;
0.0.45: but if it is a light one, it is taken to another Company. In the present one the style is pure. Do you make proof, what, in each character, my ability can effect. If I have never greedily set a high price upon my skill, and have come to the conclusion that this is my greatest gain,
0.0.50: as far as possible to be subservient to your convenience, establish in me a precedent, that the young may be anxious rather to please you than themselves.

1.1.53:
(Enter CHREMES, and MENEDEMUS with a spade in his hand, who falls to digging.) CHREMES
Although this acquaintanceship between us is of very recent date, from the time in fact of your purchasing an estate here in the neighborhood,
1.1.56: yet either your good qualities, or our being neighbors (which I take to be a sort of friendship), induces me to inform you, frankly and familiarly, that you appear to me to labor beyond your years,
1.1.60: and beyond what your affairs require. For, in the name of Gods and men, what would you have? What can be your aim? You are, as I conjecture, sixty years of age, or more. No man in these parts has a better or a more valuable estate, no one
1.1.65: more servants; and yet you discharge their duties just as diligently as if there were none at all. However early in the morning I go out, and however late in the evening I return home, I see you either digging, or plowing, or doing something, in fact, in the fields.
1.1.70:
You take respite not an instant, and are quite regardless of yourself. I am very sure that this is not done for your amusement. But really I am vexed how little work is done here. If you were to employ the time you spend in laboring yourself, in keeping your servants at work, you would profit much more.
MENEDEMUS
1.1.75:
Have you so much leisure, Chremes, from your own affairs, that you can attend to those of others—those which don’t concern you?
CHREMES
1.1.77:
I am a man, and nothing that concerns a man do I deem a matter of indifference to me. Suppose that I wish either to advise you in this matter, or to be informed myself: if what you do is right, that I may do the same; if it is not, then that I may dissuade you.
MENEDEMUS
1.1.80:
It’s requisite for me to do so; do you as it is necessary for you to do.
CHREMES
1.1.81:
Is it requisite for any person to torment himself?
MENEDEMUS
It is for me.
CHREMES
1.1.82:
If you have any affliction, I could wish it otherwise. But prithee, what sorrow is this of yours? How have you deserved so ill of yourself?
MENEDEMUS
1.1.83:
Alas! alas!
(He begins to weep.)
CHREMES
1.1.84: Do not weep, but make me acquainted with it, whatever it is.
1.1.85:
Do not be reserved; fear nothing; trust me, I tell you. Either by consolation, or by counsel, or by any means, I will aid you.
MENEDEMUS
1.1.87:
Do you wish to know this matter?
CHREMES
Yes, and for the reason I mentioned to you.
MENEDEMUS
1.1.88:
I will tell you.
CHREMES
But still, in the mean time, lay down that rake; don’t fatigue yourself.
MENEDEMUS
1.1.89:
By no means.
CHREMES
What can be your object?
(Tries to take the rake from him.)
MENEDEMUS
1.1.90:
Do leave me alone, that I may give myself no respite from my labor.
CHREMES
1.1.91:
I will not allow it, I tell you.
(Taking the rake from him.)
MENEDEMUS
Ah! that’s not fair.
CHREMES
(poising the rake.)
1.1.92:
Whew! such a heavy one as this, pray!
MENEDEMUS
Such are my deserts.
CHREMES
1.1.93:
Now speak.
(Laying down the rake.)
MENEDEMUS
I have an only son,—a young man,—alas! why did I say—I have?—rather I should say, I had one, Chremes:—
1.1.95:
whether I have him now, or not, is uncertain.
CHREMES
Why so?
MENEDEMUS
You shall know:—There is a poor old woman here, a stranger from Corinth:—her daughter, a young woman, he fell in love with, insomuch that he almost regarded her as his wife; all this took place unknown to me. When I discovered the matter, I began to reprove him, not with gentleness,
1.1.100: nor in the way suited to the love-sick mind of a youth, but with violence, and after the usual method of fathers. I was daily reproaching him,—Look you, do you expect to be allowed any longer to act thus, myself, your father, being alive; to be keeping a mistress pretty much as though your wife?
1.1.105: You are mistaken, Clinia, and you don’t know me, if you fancy that. I am willing that you should be called my son, just as long as you do what becomes you; but if you do not do so, I shall find out how it becomes me to act toward you. This arises from nothing, in fact, but too much idleness.
1.1.110: At your time of life, I did not devote my time to dalliance, but, in consequence of my poverty, departed hence for Asia, and there acquired in arms both riches and military glory. At length the matter came to this,—the youth, from hearing the same things so often, and with such severity, was overcome.
1.1.115:
He supposed that I, through age and affection, had more judgment and foresight for him than him-self. He went off to Asia, Chremes, to serve under the king.
CHREMES
1.1.118:
What is it you say?
MENEDEMUS
He departed without my knowledge—and has been gone these three months.
CHREMES
1.1.119:
Both are to be blamed—although I still think this step shows an ingenuous and enterprising disposition.
MENEDEMUS
1.1.121: When I learned this from those who were in the secret, I returned home sad, and with feelings almost over-whelmed and distracted through grief. I sit down; my servants run to me; they take off my shoes: then some make all haste to spread the couches,
1.1.125: and to prepare a repast; each according to his ability did zealously what he could, in order to alleviate my sorrow. When I observed this, I began to reflect thus:—What! are so many persons anxious for my sake alone, to pleasure myself only?
1.1.130: Are so many female servants to provide me with dress? Shall I alone keep up such an expensive establishment, while my only son, who ought equally, or even more so, to enjoy these things—inasmuch as his age is better suited for the enjoyment of them—him, poor youth, have I driven away from home by my severity!
1.1.135: Were I to do this, really I should deem myself deserving of any calamity. But so long as he leads this life of penury, banished from his country through my severity, I will revenge his wrongs upon myself, toiling, making money, saving, and laying up for him.
1.1.140: At once I set about it; I left nothing in the house, neither movables nor clothing; every thing I scraped together. Slaves, male and female, except those who could easily pay for their keep by working in the country, all of them I set up to auction and sold. I at once put up a bill
1.1.145: to sell my house. I collected somewhere about fifteen talents, and purchased this farm; here I fatigue myself: I have come to this conclusion, Chremes, that I do my son a less injury, while I am unhappy; and that it is not right for me to enjoy any pleasure here,
1.1.150:
until such time as he returns home safe to share it with me.
CHREMES
1.1.151: I believe you to be of an affectionate disposition toward your children, and him to be an obedient son, if one were to manage him rightly or prudently. But neither did you understand him sufficiently well, nor he you—a thing that happens where persons don’t live on terms of frankness together.
1.1.155:
You never showed him how highly you valued him, nor did he ever dare put that confidence in you which is due to a father. Had this been done, these troubles would never have befallen you.
MENEDEMUS
1.1.158:
Such is the fact, I confess; the greatest fault is on my side.
CHREMES
1.1.159: But still, Menedemus, I hope for the best, and
1.1.160:
I trust that he’ll be here safe before long.
MENEDEMUS
1.1.161:
Oh that the Gods would grant it!
CHREMES
They will do so. Now, if it is convenient to you—the festival of Bacchus is being kept here to-day—I wish you to give me your company.
MENEDEMUS
1.1.163:
I can not.
CHREMES
Why not? Do, pray, spare yourself a little while. Your absent son would wish you do so.
MENEDEMUS
1.1.165:
It is not right that I, who have driven him hence to endure hardships, should now shun them myself.
CHREMES
1.1.167:
It is.
CHREMES
Then kindly fare you wall.
MENEDEMUS
And you the same.
(Goes into his house.)
CHREMES
(to himself.)
He has forced tears from me, and I do pity him. But as the day is far gone, I must remind Phania, this neighbor of mine,
1.1.170:
to come to dinner. I’ll go see whether he is at home. (Goes to PHANIA’s door, makes the inquiry, and returns.) There was no occasion for me to remind him: they tell me he has been some time already at my house; it’s I myself am making my guests wait. I’ll go in-doors immediately. But what means the noise at the door of my house? I wonder who’s coming out! I’ll step aside here.
(He stands aside.)

1.2.175:
(Enter CLITIPHO, from the house of CHREMES.) CLITIPHO
(at the door, to CLINIA within.)
There is nothing, Clinia, for you to fear as yet: they have not been long by any means: and I am sure that she will be with you presently along with the messenger. Do at once dismiss these causeless apprehensions which are tormenting you.
CHREMES
(apart.)
1.2.178:
Who is my son talking to?
(Makes his appearance.)
CLITIPHO
(to himself.)
1.2.179:
Here comes my father, whom I wished to see: I’ll accost him. Father, you have met me opportunely.
CHREMES
1.2.180:
What is the matter?
CLITIPHO
Do you know this neighbor of ours, Menedemus?
CHREMES
Very well.
CLITIPHO
1.2.181:
Do you know that he has a son?
CHREMES
I have heard that he has; in Asia.
CLITIPHO
He is not in Asia, father; he is at:our house.
CHREMES
1.2.182:
What is it you say?
CLITIPHO
Upon his arrival, after he had just landed from the ship, I immediately brought him to dine with us; for from our very childhood upward I have always been on intimate terms with him.
CHREMES
1.2.184: You announce to me a great pleasure.
1.2.185:
How much I wish that Menedemus had accepted my invitation to make one of us: that at my house I might have been the first to surprise him, when not expecting it, with this delight!—and even yet there’s time enough—
CLITIPHO
1.2.187:
Take care what you do; there is no necessity, father, for doing so.
CHREMES
1.2.188:
For what reason?
CLITIPHO
Why, because he is as yet undetermined what to do with himself. He is but just arrived. He fears every thing; his father’s displeasure, and how his mistress may be disposed toward him.
1.2.190:
He loves her to distraction: on her account, this trouble and going abroad took place.
CHREMES
I know it.
CLITIPHO
1.2.191:
He has just sent a servant into the city to her, and I ordered our Syrus to go with him.
CHREMES
1.2.192:
What does Clinia say?
CLITIPHO
What does he say? That he is wretched.
CHREMES
Wretched? Whom could we less suppose so? What is there wanting for him to enjoy every thing that among men, in fact, are esteemed as blessings? Parents, a country in prosperity, friends, family, relations, riches?
1.2.195:
And yet, all these are just according to the disposition of him who possesses them. To him who knows how to use them, they are blessings; to him who does not use them rightly, they are evils.
CLITIPHO
1.2.197:
Aye, but lie always was a morose old man; and now I dread nothing more, father, than that in his displeasure he’ll be doing something to him more than is justifiable.
CHREMES
1.2.199:
What, he? (Aside.) But I’ll restrain myself; for that the other one should be in fear of his father is of service to him.
CLITIPHO
1.2.200:
What is it you are saying to yourself?
CHREMES
I’ll tell you. However the case stood, Clinia ought still to have remained at home. Perhaps his father was a little stricter than he liked: he should have put up with it. For whom ought he to bear with, if he would not bear with his own father? Was it reasonable that he should live after his son’s humor, or his son after his? And as to charging him with harshness, it is not the fact. For the severities of fathers
1.2.205: are generally of one character, those I mean who are in some degree reasonable men. They do not wish their sons to be always wenching; they do not wish them to be always carousing; they give a limited allowance; and yet all this tends to virtuous conduct. But when the mind, Clitipho, has once enslaved itself by vicious appetites, it must of necessity follow similar pursuits. This
1.2.210:
is a wise maxim, to take warning from others of what may be to your own advantage.
CLITIPHO
1.2.211:
I believe so.
CHREMES
I’ll now go hence in-doors, to see what we have for dinner. Do you, seeing what is the time of day, mind and take care not to be any where out of the way.
(Goes into his house, and exit CLITIPHO.)

2.1.213:
(Enter CLITIPHO.) CLITIPHO
(to himself.)
What partial judges are all fathers in regard to all of us young men, in thinking it reasonable for us to become old men all at once from boys,
2.1.215: and not to participate in those things which youth is naturally inclined to. They regulate us by their own desires,—such as they now are,—not as they once were. If ever I have a son, he certainly shall find in me an indulgent father. For the means both of knowing and of pardoning his faults shall be found by me; not like mine, who by means of another person, discloses to me his own sentiments.
2.1.220: I’m plagued to death,—when he drinks a little more than usual, what pranks of his own he does relate to me! Now he says, Take warning from others of what may be to your advantage. How shrewd! He certainly does not know how deaf I am at the moment when he’s telling his stories. Just now, the words of my mistress make more impression upon me. Give me this, and bring me that, she cries; I have nothing to say to her in answer, and no one is there more wretched than myself.
2.1.225:
But this Clinia, although he, as well, has cares enough of his own, still has a mistress of virtuous and modest breeding, and a stranger to the arts of a courtesan. Mine is a craving, saucy, haughty, extravagant creature, full of lofty airs. Then all that I have to give her is—fair words—for I make it a point not to tell her that I have nothing. This misfortune I met with not long since, nor does my father as yet know any thing of the matter.
(Exit.)

2.2.230:
(Enter CLINIA from the house of CHREMES.) CLINIA
(to himself.)
If my love-affairs had been prosperous for me, I am sure she would have been here by this; but I’m afraid that the damsel has been led astray here in my absence. Many things combine to strengthen this opinion in my mind; opportunity, the place, her age, a worthless mother, under whose control she is, with whom nothing but gain is precious.
(Enter CLITIPHO.)
CLITIPHO
2.2.234:
Clinia!
CLINIA
Alas! wretched me!
CLITIPHO
2.2.235:
Do, pray, take care that no one coming out of your father’s house sees you here by accident.
CLINIA
2.2.236:
I will do so; but really my mind presages I know not what misfortune.
CLITIPHO
2.2.237:
Do you persist in making up your mind upon that, before you know what is the fact?
CLINIA
2.2.238:
Had no misfortune happened, she would have been here by this.
CLITIPHO
She’ll be here presently.
CLINIA
When will that presently be?
CLITIPHO
2.2.239: You don’t consider that it is a great way fiom here. Besides, you know the ways of women,
2.2.240:
while they are bestirring themselves, and while they are making preparations a whole year passes by.
CLINIA
O Clitipho, I’m afraid—
CLITIPHO
2.2.241:
Take courage. Look, here comes Dromo, together with Syrus: they are close at hand.
(They stand aside.)

2.3.242:
(Enter SYRUS and DROMO, conversing at a distance.) SYRUS
Do you say so?
DROMO
’Tis as I told you,—
but in the mean time, while we’ve been carrying on our discourse, these women have been left behind.
CLITIPHO
(apart.)
2.3.243:
Don’t you hear, Clinia? Your mistress is close at hand.
CLINIA
(apart.)
2.3.244:
Why yes, I do hear now at last, and I see and revive, Clitipho.
DROMO
2.3.245:
No wonder; they are so encumbered; they are bringing a troop of female attendants with them.
CLINIA
(apart.)
2.3.246:
I’m undone! Whence come these female attendants?
CLITIPHO
(apart.)
Do you ask me?
SYRUS
2.3.247:
We ought not to have left them; what a quantity of things they are bringing!
CLINIA
(apart.)
Ah me!
SYRUS
2.3.248:
Jewels of gold, and clothes; it’s growing late too, and they don’t know the way. It was very foolish of us to leave them. Just go back, Dromo, and meet them. Make haste—why do you delay?
(Exit DROMO).)
CLINIA
(apart.)
2.3.250:
Woe unto wretched me!—from what high hopes am I fallen!
CLITIPHO
(apart.)
2.3.251:
What’s the matter? Why, what is it that troubles you?
CLINIA
(apart.)
Do you ask what it is? Why, don’t you see? Attendants, jewels of gold, and clothes. her too, whom I left here with only one little servant girl. Whence do you suppose that they come?
CLITIPHO
(apart.)
2.3.253:
Oh! now at last I understand you.
SYRUS
(to himself.)
2.3.254: Good Gods! what a multitude there is! Our house will hardly hold them, I’m sure.
2.3.255:
How much they will eat! how much they will drink! what will there be more wretched than our old gentleman? (Catching sight of CLINIA and CLITIPHO.) But look, I espy the persons I was wanting.
CLINIA
(apart.)
2.3.256: Oh Jupiter! Why, where is fidelity gone? While I, distractedly wandering, have abandoned my country for your sake, you, in the mean time, Antiphila, have been enriching yourself, and have forsaken me in these troubles, you for whose sake I am in extreme disgrace, and have been disobedient to my father;
2.3.260:
on whose account I am now ashamed and grieved, that he who used to lecture me about the manners of these women, advised me in vain, and was not able to wean me away from her:—which, however, I shall now do; whereas when it might have been advantageous to me to do so, I was unwilling. There is no being more wretched than I.
SYRUS
(to himself.)
2.3.263: He certainly has been misled by our words which we have been speaking here. (Aloud.) Clinia, you imagine your mistress quite different from what she really is.
2.3.265:
For both her mode of life is the same, and her disposition toward you is the same as it always was; so far as we could form a judgment from the circumstances themselves.
CLINIA
2.3.267:
How so, prithee? For nothing in the world could I rather wish for just now, than that I have suspected this without reason.
SYRUS
2.3.269: This, in the first place, then (that you may not be ignorant of any thing that concerns her); the old woman,
2.3.270:
who was formerly said to be her mother, was not so.—She is dead: this I overheard by accident from her, as we came along, while she was telling the other one.
CLITIPHO
2.3.272:
Pray, who is the other one?
SYRUS
2.3.273:
Stay; what I have begun I wish first to relate, Clitipho; I shall come to that afterward.
CLITIPHO
2.3.274:
Make haste, then.
SYRUS
First of all then,
2.3.275: when we came to the house, Dromo knocked at the door; a certain old woman came out; when she opened the door, he directly rushed in; I followed; the old woman bolted the door, and returned to her wool. On this occasion might be known, Clinia, or else on none,
2.3.280: in what pursuits she passed her life during your absence; when we thus came upon a female unexpectedly. For this circumstance then gave us an opportunity of judging of the course of her daily life; a thing which especially discovers what is the disposition of each individual.
2.3.285: We found her industriously plying at the web; plainly clad in a mourning dress, on account of this old woman, I suppose, who was lately dead; without golden ornaments, dressed, besides, just like those who only dress for themselves, and patched up with no worthless woman’s trumpery.
2.3.290:
Her hair was loose, long, and thrown back negligently about her temples. (To CLINIA.) Do you hold your peace.
CLINIA
2.3.291:
My dear Syrus, do not without cause throw me into ecstasies, I beseech you.
SYRUS
2.3.292: The old woman was spinning the woof: there was one little servant girl besides;—she was weaving together with them, covered with patched clothes,
2.3.300:
for it is a rule with those who wish to gain access to the mistress, first to bribe the maid.
CLINIA
(to SYRUS.)
2.3.302:
Go on, I beseech you; and beware of endeavoring to purchase favor by telling an untruth. What did she say, when you mentioned me?
SYRUS
2.3.304: When we told her that you had returned, and had requested her
2.3.305:
to come to you, the damsel instantly put away the web, and covered her face all over with tears; so that you might easily perceive that it really was caused by her affection for you.
CLINIA
2.3.308:
So may the Deities bless me, I know not where I am for joy! I was so alarmed before.
CLITIPHO
2.3.309:
But I was sure that there was no reason, Clinia. Come now, Syrus, tell me, in my turn, who this other lady is.
SYRUS
2.3.311:
Your Bacchis, whom we are bringing.
CLITIPHO
Ha! What! Bacchis? How now, you rascal! whither are you bringing her?
SYRUS
2.3.312:
Whither am I bringing her? To our house, to be sure.
CLITIPHO
2.3.313:
What! to my father’s?
SYRUS
To the very same.
CLITIPHO
Oh, the audacious impudence of the fellow!
SYRUS
Hark’ye, no great and memorable action is done without some risk.
CLITIPHO
2.3.315:
Look now; are you seeking to gain credit for yourself, at the hazard of my character, you rascal, in a point, where, if you only make the slightest slip, I am ruined? What would you be doing with her?
SYRUS
2.3.317:
But still—
CLITIPHO
Why still?
SYRUS
If you’ll give me leave, I’ll tell you.
CLINIA
Do give him leave.
CLITIPHO
2.3.318:
I give him leave then.
SYRUS
This affair is now just as though when—
CLITIPHO
Plague on it, what roundabout story is he beginning to tell me?
CLINIA
2.3.319:
Syrus, he says what’s right—do omit digressions; come to the point.
SYRUS
2.3.320:
Really I can not hold my tongue. Clitipho, you are every way unjust, and can not possibly be endured.
CLINIA
2.3.321:
Upon my faith, he ought to have a hearing. (To CLITIPHO.) Do be silent.
SYRUS
2.3.322: You wish to indulge in your amours; you wish to possess your mistress; you wish that to be procured wherewithal to make her presents; in getting this, you do not wish the risk to be your own. You are not wise to no purpose,—if indeed it is being wise to wish for that which can not happen.
2.3.325: Either the one must be had with the other, or the one must be let alone with the other. Now, of these two alternatives, consider which one you would prefer; although this project which I have formed, I know to be both a wise and a safe one. For there is an opportunity for your mistress to be with you at your father’s house, without fear of a discovery; besides, by these self-same means, I shall find the money which you have promised her—
2.3.330:
to effect which, you have already made my ears deaf with entreating me. What would you have more?
CLITIPHO
2.3.331:
If, indeed, this could be brought about—
SYRUS
If, indeed? You shall know it by experience.
CLITIPHO
2.3.332:
Well, well, disclose this project of yours. What is it?
SYRUS
We will pretend that your mistress is his.
(pointing to CLINIA)
CLITIPHO
2.3.333:
Very fine! Tell me, what is he to do with his own? Is she, too, to be called his, as if one was not a sufficient discredit?
SYRUS
2.3.335:
No—she shall be taken to your mother.
CLITIPHO
Why there?
SYRUS
It would be tedious, Clitipho, if I were to tell you why I do so; I have a good reason.
CLITIPHO
2.3.336:
Stuff! I see no grounds sufficiently solid why it should be for my advantage to incur this risk.
(Turning as if going.)
SYRUS
2.3.338:
Stay; if there is this risk, I have another project, which you must both confess to be free from danger.
CLITIPHO
2.3.340:
I’ll go meet her, and tell her to return home.
CLITIPHO
Ha! what was it you said?
SYRUS
2.3.341:
I’ll rid you at once of all fears, so that you may sleep at your ease upon either ear.
CLITIPHO
2.3.343:
What am I to do now?
CLINIA
What are you to do? The goods that—
CLITIPHO
Only tell me the truth, Syrus.
SYRUS
2.3.344:
Dispatch quickly; you’ll be wishing just now too late and in vain.
(Going.)
CLINIA
2.3.345:
The Gods provide, enjoy while yet you may; for you know not—
CLITIPHO
(calling.)
2.3.346:
Syrus, I say!
SYRUS
(moving on.)
Go on; I shall still do that which I said.
CLINIA
2.3.347:
Whether you may have another opportunity hereafter or ever again.
CLITIPHO
2.3.348:
I’faith, that’s true. (Calling.) Syrus, Syrus, I say, harkye, harkye, Syrus!
SYRUS
(aside.)
2.3.349:
He warms a little. (To CLITIPHO.) What is it you want?
CLITIPHO
Come back, come back.
SYRUS
(coming back to him.)
Here I am; tell me what you would have. You’ll be presently saying that this, too, doesn’t please you.
CLITIPHO
2.3.350:
Nay, Syrus, I commit myself, and my love, and my reputation entirely to you: you are the seducer; take care you don’t deserve any blame.
SYRUS
2.3.353: It is ridiculous for you to give me that caution, Clitipho, as if my interest was less at stake in this affair than yours.
2.3.355:
Here, if any ill luck should perchance befall us, words will be in readiness for you, but for this individual blows (pointing to himself). For that reason, this matter is by no means to be neglected on my part: but do prevail upon him (pointing to CLINIA) to pretend that she is his own mistress.
CLINIA
2.3.358:
You may rest assured I’ll do so. The matter has now come to that pass, that it is a case of necessity.
CLITIPHO
2.3.360:
’Tis with good reason that I love you, Clinia.
CLINIA
2.3.361:
But she mustn’t be tripping at all.
SYRUS
She is thoroughly tutored in her part.
CLITIPHO
2.3.362:
But this I wonder at, how you could so easily prevail upon her, who is wont to treat such great peoplel with scorn.
SYRUS
2.3.364: I came to her at the proper moment, which in all things is of the first importance:
2.3.365: for there I found a certain wretched captain soliciting her favors: she artfully managed the man, so as to inflame his eager passions by denial; and this, too, that it might be especially pleasing to yourself. But hark you, take care, will you, not to be imprudently impetuous.
2.3.370:
You know your father, how quick-sighted he is in these matters; and I know you, how unable you are to command yourself. Keep clear of words of double meaning, your sidelong looks, sighing, hemming, coughing, tittering.
CLITIPHO
2.3.374:
You shall have to commend me.
SYRUS
Take care of that, please.
CLITIPHO
You yourself shall be surprised at me.
SYRUS
2.3.375:
But how quickly the ladies have come up with us!
CLITIPHO
2.3.376:
Where are they? (SYRUS stands before him.) Why do you hold me back?
SYRUS
For the present she is nothing to you.
CLITIPHO
2.3.377:
I know it, before my father; but now in the mean time—
SYRUS
Not a bit the more.
CLITIPHO
2.3.378:
Do let me.
SYRUS
I will not let you, I tell you.
CLITIPHO
But only for a moment, pray.
SYRUS
I forbid it.
CLITIPHO
2.3.379:
Only to salute her.
SYRUS
If you are wise, get you gone.
CLITIPHO
I’m off.
2.3.380:
But what’s he to do?
(Pointing at CLINIA.)
SYRUS
He will stay here.
CLITIPHO
O happy man!
SYRUS
Take yourself off.
(Exit CLITIPHO.)

2.4.381:
(Enter BACCHIS and ANTIPHILA at a distance.) BACCHIS
Upon my word, my dear Antiphila, I commend you, and think you fortunate in having made it your study that your manners should be conformable to those good looks of yours: and so may the Gods bless me, I do not at all wonder if every man is in love with you. For your discourse has been a proof to me what kind of disposition you possess.
2.4.385: And when now I reflect in my mind upon your way of life, and that of all of you, in fact, who keep the public at a distance from yourselves, it is not surprising both that you are of that disposition, and that we are not; for it is your interest to be virtuous; those, with whom we are acquainted, will not allow us to be so. For our lovers, allured merely by our beauty, court us for that;
2.4.390: when that has faded, they transfer their affections elsewhere; and unless we have made provision in the mean time for the future, we live in destitution. Now with you, when you have once resolved to pass your life with one man whose manners are especially kindred to your own, those persons become attached to you. By this kindly feeling, you are truly devoted to each other;
2.4.395:
and no calamity can ever possibly interrupt your love.
ANTIPHILA
2.4.396:
I know nothing about other women: I’m sure that I have, indeed, always used every endeavor to derive my own happiness from his happiness.
CLINIA
(apart, overhearing ANTIPHILA.)
2.4.397: Ah! ’tis for that reason, my Antiphila, that you alone have now caused me to return to my native country; for while I was absent from you, all other hardships which I encountered were light to me,
2.4.400:
save the being deprived of you.
SYRUS
(apart.)
I believe it.
CLINIA
(apart.)
Syrus, I can scarce endure it! Wretch that I am, that I should not be allowed to possess one of such a disposition at my own discretion!
SYRUS
2.4.402:
Nay, so far as I understand your father, he will for a long time yet be giving you a hard task.
BACCHIS
2.4.403:
Why, who is that young man that’s looking at us?
ANTIPHILA
(seeing CLINIA.)
Ah! do support me, I entreat you!
BACCHIS
2.4.404:
Prithee, what is the matter with you?
ANTIPHILA
I shall die, alas! I shall die!
BACCHIS
Why are you thus surprised, Antiphila?
ANTIPHILA
2.4.405:
Is it Clinia that I see, or not?
BACCHIS
Whom do you see?
CLINIA
(running to embrace ANTIPHILA.)
2.4.406:
Blessings on you, my life!
ANTIPHILA
Oh my long-wished for Clinia, blessings on you!
CLINIA
How fare you, my love?
ANTIPHILA
2.4.407:
I’m overjoyed that you have returned safe.
CLINIA
And do I embrace you, Antiphila, so passionately longed for by my soul?
SYRUS
2.4.409:
Go in-doors; for the old gentleman has been waiting for us some time.
(They go into the house of CHREMES.)

3.1.410:
(Enter CHREMES from his house.) CHREMES
(to himself.)
It is now daybreak. Why do I delay to knock at my neighbor’s door, that he may learn from me the first that his son has returned? Although I am aware that the youth would not prefer this. But when I see him tormenting himself so miserably about his absence, can I conceal a joy so unhoped for,
3.1.415:
especially when there can be no danger to him from the discovery? I will not do so; but as far as I can I will assist the old man. As I see my son aiding his friend and year’s-mate, and acting as his confidant in his concerns, it is but right that we old men as well should assist each other.
(Enter MENEDEMUS from his house.)
MENEDEMUS
(to himself)
3.1.420: Assuredly I was either born with a disposition peculiarly suited for misery, or else that saying which I hear commonly repeated, that time assuages human sorrow, is false. For really my sorrow about my son increases daily; and the longer
3.1.425:
he is away from me, the more anxiously do I wish for him, and the more I miss him.
CHREMES
(apart.)
3.1.426:
But I see him coming out of his house; I’ll go speak to him. (Aloud.) Menedemus, good-morrow; I bring you news, which you would especially desire to be imparted.
MENEDEMUS
3.1.429:
Pray, have you heard any thing about my son, Chremes?
CHREMES
3.1.430:
He’s alive, and well.
MENEDEMUS
Why, where is he, pray?
CHREMES
Here, at my house, at home.
MENEDEMUS
3.1.431:
My son?
CHREMES
Such is the fact.
MENEDEMUS
Come home?
CHREMES
Certainly.
MENEDEMUS
My son, Clinia, come home?
CHREMES
3.1.432:
I say so.
MENEDEMUS
Let us go. Lead me to him, I beg of you.
CHREMES
3.1.433: He does not wish you yet to know of his return, and he shuns your presence; he’s afraid that,
3.1.435:
on account of that fault, your former severity may even be increased.
MENEDEMUS
3.1.436:
Did you not tell him how I was affected?
CHREMES
No—
MENEDEMUS
For what reason, Chremes?
CHREMES
3.1.437:
Because there you would judge extremely ill both for yourself and for him, if you were to show yourself of a spirit so weak and irresolute.
MENEDEMUS
3.1.439:
I can not help it: enough already, enough, have I proved a rigorous father.
CHREMES
Ah
3.1.440: Menedemus! you are too precipitate in either extreme, either with profuseness or with parsimony too great. Into the same error will you fall from the one side as from the other. In the first place, formerly, rather than allow your son to visit a young woman, who was
3.1.445: then content with a very little, and to whom any thing was acceptable, you frightened him away from here. After that, she began, quite against her inclination, to seek a subsistence upon the town. Now, when she can not be supported without a great expense, you are ready to give any thing. For, that you may know
3.1.450:
how perfectly she is trained to extravagance, in the first place, she has already brought with her more than ten female attendants, all laden with clothes and jewels of gold; if a satrap had been her admirer, he never could support her expenses, much less can you.
MENEDEMUS
3.1.454:
Is she at your house?
CHREMES
Is she, do you ask?
3.1.455: I have felt it; for I have given her and her retinue one dinner; had I to give them another such, it would be all over with me; for, to pass by other matters, what a quantity of wine she did consume for me in tasting only, saying thus, This wine is too acid, respected sir, do please look for something more mellow.
3.1.460:
I opened all the casks, all the vessels; she kept all on the stir: and this but a single night. What do you suppose will become of you when they are constantly preying upon you? So may the Gods prosper me, Menedemus, I do pity your lot.
MENEDEMUS
3.1.464: Let him do what he will;
3.1.465:
let him take, waste, and squander; I’m determined to endure it, so long as I only have him with me.
CHREMES
3.1.466:
If it is your determination thus to act, I hold it to be of very great foment that he should not be aware that with a full knowledge you grant him this.
MENEDEMUS
3.1.470: supply him with money through some other person; suffer yourself to be imposed upon by the artifices of his servant: although I have smelt out this too, that they are about that, and are secretly planning it among them. Syrus is always whispering with that servant of yours; they impart their plans to the young men; and it were better for you to lose
3.1.475: a talent this way, than a mina the other. The money is not the question now, but this—in what way we can supply it to the young man with the least danger. For if he once knows the state of your feelings, that you would sooner part with your life, and sooner
3.1.480: with all your money, than allow your son to leave you; whew! what an inlet will you be opening for his debauchery! aye, and so much so, that henceforth to live can not be desirable to you. For we all become worse through indulgence. Whatever comes into his head, he’ll be wishing for; nor
3.1.485:
will he reflect whether that which he desires is right or wrong. You will not be able to endure your estate and him going to ruin. You will refuse to supply him: he will immediately have recourse to the means by which he finds that he has the greatest hold upon you, and threaten that he will immediately leave you.
MENEDEMUS
3.1.490:
You seem to speak the truth, and just what is the fact.
CHREMES
3.1.491:
I’faith, I have not been sensible of sleep this night with my eyes, for thinking of this—how to restore your son to you.
MENEDEMUS
(taking his hand.)
3.1.493:
Give me your right hand. I request that you will still act in a like manner, Chremes.
CHREMES
3.1.494:
I am ready to serve you.
MENEDEMUS
Do you know what it is I now want you to do?
CHREMES
3.1.495:
Tell me.
MENEDEMUS
As you have perceived that they are laying a plan to deceive me, that they may hasten to complete it. I long to give him whatever he wants: I am now longing to behold him.
CHREMES
3.1.497: I’ll lend my endeavors. This little business is in my way. Our neighbors Simus and Crito are disputing here about boundaries;
3.1.500:
they have chosen me for arbitrator. I’ll go and tell them that I can not possibly give them my attention to-day as I had stated I would. I’ll be here immediately.
(Exit.)
MENEDEMUS
3.1.502: Pray do. (To himself.) Ye Gods, by our trust in you! That the nature of all men should be so constituted, that they can see and judge of other men’s affairs better
3.1.505:
than their own! Is it because in our own concerns we are biased either with joy or grief in too great a degree? How much wiser now is he for me, than I have been for myself!
(Re-enter CHREMES.)
CHREMES
3.1.508: I have disengaged myself, that I might lend you my services at my leisure. Syrus must be found and instructed by me in this business.
3.1.510:
Some one, I know not who, is coming out of my house: do you step hence home, that they may not perceive that we are conferring together.
(MENEDEMUS goes into his house.)

3.2.512:
(Enter SYRUS from the house of CHREMES.) SYRUS
(aloud to himself.)
Run to and fro in every direction; still, money, you must be found: a trap must be laid for the old man.
CHREMES
(apart, overhearing him.)
3.2.514: Was I deceived in saying that they were planning this?
3.2.515:
That servant of Clinia’s is somewhat dull; therefore that province has been assigned to this one of ours.
SYRUS
(in a low voice.)
3.2.517:
Who’s that speaking? (Catches sight of CGREMES.) I’m undone! Did he hear it, I wonder?
CHREMES
Syrus.
SYRUS
Well—
CHREMES
3.2.518:
What are you doing here?
SYRUS
All right. Really, I am quite surprised at you, Chremes, up so early, after drinking so much yesterday.
CHREMES
3.2.520:
Not too much, say you? Really, you’ve seen the old age of an eagle, as the saying is.
CHREMES
3.2.521:
Pooh, pooh!
SYRUS
A pleasant and agreeable woman this Courtesan.
CHREMES
3.2.522:
Why, so she seemed to me, in fact.
SYRUS
3.2.523:
And really of handsome appearance.
CHREMES
Well enough.
SYRUS
3.2.524: Not like those of former days, but as times are now, very passable:
3.2.525:
nor do I in the least wonder that Clinia doats upon her. But he has a father—a certain covetous, miserable, and niggardly person—this neighbor of ours (pointing to the house). Do you know him? Yet, as if he was not abounding in wealth, his son ran away through want. Are you aware that it is the fact, as I am saying?
CHREMES
3.2.529: How should I not be aware?
3.2.530:
A fellow that deserves the mill.
SYRUS
Who?
CHREMES
That servant of the young gentleman, I mean.
SYRUS
(aside.)
3.2.531:
Syrus! I was sadly afraid for you.
CHREMES
3.2.532:
To suffer it to come to this!
SYRUS
What was he to do?
CHREMES
Do you ask the question? He ought to have found some expedient, contrived some stratagem, by means of which there might have been something for the young man to give to his mistress,
3.2.535:
and thus have saved this crabbed old fellow in spite of himself.
SYRUS
3.2.536:
You are surely joking.
CHREMES
This ought to have been done by him, Syrus.
SYRUS
3.2.537:
How now—pray, do you commend servants, who deceive their masters?
CHREMES
Upon occasion—I certainly do commend them.
SYRUS
3.2.538:
Quite right.
CHREMES
Inasmuch as it often is the remedy for great disturbances.
3.2.540:
Then would this man’s only son have staid at home.
SYRUS
(aside.)
3.2.541:
Whether he says this in jest or in earnest, I don’t know; only, in fact, that he gives me additional zest for longing still more to trick him.
CHREMES
3.2.543: And what is he now waiting for, Syrus? Is it until his father drives him away from here a second time, when he can no longer support her expenses?
3.2.545:
Has he no plot on foot against the old gentleman?
SYRUS
He is a stupid fellow.
CHREMES
3.2.546:
Then you ought to assist him—for the sake of the young man.
SYRUS
3.2.547:
For my part, I can do so easily, if you command me; for I know well in what fashion it is usually done.
CHREMES
3.2.549:
So much the better, i’ faith.
SYRUS
’Tis not my way to tell an untruth.
CHREMES
3.2.550:
Do it then.
SYRUS
But hark you! Just take care and remember this, in case any thing of this sort should perchance happen at a future time, such are human affairs!—your son might do the same.
CHREMES
3.2.555:
but in case, none the more—You see what his age is; (aside) and truly, Chremes, if an occasion does happen, I may be able to handle you right handsomely.
CHREMES
3.2.557:
As to that, we’ll consider what is requisite when the occasion does happen. At present do you set about this matter.
(Goes into his house.)
SYRUS
(to himself.)
3.2.559: Never on any occasion did I hear my master talk more to the purpose;
3.2.560:
nor at any time could I believe that I was authorized to play the rogue with greater impunity. I wonder who it is coming out of our house?
(Stands aside.)

3.3.562:
(Enter CHREMES and CLITIPHO from the house of the former.) CHREMES
Pray, what does this mean? What behavior is this, Clitipho? Is this acting as becomes you?
CLITIPHO
3.3.563:
What have I done?
CHREMES
Did I not see you just now putting your hand into this Courtesan’s bosom?
SYRUS
(apart.)
3.3.564:
It’s all up with us—I’m utterly undone!
CLITIPHO
What, I?
CHREMES
With these self-same eyes I saw it—don’t deny it.
3.3.565:
Besides, you wrong him unworthily in not keeping your hands off: for indeed it is a gross affront to entertain a person, your friend, at your house, and to take liberties with his mistress. Yesterday, for instance, at wine, how rude you were—
SYRUS
(apart.)
3.3.568:
’Tis the truth
CHREMES
How annoying you were! So much so, that for my part, as the Gods may prosper me, I dreaded what in the end might be the consequence.
3.3.570:
I understand lovers. They resent highly things that you would not imagine.
CLITIPHO
3.3.571:
But he has full confidence in me, father, that I would not do any thing of that kind.
CHREMES
3.3.572: Be it so; still, at least, you ought to go somewhere for a little time away from their presence. Passion prompts to many a thing; your presence acts as a restraint upon doing them. I form a judgment from myself. There’s not one of my friends this day
3.3.575:
to whom I would venture, Clitipho, to disclose all my secrets. With one, his station forbids it; with another, I am ashamed of the action itself, lest I may appear a fool or devoid of shame; do you rest assured that he does the same. But it is our part to be sensible of this; and, when and where it is requisite, to show due complaisance.
SYRUS
(coming forward and whispering to CLITIPHO.)
3.3.579:
What is it he is saying?
CLITIPHO
(aside, to SYRUS.)
I’m utterly undone!
SYRUS
Clitipho, these same injunctions I gave you.
3.3.580:
You have acted the part of a prudent and discreet person.
CLITIPHO
Hold your tongue, I beg.
SYRUS
3.3.581:
Very good.
CHREMES
(approaching them.)
Syrus, I am ashamed of him.
SYRUS
I believe it; and not without reason. Why, he vexes myself even.
CLITIPHO
(to SYRUS.)
3.3.582:
Do you persist, then?
SYRUS
I’ faith, I’m saying the truth, as it appears to me.
CLITIPHO
3.3.583:
May I not go near them?
CHREMES
How now—pray, is there but one way of going near them?
SYRUS
(aside.)
3.3.584: Confusion! He’ll be betraying himself before I’ve got the money.
3.3.585:
(Aloud.) Chremes, will you give attention to me, who am but a silly person?
CHREMES
What am I to do?
SYRUS
Bid him go somewhere out of the way.
CLITIPHO
3.3.586:
Where am I to go?
SYRUS
Where you please; leave the place to them; be off and take a walk.
CLITIPHO
3.3.587:
Take a walk! where?
SYRUS
Pshaw! Just as if there was no place to walk in. Why, then, go this way, that way, where you will.
CHREMES
3.3.588:
He says right, I’m of his opinion.
CLITIPHO
3.3.589:
May the Gods extirpate you, Syrus, for thrusting me away from here.
SYRUS
(aside to CLITIPHO.)
Then
3.3.590:
do you for the future keep those hands of yours within bounds. (Exit CLITIPHO.) Really now (to CHREMES), what do you think? What do you imagine will become of him next, unless, so far as the Gods afford you the means, you watch him, correct and admonish him?
CHREMES
3.3.593:
I’ll take care of that.
SYRUS
But now, master, he must be looked after by you.
CHREMES
3.3.594:
It shall be done.
SYRUS
If you are wise,—for now he minds me less and less every day.
CHREMES
3.3.595:
What say you? What have you done, Syrus, about that matter which I was mentioning to you a short time since? Have you any plan that suits you, or not yet even?
SYRUS
3.3.596:
You mean the design upon Menedemus? I have; I have just hit upon one.
CHREMES
3.3.597:
You are a clever fellow; what is it? Tell me.
SYRUS
3.3.598:
I’ll tell you; but, as one matter arises out of another—
CHREMES
Why, what. is it, Syrus?
SYRUS
3.3.599:
This Courtesan is a very bad woman.
CHREMES
So she seems.
SYRUS
Aye, if you did but know.
3.3.600:
O shocking! just see what she is hatching. There was a certain old woman here from Corinth,—this Bacchis lent her a thousand silver drachmae.
CHREMES
3.3.602:
What then?
SYRUS
She is now dead: she has left a daughter, a young girl. She has been left with this Bacchis as a pledge for that sum.
CHREMES
3.3.604:
She has brought her hither along with her, her I mean who is now with your wife.
CHREMES
3.3.605:
What then?
SYRUS
She is soliciting Clinia at once to advance her this money; she says, however, that this girl is to be a security, that, at a future time, she will repay the thousand pieces of money.
CHREMES
3.3.606:
And would she really be a security?
SYRUS
Dear me, is it to be doubted?
3.3.607:
I think so.
CHREMES
What then do you intend doing?
SYRUS
3.3.608:
What, I? I shall go to Menedemus; I’ll tell him she is a captive from Caria, rich, and of noble family; if he redeems her, there will be a considerable profit in this transaction.
CHREMES
3.3.610:
You are in an error.
SYRUS
Why so?
CHREMES
I’ll now answer you for Menedemus—I will not purchase her.
SYRUS
3.3.611:
What is it you say? Do speak more agreeably to our wishes.
CHREMES
But there is no occasion.
SYRUS
3.3.612:
No occasion?
CHREMES
Certainly not, i’ faith.
SYRUS
How so, I wonder?
CHREMES
You shall soon know.
SYRUS
3.3.613:
Stop, stop; what is the reason that there is such a great noise at our door?
(They retire out of sight.)

4.1.614:
(Enter SOSTRATA and a NURSE in haste from the house of CHREMES, and CHREMES and SYRUS on the other side of the stage unperceived.) SOSTRATA
(holding up a ring and examining it.)
Unless my fancy deceives me, surely this is the ring which I suspect it to be, the same with which my daughter was exposed.
CHREMES
(apart.)
4.1.615:
Syrus, what is the meaning of these expressions?
SOSTRATA
4.1.616:
Nurse, how is it? Does it not seem to you the same?
NURSE
As for me, I said it was the same the very instant that you showed it me.
SOSTRATA
4.1.617:
But have you now examined it thoroughly, my dear nurse?
NURSE
Thoroughly.
SOSTRATA
4.1.618:
Then go in-doors at once, and if she has now done bathing, bring me word. I’ll wait here in the mean time for my husband.
SYRUS
(apart.)
4.1.619: She wants you, see what it is she wants;
4.1.620:
she is in a serious mood, I don’t know why; it is not without a cause—I fear what it may be.
CHREMES
What it may be? I’ faith, she’ll now surely be announcing some important trifle, with a great parade.
SOSTRATA
(turning round.)
4.1.622:
Ha! my husband!
CHREMES
Ha! my wife!
SOSTRATA
I was looking for you.
CHREMES
Tell me what you want.
SOSTRATA
4.1.623:
In the first place, this I beg of you, not to believe that I have ventured to do any thing contrary to your commands.
CHREMES
4.1.624:
Would you have me believe you in this, although so incredible? Well, I will believe you.
SYRUS
(aside.)
4.1.625:
This excuse portends I know not what offense.
SOSTRATA
4.1.626:
Do you remember me being pregnant, and yourself declaring to me, most peremptorily, that if I should bring forth a girl, you would not have it brought up.
CHREMES
4.1.627:
I know what you have done, you have brought it up.
SYRUS
(aside.)
4.1.628:
Such is the fact, I’m sure: my young master has gained a loss in consequence.
SOSTRATA
4.1.629: Not at all; but there was here an elderly woman of Corinth, of no indifferent character; to her I gave it
4.1.630:
to be exposed.
CHREMES
O Jupiter! that there should be such extreme folly in a person’s mind.
SOSTRATA
4.1.631:
Alas! what have I done?
CHREMES
And do you ask the question?
SOSTRATA
If I have acted wrong, my dear Chremes, I have done so in ignorance.
CHREMES
4.1.632: This, indeed, I know for certain, even if you were to deny it, that in every thing you both speak and act ignorantly and foolishly: how many blunders you disclose in this single affair! For, in the first place, then, if
4.1.635: you had been disposed to obey my orders, the child ought to have been dispatched; you ought not in words to have feigned her death, and in reality to have left hopes of her surviving. But that I pass over; compassion, maternal affection, I allow it. But how finely you did provide for the future! What was your meaning? Do reflect. It’s clear, beyond a doubt, that your daughter was betrayed by you to this old woman,
4.1.640:
either that through you she might make a living by her, or that she might be sold in open market as a slave. I suppose you reasoned thus: any thing is enough, if only her life is saved: what are you to do with those who understand neither law, nor right and justice? Be it for better or for worse, be it for them or against them, they see nothing except just what they please.
SOSTRATA
4.1.644: My dear Chremes, I have done wrong, I own; I am convinced. Now this I beg of you;
4.1.645:
inasmuch as you are more advanced in years than I, be so much the more ready to forgive; so that your justice may be some protection for my weakness.
CHREMES
4.1.647:
I’ll readily forgive you doing this, of course; but, Sostrata, my easy temper prompts you to do amiss. But, whatever this circumstance is, by reason of which this was begun upon, proceed to tell it.
SOSTRATA
4.1.649: As we women are all foolishly and wretchedly
4.1.650:
superstitious, when I delivered the child to her to be exposed, I drew a ring from off my finger, and ordered her to expose it, together with the child; that if she should die, she might not be without some portion of our possessions.
CHREMES
4.1.653:
That was right; thereby you proved the saving of yourself and her.
SOSTRATA
(holding out the ring.)
This is that ring.
CHREMES
4.1.654:
Whence did you get it?
SOSTRATA
From the young woman whom Bacchis brought here with her.
SYRUS
(aside.)
Ha!
CHREMES
4.1.655:
What does she say?
SOSTRATA
She gave it me to keep for her, while she went to bathe. At first I paid no attention to it; but after I looked at it, I at once recognized it, and came running to you.
CHREMES
4.1.657:
What do you suspect now, or have you discovered, relative to her?
SOSTRATA
4.1.658:
I don’t know; unless you inquire of herself whence she got it, if that can possibly be discovered.
SYRUS
(aside.)
4.1.659: I’m undone! I see more hopes from this incident than I desire.
4.1.660:
If it is so, she certainly must be ours.
CHREMES
Is this woman living to whom you delivered the child?
SOSTRATA
I don’t know.
CHREMES
4.1.661:
What account did she bring you at the time?
SOSTRATA
That she had done as I had ordered her.
CHREMES
4.1.662:
Tell me what is the woman’s name, that she may be inquired after.
SOSTRATA
Philtere.
SYRUS
(aside.)
4.1.663:
’Tis the very same. It’s a wonder if she isn’t found, and I lost.
CHREMES
Sostrata, follow me this way in-doors.
SOSTRATA
4.1.664: How much beyond my hopes has this matter turned out! How dreadfully afraid I was,
4.1.665:
Chremes, that you would now be of feelings as unrelenting as formerly you were on exposing the child.
CHREMES
4.1.666:
Many a time a man can not be such as he would be, if circumstances do not admit of it. Time has now so brought it about, that I should be glad of a daughter; formerly I wished for nothing less.
(CHREMES and SOSTRATA go into the house.)

4.2.668:
(SYRUS alone.) SYRUS
Unless my fancy deceives me, retribution will not be very far off from me; so much by this incident are my forces now utterly driven into straits;
4.2.670: unless I contrive by some means that the old man mayn’t come to know that this damsel is his son’s mistress. For as to entertaining any hopes about the money, or supposing I could cajole him, it’s useless; I shall be sufficient triumphant, if I’m allowed to escape with my sides covered. I’m vexed that such a tempting morsel has been so suddenly snatched away from my jaws. What am I to do? Or what shall I devise? I must begin upon my plan over again.
4.2.675: Nothing is so difficult, but that it may be found out by seeking. What now if I set about it after this fashion. (He considers.) That’s of no use. What, if after this fashion? I effect just about the same. But this I think will do. It can not. Yes! excellent. Bravo! I’ve found out the best of all—I’ faith, I do believe that after all I shall lay hold of this same run-away money.

4.3.679:
(Enter CLINIA at the other side of the stage.) CLINIA
(to himself.)
Nothing can possibly henceforth befall me of such consequence
4.3.680:
as to cause me uneasiness; so extreme is this joy that has surprised me. Now then I shall give myself up entirely to my father, to be more frugal than even he could wish.
SYRUS
(apart.)
4.3.682:
I wasn’t mistaken; she has been discovered, so far as I understand from these words of his. (Acvancing.) I am rejoiced that this matter has turned out for you so much to your wish.
CLINIA
4.3.684:
O my dear Syrus, have you heard of it, pray?
SYRUS
How shouldn’t I, when I was present all the while?
CLINIA
4.3.685:
Did you ever hear of any thing falling out so fortunately for any one?
SYRUS
Never.
CLINIA
4.3.686:
And, so may the Gods prosper me, I do not now rejoice so much on my own account as hers, whom I know to be deserving of any honor.
SYRUS
4.3.688: I believe it: but now, Clinia, come, attend to me in my turn. For your friend’s business as well,—it must be seen to—that it is placed in a state of security,
4.3.690:
lest the old gentleman should now come to know any thing about his mistress.
CLINIA
O Jupiter!
SYRUS
Do be quiet.
CLINIA
4.3.691:
My Antiphila will be mine.
SYRUS
Do you still interrupt me thus?
CLINIA
4.3.692:
What can I do? My dear Syrus, I’m transported with joy! Do bear with me.
SYRUS
I’ faith, I really do bear with you.
CLINIA
4.3.693:
We are blest with the life of the Gods.
SYRUS
I’m taking pains to no purpose, I doubt.
CLINIA
4.3.694:
Speak; I hear you.
SYRUS
But still you’ll not mind it.
CLINIA
I will.
SYRUS
This must be seen to, I say,
4.3.695:
that your friend’s business as well is placed in a state of security. For if you now go away from us, and leave Bacchis here, our old man will immediately come to know that she is Clitipho’s mistress; if you take her away with you, it will be concealed just as much as it has been hitherto concealed.
CLINIA
4.3.699: But still, Syrus, nothing can make more against my marriage than this;
4.3.700:
for with what face am I to address my father about it? You understand what I mean?
SYRUS
Why not?
CLINIA
4.3.701:
What can I say? What excuse can I make?
SYRUS
Nay, I don’t want you to dissemble; tell him the whole case just as it really is.
CLINIA
4.3.702:
What is it you say?
SYRUS
I bid you do this; tell him that you are in love with her, and want her for a wife: that this Bacchis is Clitipho’s mistress.
CLINIA
4.3.704: You require a thing that is fair and reasonable, and easy to be done.
4.3.705:
And I suppose, then, you would have me request my father to keep it a secret from your old man.
SYRUS
4.3.706:
On the contrary; to tell him directly the matter just as it is.
CLINIA
What? Are you quite in your senses or sober? Why, you were for ruining him outright. For how could he be in a state of security? Tell me that.
SYRUS
4.3.709:
For my part, I yield the palm to this device. Here I do pride myself exultingly, in having in myself such exquisite resources, and power of address so great, as to deceive them both by telling the truth: so that when your old man tells ours that she is his son’s mistress, he’ll still not believe him.
CLINIA
4.3.713: But yet, by these means you again cut off all hopes of my marriage; for as long as Chremes believes that she is my mistress, he’ll not give me his daughter.
4.3.715:
Perhaps you care little what becomes of me, so long as you provide for him.
SYRUS
4.3.716:
What the plague, do you suppose I want this pretense to be kept up for an age? ’Tis but for a single day, only till I have secured the money: you be quiet; I ask no more.
CLINIA
4.3.718:
Is that sufficient? If his father should come to know of it, pray, what then?
SYRUS
4.3.719:
What if I have recourse to those who say, What now if the sky were to fall?
CLINIA
4.3.720:
I’m afraid to go about it.
SYRUS
You, afraid! As if it was not in your power to clear yourself at any time you like, and discover the whole matter.
CLINIA
4.3.722:
Well, well; let Bacchis be brought over to our house.
SYRUS
Capital! she is coming out of doors.

4.4.723:
(Enter BACCHIS and PHRYGIA, from the house of CHREMES.) BACCHIS
(pretending not to see CLINIA and SYRUS.)
To a very fine purpose, upon my faith, have the promises of Syrus brought me hither, who agreed to lend me ten minae. If now he
4.4.725:
deceives me, oft as he may entreat me to come, he shall come in vain. Or else, when I’ve promised to come, and fixed the time, when he has carried word back for certain, and Clitipho is on the stretch of expectation, I’ll disappoint him and not come. Syrus will make atonement to me with his back.
CLINIA
(apart, to SYRUS.)
4.4.729:
She promises you very fairly.
SYRUS
(to CLINIA.)
But do you think she is in jest?
4.4.730:
She’ll do it, if I don’t take care.
BACCHIS
(aside.)
They’re asleep—I’faith, I’ll rouse them. (Aloud.) My dear Phrygia, did you hear about the country-seat of Charinus, which that man was showing us just now?
PHRYGIA
4.4.732:
I heard of it.
BACCHIS
(aloud.)
That it was the next to the farm here on the right-hand side.
PHRYGIA
I remember.
BACCHIS
(aloud.)
4.4.733:
Run thither post-haste; the Captain is keeping the feast of Bacchus at his house.
SYRUS
(apart.)
4.4.734:
What is she going to be at?
BACCHIS
(aloud.)
Tell him I am here very much against my inclination, and am detained;
4.4.735:
but that by some means or other I’ll give them the slip and come to him.
(PHRYGIA moves.)
SYRUS
(coming forward.)
4.4.736:
Upon my faith, I’m ruined! Bacchis, stay, stay; prithee, where are you sending her? Order her to stop.
BACCHIS
(to PHRYGIA.)
4.4.737:
Be off.
SYRUS
Why, the money’s ready.
BACCHIS
Why, then I’ll stay.
(PHRYGIA returns.)
SYRUS
4.4.738:
And it will be given you presently.
BACCHIS
Just when you please; do I press you?
SYRUS
But do you know what you are to do, pray?
BACCHIS
4.4.739:
What?
SYRUS
You must now go over to the house of Menedemus, and your equipage
4.4.740:
must be taken over thither.
BACCHIS
What scheme are you upon, you rascal?
SYRUS
What, I? Coining money to give you.
BACCHIS
4.4.741:
Do you think me a proper person for you to play upon?
SYRUS
It’s not without a purpose.
BACCHIS
(pointing to the house.)
4.4.742:
Why, have I any business then with you here?
SYRUS
O no; I’m only going to give you what’s your own.
BACCHIS
4.4.743:
Then let’s be going.
SYRUS
Follow this way. (Goes to the door of MENEDIEMUS, and calls.) Ho there! Dromo.
(Enter DROMO from the house.)
DROMO
Who is it wants me?
SYRUS
Syrus.
DROMO
What’s the matter?
SYRUS
4.4.744:
Take over all the attendants of Bacchis to your house here immediately.
DROMO
4.4.745:
Why so?
SYRUS
Ask no questions. Let them take what they brought here with them. The old gentleman will hope his expenses are lightened by their departure; for sure he little knows how much loss this trifling gain will bring him. You, Dromo, if you are wise, know nothing of what you do know.
DROMO
4.4.748:
You shall own that I’m dumb.
(CLINIA, BACCHIS, and PHRYGIA go into the house of MENEDEMUS, and DROMO follows with BACCHIS’s retinue and baggage.)

4.5.749:
(Enter CHREMES from his house.) CHREMES
(to himself)
So may the Deities prosper me, I am now concerned for the fate of Menedemus,
4.5.750: that so great a misfortune should have befallen him. To be maintaining that woman with such a retinue! Although I am well aware he’ll not be sensible of it for some days to come, his son was so greatly missed by him; but when he sees such a vast expense incurred by him
4.5.755:
every day at home, and no limit to it, he’ll wish that this son would leave him a second time. See—here comes Syrus most opportunely.
SYRUS
(to himself, as he comes forward.)
4.5.757:
Why delay to accost him?
CHREMES
Syrus.
SYRUS
Well.
CHREMES
4.5.758:
How go matters?
SYRUS
I’ve been wishing for some time for you to be thrown in my way.
CHREMES
4.5.759:
You seem, then, to have effected something, I know not what, with the old gentleman.
SYRUS
4.5.760:
As to what we were talking of a short time since? No sooner said than done.
CHREMES
4.5.761:
In real earnest?
SYRUS
In real.
CHREMES
Upon my faith, I can not forbear patting your head for it. Come here, Syrus; I’ll do you some good turn for this matter, and with pleasure.
(Patting his head.)
SYRUS
4.5.764:
But if you knew how cleverly it came into my head—
CHREMES
4.5.765:
Pshaw! Do you boast because it has turned out according to your wishes
SYRUS
4.5.766:
On my word, not I, indeed; I am telling the truth.
CHREMES
Tell me how it is.
SYRUS
4.5.767:
Clinia has told Menedemus, that this Bacchis is your Clitipho’s mistress, and that he has taken her thither with him in order that you might not come to know of it.
CHREMES
4.5.770:
Very good.
SYRUS
Tell me, please, what you think of it.
CHREMES
Extremely good, I declare.
SYRUS
Why yes, pretty fair. But listen, what a piece of policy still remains. He is then to say that he has seen your daughter—that her beauty charmed him as soon as he beheld her; and that he desires her for a wife.
CHREMES
4.5.775:
and, in fact, he’ll request that she may be asked for.
CHREMES
For what purpose, Syrus? For I don’t altogether comprehend it.
SYRUS
4.5.776:
O dear, you are so dull.
CHREMES
4.5.777:
Perhaps so.
SYRUS
Money will be given him for the wedding—with which golden trinkets and clothes—do you understand me?
CHREMES
4.5.779:
Just so.
CHREMES
But I neither give nor betroth my daughter to him.
SYRUS
4.5.780:
But why?
CHREMES
Why, do you ask me? To a fellow—
SYRUS
4.5.781:
Just as you please. I don’t mean that in reality you should give her to him, but that you should pretend it.
CHREMES
4.5.782:
Pretending is not in my way; do you mix up these plots of yours, so as not to mix me up in them. Do you think that I’ll betroth my daughter to a person to whom I will not marry her?
SYRUS
4.5.785:
I imagined so.
CHREMES
By no means.
SYRUS
It might have been cleverly managed; and I under-took this affair for the very reason, that a short time since you so urgently requested it.
CHREMES
4.5.787:
I believe you.
SYRUS
But for my part, Chremes, I take it well and good, either way.
CHREMES
4.5.788:
But still, I especially wish you to do your best for it to be brought about; but in some other way.
SYRUS
4.5.790: It shall be done: some other method must be thought of; but as to what I was telling you of,—about the money which she owes to Bacchis,—that must now be repaid her. And you will not, of course, now be having recourse to this method; What have I to do with it? Was it lent to me? Did I give any orders? Had she the power to pawn my daughter
4.5.795:
without my consent? They quote that saying, Chremes, with good reason, Riorous law is often rigorous injustice.
CHREMES
4.5.797:
I will not do so.
SYRUS
On the contrary, though others were at liberty, you are not at liberty; all think that you are in good and very easy circumstances.
CHREMES
4.5.799:
Nay rather, I’ll at once carry it to her myself.
SYRUS
Why no; request your son in preference.
CHREMES
4.5.800:
For what reason?
SYRUS
Why, because the suspicion of being in love with her has been transferred to him with Menedemus.
CHREMES
4.5.801:
What then?
SYRUS
Because it will seem to be more like probability when he gives it her; and at the same time I shall effect more easily what I wish. Here he comes too; go, and bring out the money.
CHREMES
4.5.804:
I’ll bring it.
(Goes into his house.)

4.6.805:
(Enter CLITIPHO.) CLITIPHO
(to himself.)
There is nothing so easy but that it becomes difficult when you do it with reluctance. As this walk of mine, for instance, though not fatiguing, it has reduced me to weariness. And now I dread nothing more than that I should be packed off somewhere hence once again, that I may not have access to Bacchis.
4.6.810:
May then all the Gods and Goddesses, as many as exist, confound you, Syrus, with these stratagems and plots of yours. You are always devising something of this kind, by means of which to torture me.
SYRUS
4.6.813:
Will you not away with you—to where you deserve? How nearly had your forwardness proved my ruin!
CLITIPHO
4.6.815:
Upon my faith, I wish it had been so; just what you deserve.
SYRUS
Deserve? How so? Really, I’m glad that I’ve heard this from you before you had the money which I was just going to give you.
CLITIPHO
4.6.818:
What then would you have me to say to you? You’ve made a fool of me; brought my mistress hither, whom I’m not allowed to touch—
SYRUS
4.6.820:
Well, I’m not angry then. But do you know where Bacchis is just now?
CLITIPHO
4.6.821:
At our house.
SYRUS
No.
CLITIPHO
Where then?
SYRUS
At Clinia’s.
CLITIPHO
4.6.822:
I’m ruined!
SYRUS
Be of good heart; you shall presently carry to her the money that you promised her.
CLITIPHO
4.6.823:
You do prate away.—Where from?
SYRUS
From your own father.
CLITIPHO
4.6.824:
Perhaps you are joking with me.
SYRUS
The thing itself will prove it.
CLITIPHO
4.6.825:
Indeed, then, I am a lucky man. Syrus, I do love you from my heart.
SYRUS
4.6.826: But your father’s coming out. Take care not to express surprise at any thing, for what reason it is done; give way at the proper moment; do what he orders, and say but little.

4.7.829:
(Enter CHREMES from the house, with a bag of money.) CHREMES
Where’s Clitipho now?
SYRUS
(aside to CLITIPHO.)
Say—here I am.
CLITIPHO
Here am I.
CHREMES
(to SYRUS.)
4.7.830:
Have you told him how it is?
SYRUS
I’ve told him pretty well every thing.
CHREMES
4.7.831:
Take this money, and carry it.
(Holding out the bag.)
SYRUS
(aside to CLITIPHO.)
Go—why do you stand still, you stone; why don’t you take it?
CLITIPHO
4.7.832:
Very well, give it me.
(Receives the bag.)
SYRUS
(to CLITIPHO.)
Follow me this way directly. (To CHREMES.) You in the mean while will wait here for us till we return; for there’s no occasion for us to stay there long.
(CLITIPHO and SYRUS go into the house of MENEDEMUS.)
CHREMES
(to himself.)
4.7.835: My daughter, in fact, has now had ten minae from me, which I consider as paid for her board; another ten will follow these for clothes; and then she will require two talents for her portion. How many things, both just and unjust, are sanctioned by custom!
4.7.840: Now I’m obliged, neglecting my business, to look out for some one on whom to bestow my property, that has been acquired by my labor.

4.8.842:
(Enter MENEDEMUS from his house.) MENEDEMUS
(to CLINIA within.)
My son, I now think myself the happiest of all men, since I find that you have returned to a rational mode of life.
CHREMES
(aside.)
4.8.845:
preserve, so far as in you lies, my son, myself, and my family.
CHREMES
4.8.846:
Tell me what you would have me do.
MENEDEMUS
You have this day found a daughter.
CHREMES
4.8.847:
What then?
MENEDEMUS
Clinia wishes her to be given him for a wife.
CHREMES
4.8.848:
Prithee, what kind of a person are you?
MENEDEMUS
Why?
CHREMES
Have you already forgotten what passed between us, concerning a scheme,
4.8.850:
that by that method some money might be got out of you?
MENEDEMUS
I remember.
CHREMES
4.8.851:
That self-same thing they are now about.
MENEDEMUS
What do you tell me, Chremes? Why surely, this Courtesan, who is at my house, is Clitipho’s mistress.
CHREMES
4.8.853: So they say, and you believe it all; and they say that he is desirous of a wife, in order that, when I have betrothed her,
4.8.855:
you may give him money, with which to provide gold trinkets and clothing, and other things that are requisite.
MENEDEMUS
4.8.856:
That is it, no doubt; that money will be given to his mistress.
CHREMES
Of course it is to be given.
MENEDEMUS
4.8.857: Alas! in vain then, unhappy man, have I been overjoyed; still however, I had rather any thing than be deprived of him. What answer now shall I report from you, Chremes,
4.8.860:
so that he may not perceive that I have found it out, and take it to heart?
CHREMES
4.8.861:
To heart, indeed! you are too indulgent to him, Menedemus.
MENEDEMUS
Let me go on; I have now begun: assist me in this throughout, Chremes.
CHREMES
4.8.863:
Say then, that you have seen me, and have treated about the marriage.
MENEDEMUS
4.8.865:
that as a son-in-law he meets my approbation; in fine, too, if you like, tell him also that she has been promised him.
MENEDEMUS
4.8.866:
Well, that’s what I wanted—
CHREMES
4.8.867:
That he may the sooner ask of you, and you may as soon as possible give him what you wish.
MENEDEMUS
4.8.868:
It is my wish.
CHREMES
Assuredly, before very long, according as I view this matter, you’ll have enough of him.
4.8.870:
But, however that may be, if you are wise, you’ll give to him cautiously, and a little at a time.
MENEDEMUS
4.8.871:
I’ll do so.
CHREMES
Go in-doors and see how much he requires. I shall be at home, if you should want me for any thing.
MENEDEMUS
4.8.872:
I certainly do want you; for I shall let you know whatever I do.
(They go into their respective houses.)

5.1.875:
but this assistant, prompter, and director of mine, Chremes, outdoes me in that. Any one of those epithets which are applied to a fool is suited to myself, such as dolt, post, ass, lump of lead; to him not one can apply; his stupidity surpasses them all.
(Enter CHREMES, speaking to SOSTRATA within.)
CHREMES
5.1.879: Hold now, do, wife, leave off dinning the Gods with thanksgivings
5.1.880:
that your daughter has been discovered; unless you judge of them by your own disposition, and think that they understand nothing, unless the same thing has been told them a hundred times. But, in the mean time, why does my son linger there so long with Syrus?
MENEDEMUS
5.1.883:
What persons do you say are lingering?
CHREMES
Ha! Menedemus, you have come opportunely. Tell me, have you told Clinia what I said?
MENEDEMUS
5.1.885:
What did he say?
MENEDEMUS
He began to rejoice, just like people do who wish to be married.
CHREMES
(laughing.)
5.1.886:
Ha! ha! ha!
MENEDEMUS
Why are you laughing?
CHREMES
The sly tricks of my servant, Syrus, just came into my mind.
MENEDEMUS
5.1.887:
Did they?
CHREMES
