The rogue can even mould the countenances of people.
MENEDEMUS
5.1.888:
That my son is pretending that he is overjoyed, is it that you mean?
CHREMES
Just so.
(Laughing.)
MENEDEMUS
The very same thing came into my mind.
CHREMES
5.1.889:
A crafty knave!
MENEDEMUS
Still more would you think such to be the fact, if you knew more.
CHREMES
5.1.890:
Do you say so?
MENEDEMUS
Do you give attention then?
CHREMES
Just stop—first I want to know this, what money you have squandered; for when you told your son that she was promised, of course Dromo would at once throw in a word that golden jewels, clothes, and attendants would be needed for the bride, in order that you might give the money.
MENEDEMUS
5.1.894:
No.
CHREMES
How, no?
MENEDEMUS
No, I tell you.
CHREMES
Nor yet your son himself?
MENEDEMUS
Not in the slightest, Chremes.
5.1.895:
He was only the more pressing on this one point, that the match might be concluded to-day.
CHREMES
5.1.896:
You say what’s surprising. What did my servant Syrus do? Didn’t even he say any thing?
MENEDEMUS
Nothing at all.
CHREMES
5.1.897:
For what reason, I don’t know.
MENEDEMUS
For my part, I wonder at that, when you know other things so well. But this same Syrus has moulded your son, too, to such perfection, that there could not be even the slightest suspicion that she is Clinia’s mistress!
CHREMES
5.1.900:
What do you say?
MENEDEMUS
Not to mention, then, their kissing and embracing; that I count nothing.
CHREMES
5.1.901:
What more could be done to carry on the cheat?
MENEDEMUS
Pshaw!
CHREMES
What do you mean?
MENEDEMUS
Only listen. In the inner part of my house there is a certain room at the back; into this a bed was brought, and was made up with bed-clothes.
CHREMES
5.1.904:
What took place after this?
MENEDEMUS
No sooner said than done, thither went Clitipho.
CHREMES
5.1.905:
Alone?
MENEDEMUS
Alone.
CHREMES
I’m alarmed.
MENEDEMUS
Bacchis followed directly.
CHREMES
5.1.906:
Alone?
MENEDEMUS
Alone.
CHREMES
I’m undone!
MENEDEMUS
When they had gone into the room, they shut the door.
CHREMES
Well—did Clinia see all this going on?
MENEDEMUS
5.1.907:
How shouldn’t he? He was with me.
CHREMES
5.1.908:
Bacchis is my son’s mistress, Menedemus I’m undone.
MENEDEMUS
5.1.909:
Why so?
CHREMES
I have hardly substance to suffice for ten days.
MENEDEMUS
5.1.910:
What! are you alarmed at it, because he is paying attention to his friend?
CHREMES
5.1.911:
His she-friend rather.
MENEDEMUS
If he really is paying it.
CHREMES
Is it a matter of doubt to you? Do you suppose that there is any person of so accommodating and tame a spirit as to suffer his own mistress, himself looking on, to—
MENEDEMUS
(chuckling and speaking ironically.)
5.1.914:
Why not? That I may be imposed upon the more easily.
CHREMES
5.1.915:
Do you laugh at me? You have good reason. How angry I now am with myself! How many things gave proof, whereby, had I not been a stone, I might have been fully sensible of this? What was it I saw? Alas! wretch that I am! But assuredly they shall not escape my vengeance if I live; for this instant—
MENEDEMUS
5.1.919: Can you not contain yourself? Have you no respect for yourself?
5.1.920:
Am I not a sufficient example to you?
CHREMES
For very anger, Menedemus, I am not myself.
MENEDEMUS
5.1.921:
For you to talk in that manner! Is it not a shame for you to be giving advice to others, to show wisdom abroad and yet be able to do nothing for yourself?
CHREMES
5.1.924:
What shall I do?
MENEDEMUS
That which you said I failed to do:
5.1.925:
make him sensible that you are his father; make him venture to intrust every thing to you, to seek and to ask of you; so that he may look for no other resources and forsake you.
CHREMES
5.1.928: Nay, I had much rather he would go any where in the world, than by his debaucheries here reduce his father to beggary!
5.1.930:
For if I go on supplying his extravagance, Menedemus, in that case my circumstances will undoubtedly be soon reduced to the level of your rake.
MENEDEMUS
5.1.932:
What evils you will bring upon yourself in this affair, if you don’t act with caution! You’ll show yourself severe, and still pardon him at last; that too with an ill grace.
CHREMES
5.1.934:
Ah! you don’t know how vexed I am.
MENEDEMUS
Just as you please.
5.1.935:
What about that which I desire—that she may be married to my son? Unless there is any other step that you would prefer.
CHREMES
5.1.936:
On the contrary, both the son-in-law and the connection are to my taste.
MENEDEMUS
5.1.937:
What portion shall I say that you have named for your daughter? Why are you silent?
CHREMES
5.1.938:
Portion?
MENEDEMUS
I say so.
CHREMES
Alas!
MENEDEMUS
Chremes, don’t be at all afraid to speak, if it is but a small one. The portion is no consideration at all with us.
CHREMES
5.1.940:
I did think that two talents were sufficient, according to my means. But if you wish me to be saved, and my estate and my son, you must say to this effect, that I have settled all my property on her as her portion.
MENEDEMUS
5.1.942:
What scheme are you upon?
CHREMES
5.1.943:
Pretend that you wonder at this, and at the same time ask him the reason why I do so.
MENEDEMUS
5.1.944:
Why, really, I can’t conceive the reason for your doing so.
CHREMES
5.1.945:
Why do I do so? To check his feelings, which are now hurried away by luxury and wantonness, and to bring him down so as not to know which way to turn himself.
MENEDEMUS
5.1.947:
What is your design?
CHREMES
Let me alone, and give me leave to have my own way in this matter.
MENEDEMUS
I do give you leave: is this your desire?
CHREMES
5.1.948:
It is so.
MENEDEMUS
Then be it so.
CHREMES
And now let your son prepare to fetch the bride. The other one shall be schooled in such language as befits children. But Syrus—
MENEDEMUS
5.1.950:
What of him?
CHREMES
What? If I live, I will have him so handsomely dressed, so well combed out, that he shall always remember me as long as he lives; to imagine that I’m to be a laughing-stock and a plaything for him! So may the Gods bless me! he would not have dared to do to a widow-woman the things which he has done to me.
(They go into their respective houses.)

5.2.954:
(Enter MENEDEMUS, with CLITIPHO and SYRUS.) CLITIPHO
Prithee, is it really the fact, Menedemus, that my father can,
5.2.955:
in so short a space of time, have cast off all the natural affection of a parent for me? For what crime? What so great enormity have I, to my misfortune, committed? Young men generally do the same.
MENEDEMUS
5.2.957:
I am aware that this must be much more harsh and severe to you, on whom it falls; but yet I take it no less amiss than you. How it is so I know not, nor can I account for it, except that from my heart I wish you well.
CLITIPHO
5.2.960:
Did not you say that my father was waiting here?
(Enter CHREMES from his house.)
MENEDEMUS
See, here he is.
(MENEDEMUS goes into his house.)
CHREMES
Why are you blaming me, Clitipho? Whatever I have done in this matter, I had a view to you and your imprudence. When I saw that you were of a careless disposition, and held the pleasures of the moment of the first importance, and did not look forward to the future, I took measures that you might neither want nor be able to waste this which I have.
5.2.965:
When, through your own conduct, it was not allowed me to give it you, to whom I ought before all, I had recourse to those who were your nearest relations; to them I have made over and intrusted every thing. There you’ll always find a refuge for your folly; food, clothing, and a roof under which to betake yourself.
CLITIPHO
5.2.969:
It is better than that, you being my heir, Bacchis should possess this estate of mine.
SYRUS
(apart.)
5.2.970:
I’m ruined irrevocably!—Of what mischief have I, wretch that I am, unthinkingly been the cause?
CLITIPHO
5.2.971:
Would I were dead!
CHREMES
Prithee, first learn what it is to live. When you know that, if life displeases you, then try the other.
SYRUS
5.2.973:
Master, may I be allowed—?
CHREMES
Say on.
SYRUS
But may I safely?
CHREMES
Say on.
SYRUS
What injustice or what madness is this, that that in which I have offended, should be to his detriment?
CHREMES
5.2.975:
Don’t you mix yourself up in it; no one accuses you, Syrus, nor need you look out for an altar, or for an intercessor for yourself.
SYRUS
5.2.976:
What is your design?
CHREMES
I am not at all angry either with you, (to SYRUS), or with you (to CLITIPHO); nor is it fair that you should be so with me for what I am doing.
(He goes into his house.)
SYRUS
5.2.978:
He’s gone. I wish I had asked him—
CLITIPHO
What, Syrus?
SYRUS
Where I am to get my subsistence; he has so utterly cast us adrift. You are to have it, for the present, at your sister’s, I find.
CLITIPHO
5.2.980:
Has it then come to this pass, Syrus—that I am to be in danger even of starving?
SYRUS
5.2.981:
So we only live, there’s hope—
CLITIPHO
What hope?
SYRUS
That we shall be hungry enough.
CLITIPHO
5.2.982:
Do you jest in a matter so serious, and not give me any assistance with your advice?
SYRUS
5.2.983:
On the contrary, I’m both now thinking of that, and have been about it all the time your father was speaking just now; and so far as I can perceive—
CLITIPHO
5.2.984:
What?
SYRUS
It will not be wanting long.
(He meditates.)
CLITIPHO
5.2.985:
What is it, then?
SYRUS
It is this—I think that you are not their son.
CLITIPHO
How’s that, Syrus? Are you quite in your senses?
SYRUS
5.2.986:
I’ll tell you what’s come into my mind; be you the judge. While they had you alone, while they had no other source of joy more nearly to affect them, they indulged you, they lavished upon you. Now a daughter has been found, a pretense has been found in fact on which to turn you adrift.
CLITIPHO
5.2.990:
It’s very probable.
SYRUS
Do you suppose that he is so angry on account of this fault?
CLITIPHO
5.2.991:
I do not think so.
SYRUS
Now consider another thing. All mothers are wont to be advocates for their sons when in fault, and to aid them against a father’s severity; ’tis not so here.
CLITIPHO
5.2.993:
You say true; what then shall I now do, Syrus?
SYRUS
5.2.994: Question them on this suspicion; mention the matter without reserve;
5.2.995:
either, if it is not true, you’ll soon bring them both to compassion, or else you’ll soon find out whose son you are.
CLITIPHO
5.2.996:
You give good advice; I’ll do so.
(He goes into the house of CHREMES.)
SYRUS
(to himself.)
Most fortunately did this come into my mind. For the less hope the young man entertains, the greater the difficulty with which he’ll bring his father to his own terms. I’m not sure even, that he may not take a wife, and then no thanks for Syrus.
5.2.1000:
But what is this? The old man’s coming out of doors; I’ll be off. What has so far happened, I am surprised at, that he didn’t order me to becarried off from here: now I’ll away to Menedemus here, I’ll secure him as my intercessor; I can put no trust in our old man.
(Goes into the house of MENEDEMUS.)

5.3.1003:
(Enter CHREMES and SOSTRATA from the house.) SOSTRATA
Really, sir, if you don’t take care, you’ll be causing some mischief to your son; and indeed I do wonder at it,
5.3.1005:
my husband, how anything so foolish could ever come into your head.
CHREMES
5.3.1006:
Oh, you persist in being the woman? Did I ever wish for any one thing in all my life, Sostrata, but that you were my contradicter on that occasion? And yet if I were now to ask you what it is that I have done amiss, or why you act thus, you would not know in what point you are now so obstinately opposing me in your folly.
SOSTRATA
5.3.1010:
Yes, rather, I should have said you do know; inasmuch as either expression amounts to the same thing.
SOSTRATA
5.3.1011:
Alas! you are unreasonable to expect me to be silent in a matter of such importance.
CHREMES
5.3.1012:
I don’t expect it; talk on then, I shall still do it not a bit the less.
SOSTRATA
5.3.1013:
Will you do it?
CHREMES
Certainly.
SOSTRATA
Don’t you see how much evil you will be causing by that course?—He suspects himself to be a foundling.
CHREMES
5.3.1014:
Do you say so?
SOSTRATA
Assuredly it will be so.
CHREMES
5.3.1015:
Admit it.
SOSTRATA
Hold now—prithee, let that be for our enemies. Am I to admit that he is not my son who really is?
CHREMES
5.3.1017:
What! are you afraid that you can not prove that he is yours, whenever you please?
SOSTRATA
5.3.1018:
Because my daughter has been found?
CHREMES
No; but for a reason why it should be much sooner believed—because he is just like you in disposition,
5.3.1020: you will easily prove that he is your child; for he is exactly like you; why, he has not a single vice left him but you have just the same. Then, besides, no woman could have been the mother of such a son but yourself. But he’s coming out of doors, and how demure! When you understand the matter, you may form your own conclusions.

5.4.1024:
(Enter CLITIPHO from the house of CHREMES.) CLITIPHO
If there ever was any time, mother, when I caused you pleasure,
5.4.1025:
being called your son by your own desire, I beseech: you to remember it, and now to take compassion on me in my distress. A thing I beg and request—do discover to me my parents.
SOSTRATA
5.4.1028:
I conjure you, my son, not to entertain that notion in your mind, that you are another person’s child.
CLITIPHO
5.4.1029:
I am.
SOSTRATA
Wretch that I am! (Turning to CHREMES.) Was it this that you wanted, pray?
5.4.1030:
(To CLITIPHO.) So may you be the survivor of me and of him, you are my son and his; and henceforth, if you love me,take care that I never hear that speech from you again.
CHREMES
5.4.1032:
But I say, if you fear me, take care how I find these propensities existing in you.
CLITIPHO
5.4.1033:
What propensities?
CHREMES
If you wish to know, I’ll tell you; being a trifler, an idler, a cheat, a glutton, a debauchee, a spendthrift—Believe me, and believe that you are our son.
CLITIPHO
5.4.1035:
This is not the language of a parent.
CHREMES
If you had been born from my head, Clitipho, just as they say Minerva was from Jove’s, none the more on that account would I suffer myself to be disgraced by your profligacy.
SOSTRATA
5.4.1038:
May the Gods forbid it.
CHREMES
I don’t know as to the Gods; so far as I shall be enabled, I will carefully prevent it. You are seeking that which you possess—parents; that which you are in want of you don’t seek—
5.4.1040:
in what way to pay obedience to a father, and to preserve what he acquired by his industry. That you by trickery should bring before my eyes—I am ashamed to mention the unseemly word in her presence (pointing to SOSTRATA), but you were not in any degree ashamed to act thus.
CLITIPHO
(aside.)
5.4.1043: Alas! how thoroughly displeased I now am with myself! How much ashamed! nor do I know how to make a beginning to pacify him.

5.5.1045:
(Enter MENEDEMUS from his house.) MENEDEMUS
(to himself.)
Why really, Chremes is treating his son too harshly and too unkindly. I’m come out, therefore, to make peace between them. Most opportunely I see them both.
CHREMES
5.5.1047:
Well, Menedemus, why don’t you order my daughter to be sent for, and close with the offer of the portion that I mentioned?
SOSTRATA
5.5.1048:
My husband, I entreat you not to do it.
CLITIPHO
5.5.1050:
do let then prevail upon you.
CHREMES
Am I knowingly to make my property a present to Bacchis? I’ll not do it.
MENEDEMUS
5.5.1051:
Why, we would not suffer it.
CLITIPHO
If you desire me to live, father, do forgive me.
SOSTRATA
5.5.1052:
Do, my dear Chremes.
MENEDEMUS
Come, Chremes, pray, don’t be so obdurate.
CHREMES
5.5.1053:
What am I to do here? I see I am not allowed to carry this through, as I had intended.
MENEDEMUS
5.5.1054:
You are acting as becomes you.
CHREMES
On this condition, then, I’ll do it; if he does
5.5.1055:
that which I think it right he should do.
CLITIPHO
Father, I’ll do any thing; command me.
CHREMES
5.5.1056:
You must take a wife.
CLITIPHO
Father—
CHREMES
I’ll hear nothing.
MENEDEMUS
I’ll take it upon myself; he shall do so.
CHREMES
5.5.1057:
I don’t hear any thing from him as yet.
CLITIPHO
(aside.)
I’m undone!
SOSTRATA
Do you hesitate, Clitipho?
CHREMES
5.5.1058:
Nay, just as he likes.
MENEDEMUS
He’ll do it all.
SOSTRATA
This course, while you are making a beginning, is disagreeable, and while you are unacquainted with it. When you have become acquainted with it, it will become easy.
CLITIPHO
5.5.1060:
My son, upon my honor I’ll give you that charming girl, whom you may soon become attached to, the daughter of our neighbor Phanocrata.
CLITIPHO
5.5.1061:
What! that red-haired girl, with cat’s eyes, freckled face, and hooked nose? I can not, father.
CHREMES
5.5.1063:
Heyday! how nice he is! You would fancy he had set his mind upon it.
SOSTRATA
I’ll name another.
CLITIPHO
5.5.1064:
Why no—since I must marry, I myself have one that I should pretty nearly make choice of.
SOSTRATA
5.5.1065:
Now, son, I commend you.
CLITIPHO
The daughter of Archonides here.
SOSTRATA
5.5.1066:
I’m quite agreeable.
CLITIPHO
Father, this now remains.
CHREMES
What is it?
CLITIPHO
I want you to pardon Syrus for what he has done for my sake.
CHREMES
5.5.1067:
Be it so.
(To the Audience.) Fare you well, and grant us your applause.

0.0.1:
THE PROLOGUE
IF there is any one who desires to please as many good men as possible, and to give offense to extremely few, among those does our Poet enroll his name.
0.0.4: Next, if there is one who thinks that language too harsh is here applied to him, let him bear this in mind—
0.0.6: that it is an answer, not an attack; inasmuch as he has himself been the first aggressor; who, by translating plays verbally, and writing them in bad Latin, has made out of good Greek Plays Latin ones by no means good. Just as of late he has published the Phasma [the Apparition] of Menander;
0.0.10: and in the Thesaurus [the Treasure] has described him from whom the gold is demanded, as pleading his cause why it should be deemed his own, before the person who demands it has stated how this treasure belongs to him, or how it came into the tomb of his father. Henceforward, let him not deceive himself, or fancy thus,
0.0.15: I have now done with it; there’s nothing that he can say to me. I recommend him not to be mistaken, and to refrain from provoking me. I have many other points, as to which for the present he shall be pardoned, which, however, shall be brought forward hereafter, if he persists in attacking me,
0.0.19: as he has begun to do. After the Aediles had purchased the Eunuch of Menander, the Play which we are about to perform, he managed to get an opportunity of viewing it. When the magistrates were present it began to be performed. He exclaimed that a thief, no Poet, had produced the piece, but still had not deceived him;
0.0.25: that, in fact, it was the Colax, an old Play of Plautus; and that from it were taken the characters of the Parasite and the Captain. If this is a fault, the fault is the ignorance of the Poet; not that he intended to be guilty of theft. That so it is, you will now be enabled to judge.
0.0.30: The Colax is a Play of Meander’s; in it there is Colax, a Parasite, and a braggart Captain: he does not deny that he has transferred these characters into his Eunuch from the Greek; but assuredly he does deny this, that he was aware that those pieces had been already translated into Latin.
0.0.35: But if it is not permitted us to use the same characters as others, how can it any more be allowed to represent hurrying servants, to describe virtuous matrons, artful courtesans, the gluttonous parasite, the braggart captain, the infant palmed off, the old man cajoled by the servant,
0.0.40: about love, hatred, suspicion? In fine, nothing is said now that has not been said before. Wherefore it is but just that you should know this, and make allowance, if the moderns do what the ancients used to do. Grant me your attention, and give heed in silence,
0.0.45: that you may understand what the Eunuch means.

1.1.46:
(Enter PHAEDRIA and PARMENO.) PHAEDRIA
What then, shall I do? Ought I not to go, not now even, when I am sent for of her own accord? Or ought I rather so to behave myself as not to put up with affronts from Courtesans? She shut her door against me; she now invites me back. Ought I to return? No; though she should implore me.
PARMENO
1.1.50: l’faith, if indeed you only can, there’s nothing better or more spirited; but if you begin, and can not hold out stoutly, and if, when you can not endure it, while no one asks you, peace being not made, you come to her of your own accord, showing that you love her, and can not endure it, you are done for; it’s all over with you;
1.1.55: you are ruined outright. She’ll be jilting you, when she finds you overcome. Do you then, while there’s time, again and again reflect upon this, master, that a matter, which in itself admits of neither prudence nor moderation, you are unable to manage with prudence. In love there are all these evils; wrongs,
1.1.60: suspicions, enmities reconcilements, war, then peace; if you expect to render these things, naturally uncertain, certain by dint of reason, you wouldn’t effect it a bit the more than if you were to use your endeavors to be mad with reason. And, what you are now, in anger, meditating to yourself,
1.1.65: What! I to her? Who—him! Who—me! Who wouldn’t? Only let me alone; I had rather die; she shall find out what sort of a person I am; these expressions, upon my faith, by a single false tiny tear, which, by rubbing her eyes, poor thing, she can hardly squeeze out perforce, she will put an end to; and she’ll be the first to accuse you; and you will be
1.1.70:
too ready to give satisfaction to her.
PHAEDRIA
O disgraceful conduct! I now perceive, both that she is perfidious, and that I am a wretched man. I am both weary of her, and burn with passion; knowing and fully sensible, alive and seeing it, I am going to ruin; nor do I know what I am to do.
PARMENO
1.1.74: What you are to do? Why, only to redeem yourself, thus captivated,
1.1.75:
at the smallest price you can; if you can not at a very small, rate, still for as little as you can; and do not afflict yourself.
PHAEDRIA
1.1.76:
Do you persuade me to this?
PARMENO
If you are wise. And don’t be adding to the troubles which love itself produces; those which it does produce, bear patiently. But see, here she is coming herself, the downfall of our fortunes,—
1.1.80: for that which we ought ourselves to enjoy she intercepts.

1.2.81:
(Enter THAIS from her house.) THAIS
(to herself, not seeing them.)
Ah wretched me! I fear lest Phaedria should take it amiss or otherwise than I intended it, that he was not admitted yesterday.
PHAEDRIA
(aside to PARMENO.)
1.2.83:
I’m trembling and shivering all over, Parmeno, at the sight of her.
PARMENO
(apart.)
1.2.85:
only approach this fire, you’ll soon be warmer than you need.
THAIS
(turning round.)
1.2.86:
Who is it that’s speaking here? What, are you here, my Phaedria? Why are you standing here? Why didn’t you come into the house at once?
PARMENO
(whispering to PHAEDRIA.)
1.2.87:
But not a word about shutting you out!
THAIS
1.2.89: Of course, it’s because this door is always open to me,
1.2.90:
or because I’m the highest in your favor?
THAIS
Pass those matters by.
PHAEDRIA
1.2.91:
How pass them by? O Thais, Thais, I wish that I had equal affection with yourself, and that it were in like degree, that either this might distress you in the same way that it distresses me, or that I might be indifferent at this being done by you.
THAIS
1.2.95:
Prithee, don’t torment yourself, my life, my Phaedria. Upon my faith, I did it, not because I love or esteem any person more than you; but the case was such that it was necessary to be done.
PARMENO
(ironically.)
1.2.98:
I suppose that, poor thing, you shut him out of doors, for love, according to the usual practice.
THAIS
1.2.99: Is it thus you act, Parmeno? Well, well. (To PHAEDRIA.) But listen—the reason for which
1.2.100:
I desired you to be sent for hither—
PHAEDRIA
Go on.
THAIS
First tell me this; can this fellow possibly hold his tongue?
(pointing to PARMENO.)
PARMENO
1.2.101: What, I? Perfectly well. But, hark you, upon these conditions I pledge my word to you; the truth that I hear, I’m silent upon, and retain it most faithfully; but if I hear what’s false and without foundation, it’s out at once;
1.2.105:
I’m full of chinks, and leak in every direction. Therefore, if you wish it to be kept secret, speak the truth.
THAIS
1.2.107:
My mother was a Samian; she lived at Rhodes—
PARMENO
1.2.108:
That may be kept a secret.
THAIS
There, at that period, a certain merchant made present to my mother of a little girl,
1.2.110:
who had been stolen away from Attica here.
PARMENO
What, a citizen?
THAIS
I think so; we do not know for certain: she herself used to mention her mother’s and her father’s name; her country and other tokens she didn’t know, nor, by reason of her age, was she able. The merchant added this: that he had heard from the kidnappers
1.2.115: that she had been carried off from Sunium. When my mother received her, she began carefully to teach her every thing, and to bring her up, just as though she had been her own daughter. Most persons supposed that she was my sister.
1.2.119:
Thence I came hither with that stranger, with whom alone at that period I was connected; he left me all which I now possess—
PARMENO
1.2.121:
Both these things are false; out it goes.
THAIS
How so?
PARMENO
Because you were neither content with one, nor was he the only one to make you presents; for he likewise (pointing to PHAEDRIA) brought a pretty considerable share to you.
THAIS
1.2.124: Such is the fact; but do allow me to arrive at the point I wish.
1.2.125:
In the mean time, the Captain, who had begun to take a fancy to me, set out to Caria; since when, in the interval, I became acquainted with you. You yourself are aware how very dear I have held you; and how I confess to you all my nearest counsels.
PHAEDRIA
1.2.129:
Nor will Parmeno be silent about that.
PARMENO
O, is that a matter of doubt?
THAIS
1.2.130: Attend; I entreat you. My mother died there recently; her brother is somewhat greedy after wealth. When he saw that this damsel was of beauteous form and understood music, hoping for a good price, he forthwith put her up for sale, and sold her. By good fortune
1.2.135: this friend of mine was present; he bought her as a gift to me, not knowing or suspecting any thing of all this. He returned; but when he perceived that I had formed a connection with you as well, he feigned excuses on purpose that he might not give her; he said that if he could feel confidence that he should be preferred to yourself
1.2.140:
by me, so as not to apprehend that, when I had received her, I should forsake him, then he was ready to give her to me; but that he did fear this. But, so far as I can conjecture, he has set his affections upon the girl.
PHAEDRIA
1.2.144: Nothing; for I have made inquiry. Now, my Phaedria,
1.2.145: there are many reasons why I could wish to get her away from him. In the first place, because she was called my sister; moreover, that I may restore and deliver her to her friends. I am a lone woman; I have no one here, neither acquaintance nor relative; wherefore, Phaedria, I am desirous by my good offices to secure friends.
1.2.150:
Prithee, do aid me in this, in order that it may be the more easily effected. Do allow him for the few next days to have the preference with me. Do you make no answer?
PHAEDRIA
1.2.152:
Most vile woman! Can I make you any answer after such behavior as this?
PARMENO
1.2.154:
Well done, my master, I commend you; (aside) he’s galled at last. (To PHAEDRIA.) You show yourself a man.
PHAEDRIA
1.2.155: I was not aware what you were aiming at; she was carried away from here, when a little child; my mother brought her up as though her own; she was called my sister; I wish to get her away, that I may restore her to her friends. The meaning is, that all these expressions, in fine, now amount to this, that I am shut out, he is admitted. For what reason?
1.2.160:
Except that you love him more than me: and now you are afraid of her who has been brought hither, lest she should win him, such as he is, from yourself.
THAIS
1.2.162:
I, afraid of that?
PHAEDRIA
What else, then, gives you concern? Let me know. Is he the only person who makes presents? Have you found my bounty shut against you?
1.2.165: Did I not, when you told me that you wished for a servant-maid from Aethiopia, setting all other matters aside, go and seek for one? Then you said that you wanted a Eunuch, because ladies of quality alone make use of them; I found you one. I yesterday paid twenty minae for them both.
1.2.170:
Though slighted by you, I still kept these things in mind; as a reward for so doing, I am despised by you.
THAIS
1.2.171:
Phaedria, what does this mean? Although I wish to get her away, and think that by these means it could most probably be effected; still, rather than make an enemy of you, I’ll do as you request me.
PHAEDRIA
1.2.175:
I only wish that you used that expression from your heart and truthfully, rather than make an enemy of you. If I could believe that this was said sincerely, I could put up with any thing.
PARMENO
(aside.)
1.2.178:
He staggers; how instantaneously is he vanquished by a single expression!
THAIS
1.2.179: I, wretched woman, not speak from my heart? What, pray,
1.2.180:
did you ever ask of me in jest, but that you carried your point? I am unable to obtain even this of you, that you would grant me only two days.
PHAEDRIA
1.2.182:
If, indeed, it is but two days; but don’t let these days become twenty.
THAIS
1.2.184:
Assuredly not more than two days, or—
PHAEDRIA
Or? I won’t have it.
THAIS
1.2.185:
It shall not be; only do allow me to obtain this of you.
PHAEDRIA
Of course that which you desire must be done.
THAIS
1.2.186:
I love you as you deserve; you act obligingly.
PHAEDRIA
(to PARMENO.)
I shall go into the country; there I shall worry myself for the next two days: I’m resolved to do so; Thais must be humored. Do you, Parmeno, take care that they are brought hither.
PARMENO
1.2.190:
For the next two days then, Thais, adieu.
THAIS
And the same to you, my Phaedria; do you desire aught else?
PHAEDRIA
1.2.191: What should I desire? That, present with the Captain, you may be as if absent; that night and day you may love me; may feel my absence; may dream of me; may be impatient for me; may think about me;
1.2.195:
may hope for me; may centre your delight in me; may be all in all with me; in fine, if you will, be my very life, as I am yours.
(Exeunt PHAEDRIA and PARMENO.
THAIS
(to herself.)
1.2.197: Ah wretched me! perhaps now he puts but little faith in me, and forms his estimate of me from the dispositions of other women. By my troth, I, who know my own self, am very sure of this,
1.2.200: that I have not feigned any thing that’s false, and that no person is dearer to my heart than this same Phaedria; and whatever in the present case I have done, for this girl’s sake have I done it; for I trust that now I have pretty nearly discovered her brother, a young man of very good family;
1.2.205:
and he has appointed this day to come to me at my house. I’ll go hence in-doors, and wait until he comes.
(She goes into her house.)

2.1.207:
(Enter PHAEDRIA and PARMENO.) PHAEDRIA
Mind that those people are taken there, as I ordered.
PARMENO
I’ll do so.
PHAEDRIA
And carefully.
PARMENO
2.1.208:
It shall be done.
PHAEDRIA
And with all speed.
PARMENO
It shall be done.
PHAEDRIA
Have you had sufficient instructions?
PARMENO
Dear me! to ask the question, as though it were a matter of difficulty.
2.1.210:
I wish that you were able, Phaedria, to find any thing as easily as this present will be lost.
PHAEDRIA
2.1.211:
Together with it, I myself am lost, which concerns me more nearly. Don’t bear this with such a feeling of vexation.
PARMENO
2.1.212:
By no means; on the contrary, I’ll see it done. But do you order any thing else?
PHAEDRIA
2.1.214:
Set off my present with words, as far as you can; and so far as you are able, do drive away that rival of mine from her.
PARMENO
2.1.216:
Pshaw! I should have kept that in mind, even if you hadn’t reminded me.
PHAEDRIA
I shall go into the country and remain there.
PARMENO
2.1.217:
I agree with you.
(Moves as if going.)
PHAEDRIA
But hark you!
PARMENO
What is it you want?
PHAEDRIA
Are you of opinion that I can muster resolution and hold out so as not to come back within the time?
PARMENO
2.1.218:
What, you? Upon my faith, I don’t think so; for either you’ll be returning at once, or by-and-by, at night, want of sleep will be driving you hither.
PHAEDRIA
2.1.220:
I’ll do some laborious work, that I may be continually fatigued, so as to sleep in spite of myself.
PARMENO
2.1.221:
When wearied, you will be keeping awake; by this you will be making it worse.
PHAEDRIA
Oh, you talk to no purpose, Parmeno: this softness of spirit, upon my faith, must be got rid of; I indulge myself too much. Could I not do without her, pray, if there were the necessity, even for a whole three days?
PARMENO
2.1.223:
Whew! an entire three days! Take care what you are about.
PHAEDRIA
2.1.224:
My mind is made up.
(Exit.)
PARMENO
(to himself.)
2.1.225: Good Gods! What a malady is this! That a man should become so changed through love, that you wouldn’t know him to be the same person! Not any one was there less inclined to folly than he, and no one more discreet or more temperate. But who is it that’s coming this way? Heyday! surely this is Gnatho, the Captain’s Parasite; he’s bringing along with him the damsel as a present to her. Heavens!
2.1.230:
How beautiful! No wonder if I make but a sorry figure here to-day with this decrepit Eunuch of mine. She surpasses Thais herself.
(Stands aside.)

2.2.232:
(Enter GNATHO at a distance, leading PAMPHILA.) GNATHO
(to himself.)
Immortal Gods! how much does one man excel another! What a difference there is between a wise person and a fool! This strongly came into my mind from the following circumstance. As I was, coming along to-day, I met a certain person of this place, of my own rank and station,
2.2.235: no mean fellow, one who, like myself, had guttled away his paternal estate; I saw him, shabby, dirty, sickly, beset with rags and years;—What’s the meaning of this garb? said I; he answered, Because, wretch that I am, I’ve lost what I possessed: see to what I am reduced,—all my acquaintances and friends forsake me. On this I felt contempt for him in: comparison with myself. What! said I, you pitiful sluggard,
2.2.240: have you so managed matters as to have no hope left? Have you lost your wits together with your estate? Don’t you see me, who have risen from the same condition? What a complexion I have, how spruce and well dressed, what portliness of person? I have every thing, yet have nothing; and although I possess nothing, still, of nothing am I in want. But I, said he, unhappily, can neither be a butt nor submit to blows.
2.2.245: What! said I, do you suppose it is managed by those means? You are quite mistaken. Once upon a time, in the early ages, there was a calling for that class; this is a new mode of coney-catching; I, in fact, have been the first to strike into this path. There is a class of men who strive to be the first in every thing, but are not; to these I make my court; I do not present myself to them to be laughed at;
2.2.250:
but I am the first to laugh with them, and at the same time to admire their parts: whatever they say, I commend; if they contradict that self-same thing, I commend again. Does any one deny? I deny: does he affirm? I affirm: in fine, I have so trained myself as to humor them in every thing. This calling is now by far the most productive.
PARMENO
(apart.)
2.2.254:
A clever fellow, upon my faith! From being fools he makes men mad outright.
GNATHO
(to himself, continuing.)
2.2.255: While we were thus talking, in the mean time we arrived at the market-place; overjoyed, all the confectioners ran at once to meet me; fishmongers, butchers, cooks, sausage-makers, and fishermen, whom, both when my fortunes were flourishing and when they were ruined, I had served, and often serve still: they complimented me, asked me to dinner, and gave me a hearty welcome.
2.2.260:
When this poor hungry wretch saw that I was in such great esteem, and that I obtained a living so easily, then the fellow began to entreat me that I would allow him to learn this method of me; I bade him become my follower if he could; as the disciples of the Philosophers take their names from the Philosophers themselves, so too, the Parasite; ought to be called Gnathonics.
PARMENO
(apart to the Audience.)
2.2.265:
Do you see the effects of ease and feeding at another’s cost?
GNATHO
(to Iimself, continuing.)
But why do I delay to take this girl to Thais, and ask her to come to dinner? (Aside, on seeing PARMENO.) But I see Parmeno, our rival’s servant, waiting before the door of Thais with a sorrowful air; all’s safe; no doubt these people are finding a cold welcome. I’m resolved to have some sport with this knave.
PARMENO
(aside.)
2.2.269: They fancy that, through this present,
2.2.270:
Thais is quite their own.
GNATHO
(accosting PARMENO.)
With his very best wishes Gnatho greets Parmeno, his very good friend.—What are you doing?
PARMENO
2.2.271:
I’m standing.
GNATHO
So I perceive. Pray, do you see any thing here that don’t please you?
PARMENO
2.2.272:
Yourself.
GNATHO
I believe you,—but any thing else, pray?
PARMENO
2.2.273:
Why so?
GNATHO
Because you are out of spirits.
PARMENO
Not in the least.
GNATHO
Well, don’t be so; but what think you of this slave?
(pointing to her.)
PARMENO
2.2.274:
Really, not amiss.
GNATHO
(aside.)
I’ve galled the fellow.
PARMENO
(aside, on overhearing him.)
How mistaken you are in your notion!
GNATHO
2.2.275:
How far do you suppose this gift will prove acceptable to Thais?
PARMENO
It’s this you mean to say now, that we are discarded there. Hark you, there are vicissitudes in all things.
GNATHO
2.2.277:
For the next six months, Parmeno, I’ll set you at ease; you sha’n’t have to be running to and fro, or sitting up till daylight. Don’t I make you happy?
PARMENO
2.2.279:
Me? O prodigiously!
GNATHO
That’s my way with my friends.
PARMENO
I commend you.
GNATHO
2.2.280:
I’m detaining you; perhaps you were about to go somewhere else.
PARMENO
2.2.281:
Nowhere.
GNATHO
In that case then, lend me your services a little; let me be introduced to her.
PARMENO
2.2.282:
Very well; (GNATHO knocks at the door, which immediately opens) now the door is open for you, (aside) because you are bringing her.
GNATHO
(going into the house of THAIS, ironically.)
2.2.283:
Should you like any one to be called out from here?
(Goes in with PAMPHILA, and shuts the door.)
PARMENO
(to himself.)
Only let the next two days go by; you who, at present, in such high favor, are opening the door with one little finger,
2.2.285:
assuredly I’ll cause to be kicking at that door full oft, with your heels, to no purpose.
(Re-enter GNATHO from the house.)
GNATHO
2.2.286:
Still standing here, Parmeno? Why now, have you been left on guard here, that no go-between might perchance be secretly running from the Captain to her?
(Exit.)
PARMENO
2.2.288: Smartly said; really they ought to be wonderful things to please the Captain. But I see my master’s youngest son coming this way;
2.2.290: I wonder why he has come away from the Piraeus, for he is at present on guard there in the public service. It’s not for nothing; he’s coming in a hurry, too; I can’t imagine why he’s looking around in all directions.

2.3.292:
(Enter CHAEREA on the other side of the stage, in haste.) CHAEREA
(to himself.)
I’m utterly undone! The girl is nowhere; nor do I know where I am myself, to have lost sight of her. Where to inquire for her, where to search for her, whom to ask, which way to turn,
2.3.295:
I’m at a loss. I have only this hope; wherever she is, she can not long be concealed. O what beauteous features! from this moment I banish all other women from my thoughts; I can not endure these every-day beauties.
PARMENO
(apart.)
2.3.297: Why look, here’s the other one. He’s saying something, I don’t know what, about love.
2.3.298: O unfortunate old man, their father! This assuredly is a youth, who, if he does begin, you will say that
2.3.300:
the other one was mere play and pastime, compared with what the madness of this one will cause.
CHAEREA
(to himself, aloud.)
2.3.301:
May all the Gods and Goddesses confound that old fellow who detained me to-day, and me as well who stopped for him, and in fact troubled myself a straw about him. But see, here’s Parmeno. (Addressing him.) Good-morrow to you.
PARMENO
2.3.303:
Why are you out of spirits, and why in such a hurry? Whence come you?
CHAEREA
2.3.304: What, I? I’faith, I neither know whence I’m come, nor whither I’m going;
2.3.305:
so utterly have I lost myself.
PARMENO
2.3.306:
How, pray?
CHAEREA
I’m in love.
PARMENO
(starting.)
Ha!
CHAEREA
Now, Parmeno, you may show what sort of a man you are. You know that you often promised me to this effect: Chaerea, do you only find some object to fall in love with; I’ll make you sensible of my usefulness in such matters, when I used to be storing up my father’s provisions for you on the sly in your little room.
PARMENO
2.3.315:
although their constitutions are good, by their treatment they make them as slight as bulrushes; and so for that reason they are admired, forsooth.
PARMENO
2.3.316:
What sort of a girl is this one of yours?
CHAEREA
A new style of beauty.
PARMENO
(ironically.)
Astounding!
CHAEREA
2.3.317:
Her complexion genuine, her flesh firm and full of juiciness.
PARMENO
Her age?
CHAEREA
Her age Sixteen.
PARMENO
2.3.318:
The very flower of youth.
CHAEREA
Do you make, it your care to obtain her for me either by force, stealth, or entreaty; so that I only gain her, it matters not how to me.
PARMENO
2.3.320:
Well, but to whom does the damsel belong?
CHAEREA
That, i’faith, I don’t know.
PARMENO
Whence did she come?
CHAEREA
That, just as much.
PARMENO
Where does she live?
CHAEREA
2.3.321:
Nor yet do I know that.
PARMENO
Where did you see her?
CHAEREA
In the street.
PARMENO
How did you come to lose her?
CHAEREA
2.3.322: Why, that’s what I was just now fretting myself about; and I do not believe that there is one individual to whom all good luck is a greater stranger than to myself.
2.3.325:
What ill fortune this is!
I’m utterly undone!
PARMENO
What’s the matter?
CHAEREA
Do you ask me? Do you know Archidemides, my father’s kinsman and years’-mate?
PARMENO
2.3.327:
Why not?
CHAEREA
He, while I was in full pursuit of her, met me.
PARMENO
2.3.328:
Unseasonably, upon my faith.
CHAEREA
Aye, unhappily, rather; for other ordinary matters are to be called unseasonable, Parmeno.
2.3.330:
It would be safe for me to make oath that I have not seen him for fully these six or seven months, until just now, when I least wanted, and there was the least occasion. Come now! isn’t this like a fatality? What do you say?
PARMENO
2.3.334: At once he came running up to me, from a considerable distance,
2.3.335: stooping, palsied, hanging his lip, and wheezing. Halloo, Chaerea! halloo! said he; I’ve something to say to you. I stopped. Do you know what it is I want with you? said he. Say on, said I. To-morrow my cause comes on, said he. What then? Be sure and tell your father to remember and be my advocate in the morning.
2.3.340:
In talking of this, an hour elapsed. I inquired if he wanted any thing else. That’s all, said he. I left him. When I looked in this direction for the damsel, she had that very instant turned this way down this street of ours.
PARMENO
(aside.)
2.3.343:
It’s a wonder if he doesn’t mean her who has just now been made a present of to Thais here.
CHAEREA
2.3.344:
When I got here, she was nowhere to be seen.
PARMENO
2.3.345:
Some attendants, I suppose, were accompanying the girl?
CHAEREA
2.3.346:
Yes; a Parasite, and a female servant.
PARMENO
(apart.)
It’s the very same. (To CHAEREA.) It’s all over with you; make an end of it; you’ve said your last.
CHAEREA
2.3.347:
You are thinking about something else.
PARMENO
2.3.348:
Indeed I’m thinking of this same matter.
CHAEREA
Pray, tell me, do you know her, or did you see her?
PARMENO
2.3.349:
I did see, and I do know her, I am aware to what house she has been taken.
CHAEREA
2.3.350:
What, my dear Parmeno, do you know her,
and are you aware where she is?
PARMENO
2.3.351:
She has been brought here (pointing) to the house of Thais the Courtesan. She has been made a present to her.
CHAEREA
2.3.352:
What opulent person is it, to be presenting a gift so precious as this?
PARMENO
The Captain Thraso, Phaedria’s rival.
CHAEREA
2.3.353:
An unpleasant business for my brother, it should seem.
PARMENO
2.3.354:
Aye, and if you did but know what present he is pitting against this present, you would say so still more.
CHAEREA
2.3.355:
Troth now, what is it, pray?
PARMENO
A Eunuch.
CHAEREA
What! that unsightly creature, pray, that he purchased yesterday, an old woman?
PARMENO
2.3.357:
That very same.
CHAEREA
To a certainty, the gentleman will be bundled out of doors, together with his present; but I wasn’t aware that this Thais is our neighbor.
PARMENO
2.3.358:
It isn’t long since she came.
CHAEREA
2.3.359: Unhappy wretch that I am! never to have seen her, even. Come now, just tell me,
2.3.360:
is she as handsome as she is reported to be?
PARMENO
Quite.
CHAEREA
But nothing in comparison with this damsel of mine?
PARMENO
Another thing altogether.
CHAEREA
2.3.361:
Troth now, Parmeno, prithee do contrive for me to gain possession of her.
PARMENO
I’ll do my best, and use all my endeavors; I’ll lend you my assistance. (Going.) Do you want any thing else with me?
CHAEREA
2.3.362:
Where are you going now?
PARMENO
Home; to take those slaves to Thais, as your brother ordered me.
CHAEREA
2.3.364:
Oh, lucky Eunuch that! really, to be sent as a present to that house!
PARMENO
2.3.365:
Why so?
CHAEREA
Do you ask? He will always see at home a fellow-servant of consummate beauty, and be conversing with her; he will be in the same house with her; sometimes he will take his meals with her; sometimes sleep near her.
PARMENO
2.3.368:
What now, if you yourself were to be this fortunate person?
CHAEREA
By what means, Parmeno? Tell me.
PARMENO
2.3.369:
Do you assume his dress.
CHAEREA
His dress! Well, what then?
PARMENO
2.3.370:
I’ll take you there instead of him.
CHAEREA
(musing.)
I hear you.
PARMENO
I’ll say that you are he.
CHAEREA
I understand you.
PARMENO
2.3.371:
You may enjoy those advantages which you just now said lie would enjoy; you may take your meals together with her, be in company with her, touch her, dally with her, and sleep by her side; as not one of these women is acquainted with you, nor yet knows who you are. Besides, you are of an age and figure that you may easily pass for a eunuch.
CHAEREA
2.3.375:
You speak to the purpose; I never knew better counsel given. Well, let’s go in at once; dress me up, take me away, lead me to her, as fast as you can.
PARMENO
2.3.377:
What do you mean? Really, I was only joking.
CHAEREA
You talk nonsense.
PARMENO
I’m undone! Wretch that I am! what have I done? (CHAEREA pushes him along.) Whither are you pushing me? You’ll throw me down presently. I entreat you, be quiet.
CHAEREA
2.3.379:
Let’s be off.
(Pushes him.)
PARMENO
Do you still persist?
CHAEREA
I am resolved upon it.
PARMENO
Only take care that this isn’t too rash a project.
CHAEREA
2.3.380:
Certainly it isn’t; let me alone for that.
PARMENO
Aye, but I shall have to pay the penalty for this?
CHAEREA
Pshaw!
PARMENO
2.3.381:
We shall be guilty of a disgraceful action.
CHAEREA
What, is it disgraceful to be taken to the house of a Courtesan, and to return the compliment upon those tormentors who treat us and our youthful age so scornfully, and who are always tormenting us in every way;—to dupe them just as we are duped by them?
2.3.385:
Or is it right and proper that in preference my father should be wheedled out of his money by deceitful pretexts? Those who knew of this would blame me; while all would think the other a meritorious act.
PARMENO
2.3.387:
What’s to be done in such case? If you are determined to do it, you must do it: but don’t you by-and-by be throwing the blame upon me.
CHAEREA
2.3.388:
I shall not do so.
PARMENO
Do you order me, then?
CHAEREA
I order, charge, and command you; I will never disavow my authorizing you.
PARMENO
2.3.389:
Follow me; may the Gods prosper it!
(They go into the house of LACHES.)

3.1.390:
(Enter THRASO and GNATHO.) THRASO
Did Thais really return me many thanks?
GNATHO
3.1.391:
Exceeding thanks.
THRASO
Was she delighted, say you?
GNATHO
Not so much, indeed, at the present itself, as because it was given by you; really, in right earnest, she does exult at that.
(Enter PARMIENO unseen, from LACHES’ house.)
PARMENO
(apart.)
3.1.393:
I’ve come here to be on the look-out, that when there is an opportunity I may take the presents. But see, here’s the Captain.
THRASO
3.1.394: Undoubtedly it is the case with me
3.1.395:
, that every thing I do is a cause for thankfulness.
GNATHO
3.1.396:
Upon my faith, I’ve observed it.
THRASO
The most mighty King, even, always used to give me especial thanks for whatever I did; but not so to others.
GNATHO
3.1.398:
He who has the wit that you have, often by his words appropriates to himself the glory that has been achieved by the labor of others.
THRASO
3.1.400:
You’ve just hit it.
GNATHO
The king, then, kept you in his eye.
THRASO
Just so.
GNATHO
3.1.401:
To enjoy your society.
THRASO
True; he intrusted to me all his army, all his state secrets.
GNATHO
3.1.402:
Astonishing!
THRASO
Then if, on any occasion, a surfeit of society, or a dislike of business, came upon him, when he was desirous to take some recreation; just as though—you understand?
GNATHO
3.1.405:
just as though on occasion he would rid his mind of those anxieties.
THRASO
You have it. Then he used to take me aside as his only boon companion.
GNATHO
3.1.406:
Whew! You are telling of a King of refined taste.
THRASO
3.1.407:
Aye, he is a person of that sort; a man of but very few acquaintanceships.
GNATHO
(aside.)
3.1.408:
Indeed, of none, I fancy, if he’s on intimate terms with you.
THRASO
3.1.410:
and attacked me privately. I don’t care one straw. They envied me dreadfully; but one in particular, whom the King had appointed over the Indian elephants. Once, when he became particularly troublesome, Prithee, Strato, said I, are you so fierce because you hold command over the wild beasts?
GNATHO
3.1.415:
Cleverly said, upon my faith, and shrewdly. Astounding! You did give the fellow a home thrust. What said he?
THRASO
3.1.417:
How could he be otherwise?
PARMENO
(apart.)
Ye Gods, by our trust in you! a lost and miserable fellow the one, and the other a scoundrel.
THRASO
3.1.418: Well then, about that: matter, Gnatho, the way in which I touched up the Rhodian at a banquet—
3.1.420:
did I never tell you?
GNATHO
Never; but pray, do tell me. (Aside.) I’ve heard it more than a thousand times already.
THRASO
3.1.421: There was in my company at a banquet, this young man of Rhodes, whom I’m speaking of. By chance I had a mistress there; he began to toy with her, and to annoy me. What are you doing, sir impudence? said I to the fellow;
3.1.425:
a hare yourself, and looking out for game?
GNATHO
(pretending to laugh very heartily.)
Ha, ha, ha!
THRASO
3.1.426:
What’s the matter?
GNATHO
How apt, how smart, how clever; nothing could be more excellent. Prithee, was this a saying of yours? I fancied it was an old one.
THRASO
3.1.428:
Did you ever hear it before?
GNATHO
Many a time; and it is mentioned among the first-rate ones.
THRASO
It’s my own.
GNATHO
3.1.429:
I’m sorry though that it was said to a thoughtless young man, and one of respectability.
PARMENO
(apart.)
3.1.430:
May the Gods confound you!
GNATHO
Pray, what did he do?
THRASO
Quite disconcerted. All who were present were dying with laughter; in short, they were all quite afraid of me.
GNATHO
3.1.433:
But hark you, had I best clear myself of this to Thais, as to her suspicion that I’m fond of this girl?
GNATHO
3.1.435:
on the contrary, rather increase her jealousy.
THRASO
Why so?
GNATHO
Do you ask me? Don’t you see, if on any occasion she makes mention of Phaedria or commends him, to provoke you—
THRASO
3.1.438: That such may not be the case, this method is the only remedy. When she speaks of Phaedria, do you instantly mention Pamphila.
3.1.440:
If at any time she says, Let’s invite Phaedria to make one, do you say, Let’s ask Pamphila to sing. If she praises his good looks, do you, on the other hand, praise hers. In short, do you return like for like, which will mortify her.
THRASO
3.1.445:
If, indeed, she loved me, this might be of some use, Gnatho.
GNATHO
3.1.446:
Since she is impatient for and loves that which you give her, she already loves you; as it is, then, it is an easy matter for her to feel vexed. She will be always afraid lest the presents which she herself is now getting, you may on some occasion be taking elsewhere.
THRASO
3.1.450:
Well said; that never came into my mind.
GNATHO
3.1.451: Nonsense. You never thought about it; else how much more readily would you yourself have hit upon it, Thraso!

3.2.453:
(Enter THAIS from her house, attended by PYTHIAS.) THAIS
(as she comes out.)
I thought I just now heard the Captain’s voice. And look, here he is. Welcome, my dear Thraso.
THRASO
3.2.455:
my sweet one, how are you? How much do you love me in return for that music girl?
PARMENO
(apart.)
3.2.456:
How polite! What a beginning he has made on meeting her!
THAIS
3.2.457:
Very much, as you deserve.
GNATHO
3.2.458:
Let’s go to dinner then. (To THRASO.) What do you stand here for?
PARMENO
(apart.)
Then there’s the other one: you would declare that he was born for his belly’s sake.
THRASO
3.2.459:
When you please; I sha’n’t delay.
PARMENO
(apart.)
3.2.460:
I’ll accost them, and pretend as though I had just come out. (He comes forward.) Are you going any where, Thais?
THAIS
3.2.461:
Ha! Parmeno; well done; just going out for the day.
PARMENO
3.2.462:
Where?
THAIS
(aside, pointing at THRASO.)
Why! don’t you see him?
PARMENO
(aside.)
3.2.463:
I see him, and I’m sorry for it. (Aloud.) Phaedria’s presents are ready for you when you please.
THRASO
(impatiently.)
3.2.464:
Why are we to stand here? Why don’t we be off?
PARMENO
(to THRASO.)
3.2.465:
Troth now, pray, do let us, with your leave, present to her the things we intend, and accost and speak to her.
THRASO
(ironically.)
3.2.467:
Very fine presents, I suppose, or at least equal to mine.
PARMENO
3.2.468:
The fact will prove itself. (Goes to the door of LACHES’ house and calls.) Ho there! bid those people come out of doors at once, as I ordered.
(Enter from the house a BLACK GIRL.)
PARMENO
3.2.470:
Do you step forward this way. (To THAIS.) She comes all the way from Aethiopia.
THRASO
(contemptuously.)
Here are some three minae in value.
GNATHO
3.2.471:
Hardly so much.
PARMENO
Where are you, Dorus? Step this way. (Enter CHAEREA from the house, dressed like the EUNUCH.) There’s a Eunuch for you—of what a genteel appearance! of what a prime age!
THAIS
3.2.473:
God bless me, he’s handsome.
PARMENO
What say you, Gnatho? Do you see any thing to find fault with? And what say you, Thraso?
3.2.475:
(Aside.) They hold their tongues; they praise him sufficiently thereby. (To THAIS.) Make trial of him in literature, try him in exercises, and in music; I’ll warrant him well skilled in what it becomes a gentleman to know.
THRASO
3.2.478:
That Eunuch, if occasion served, even in my sober senses, I—
PARMENO
3.2.479: And he who has sent these things makes no request that
3.2.480:
you will live for him alone, and that for his own sake others may be excluded; he neither tells of battles nor shows his scars, nor does he restrict you as (looking at THRASO) a certain person does; but when it is not inconvenient, whenever you think fit, whenever you have the time, he is satisfied to be admitted.
THRASO
(to GNATHO, contemptuously.)
3.2.485:
It appears that this is the servant of some beggarly, wretched master.
GNATHO
3.2.486:
Why, faith, no person, I’m quite sure of that, could possibly put up with him, who had the means to get another.
PARMENO
3.2.488: You hold your tongue—a fellow whom I consider beneath all men of the very lowest grade: for when you can bring yourself to flatter that fellow (pointing at THRASO),
3.2.490:
I do believe you could pick your victuals out of the very flames.
THRASO
3.2.491:
Are we to go now?
THAIS
I’ll take these in-doors first (pointing to CHAEREA and the AETHIOPIAN), and at the same time I’ll order what I wish; after that I’ll return immediately.
(Goes into the house with PYTHIAS, CHAEREA, and the SLAVE.)
THRASO
(to GNATHO.)
3.2.493:
I shall be off. Do you wait for her.
PARMENO
It is not a proper thing for a general to be walking in the street with a mistress.
THRASO
3.2.495:
Why should I use many words with you? You are the very ape of your master.
(Exit PARMENO.)
GNATHO
(laughing.)
3.2.496:
Ha, ha, ha!
THRASO
What are you laughing at?
GNATHO
At what you were mentioning just now; that saying, too, about the Rhodian, recurred to my mind. But Thais is coming out.
THRASO
3.2.498:
You go before; take care that every thing is ready at home.
GNATHO
3.2.499:
Very well.
(Exit.)
THAIS
(Re-enter THAIS, with PYTHIAS and FEMALE ATTENDANTS.)
Take care, Pythias,
3.2.500:
and be sure that if Chremes should happen to come, to beg him to wait; if that is not convenient, then to come again; if he can not do that, bring him to me.
PYTHIAS
3.2.505:
be sure that you keep at home.
THRASO
Let us begone.
THAIS
(to her attendants.)
You follow me.
(Exeunt THAIS and THRASO, followed by the Attendants. PYTHIAS goes into the house.)

3.3.506:
(Enter CHREMES.) CHREMES
(to himself.)
Why, really, the more and more I think of it, I shouldn’t be surprised if this Thais should be doing me some great mischief; so cunningly do I perceive myself beset by her. Even on the occasion when she first requested me to be fetched to her
3.3.510: (any one might ask me, What business had you with her? Really I don’t know.) When I came, she found an excuse for me to remain there; she said that she had been offering a sacrifice, and that she was desirous to speak upon some important business with me. Even then I had a suspicion that all these things were being done for her artful purposes. She takes her place beside
3.3.515: me; pays every attention to me; seeks and opportunity of conversation. When the conversation flagged, she turned off to this point—how long since my father and mother died? I said that it was now a long time ago. Whether I had any country-house at Sunium, and how far from the sea? I suppose that this has taken her fancy, and she expects to get it away from me.
3.3.520: Then at last, whether any little sister of mine had been lost from there; whether any person was with her; what she had about her when she was lost; whether any one could recognize her. Why should she make these inquiries? Unless, perhaps, she pretends—so great is her assurance—that she herself is the same person that was formerly lost when a little girl.
3.3.525: But if she is alive, she is sixteen years old, not older; whereas Thais is somewhat older than I am. She has sent to press me earnestly to come. Either let her speak out what she wants, or not be troublesome; I assuredly shall not come a third time (knocking at the door of THAIS). Ho! there, ho! there! Is any one here?
3.3.530:
It’s I, Chremes.
(Enter PYTHIAS from the house.)
PYTHIAS
O most charming, dear creature!
CHREMES
(apart.)
3.3.531:
I said there was a design upon me.
PYTHIAS
Thais entreated you most earnestly to come again to-morrow.
CHREMES
3.3.532:
I’m going into the country.
PYTHIAS
3.3.533:
Do, there’s a dear sir.
CHREMES
I can not, I tell you.
PYTHIAS
Then stay here at our house till she comes back.
CHREMES
3.3.534:
Nothing less likely.
PYTHIAS
Why, my dear Chremes?
(Taking hold of him.)
CHREMES
(shaking her off.)
3.3.535:
Away to perdition with you!
PYTHIAS
If you are so determined about it, pray do step over to the place where she is.
CHREMES
3.3.536:
I’ll go there.
PYTHIAS
(calling at the door.)
3.3.537:
Here, Dorias (DORIAS enters), show this person directly to the Captain’s.
(Exit CHREMES with DORIAS, PYTHIAS goes into the house.)

3.4.540: our rings were given as pledges; the place and time arranged. The time has now gone by; at the place appointed there was nothing ready. The fellow himself is nowhere to be met with; I neither know what to say nor what to suppose. Now the rest have commissioned me with his business, to look for him. I’ll go see, therefore, if he’s at home. But who’s this, I wonder, coming out of Thais’s?
3.4.545:
Is it he, or is it not? ’Tis the very man! What sort of being is this? What kind of garb is this? What mischief is going on now? I can not sufficiently wonder or conjecture. But, whatever it is, I should like first at a distance to try and find out.
(He stands apart.)

3.5.548:
(Enter CHAEREA from the house of Thais, in the EUNUCH’s dress.) CHAEREA
(looking around, then aloud to himself.)
Is there any body here? There’s no one. Is there any one following me from there? There’s not a person. Now am I not at liberty to give vent to these raptures? O supreme Jupiter!
3.5.550: now assuredly is the time for me to meet my death, when I can so well endure it; lest my life should sully this ecstasy with some disaster. But is there now no inquisitive person to be intruding upon me, to be following me wherever I do, to be deafening me, worrying me to death, with asking questions; why thus transported, or why so overjoyed, whither I’m going, whence I’m come, where
3.5.555:
I got this garb, what is my object, whether I’m in my senses or whether downright mad?
ANTIPHO
(apart.)
3.5.556:
I’ll accost him, and I’ll do him the favor which I see he’s wishing for. (Accosting him.) Chaerea, why are you thus transported? What’s the object of this garb? Why is it that you’re so overjoyed? What is the meaning of this? Are you quite right in your senses? Why do you stare at me? What have you to say?
CHAEREA
3.5.559: O joyous day! O welcome, my friend!
3.5.560:
There’s not one in all the world whom I would rather wish to see at this moment that yourself.
ANTIPHO
3.5.561:
Pray, do tell me what all this means.
CHAEREA
Nay rather, i’faith, I beg of you to listen to me. Do you know the mistress whom my brother is so fond of?
ANTIPHO
3.5.562:
I know her; I suppose you mean Thais?
CHAEREA
3.5.563:
The very same.
ANTIPHO
So far I recollect.
CHAEREA
To-day a certain damsel was presented to her. Why now should I extol or commend her beauty to you, Antipho,
3.5.565:
since you yourself know how nice a judge of beauty I am? I have been smitten by her.
ANTIPHO
3.5.566:
Do you say so?
CHAEREA
If you saw her, I am sure you would say she’s exquisite. What need of many words? I fell in love with her. By good luck there was at our house a certain Eunuch, whom my brother had purchased for Thais, and he had not as yet been sent to her. On this occasion, Parmeno,
3.5.570:
our servant, made a suggestion to me, which I adopted.
ANTIPHO
What was it?
CHAEREA
Be quiet, and you shall hear the sooner; to change clothes with him, and order myself to be taken there in his stead.
ANTIPHO
3.5.572:
What, instead of the Eunuch?
CHAEREA
The fact.
ANTIPHO
To receive what advantage, pray, from this plan?
CHAEREA
3.5.573: Do you ask? That I might see, hear, and be in company with her whom I loved, Antipho. Is that a slight motive, or a poor reason? I was presented to the woman.
3.5.575:
She, as soon as she received me, joyfully took me home to her house and intrusted the damsel—
ANTIPHO
3.5.576:
To whom? To you?
CHAEREA
To me.
ANTIPHO
(ironically.)
In perfect safety, at all events.
CHAEREA
3.5.577:
She gave orders that no male was to come near her, and commanded me not to stir away from her; that I was to remain alone with her in the inner apartments. Looking bashfully on the ground, I nodded assent.
ANTIPHO
(ironically.)
3.5.579:
Poor fellow!
CHAEREA
(continuing.)
I am going out, said she, to dinner.
3.5.580: She took her maids with her; a few novices of girls remained, to be about her. These immediately made preparations for her to bathe. I urged them to make haste. While preparations were being made, the damsel sat in a room looking up at a certain painting, in which was represented how Jove is said once to have sent a golden shower into the bosom of Danaë.
3.5.585: I myself began to look at it as well, and as he had in former times played the like game, I felt extremely delighted that a God should change himself into money, and slily come through the tiles of another person’s house, to deceive the fair one by means of a shower. But what God was this? He who shakes the most lofty temples of heaven with his thunders.
3.5.590: Was I, a poor creature of a mortal, not to do the same? Certainly, I was to do it, and without hesitation. While I was thinking over these matters with myself, the damsel meantime was fetched away to bathe; she went, bathed, and came back; after which they laid her on a couch. I stood waiting to see if they gave me any orders. One came up, Here, Dorus, said she, take this fan, and let her have a little air in this fashion, while we are bathing;
3.5.595:
when we have bathed, if you like, you may bathe too. With a demure air I took it.
ANTIPHO
3.5.596:
Really, I should very much have liked to see that impudent face of yours just then, and what figure a great donkey like you made, holding a fan!
CHAEREA
(continuing.)
3.5.598: Hardly had she said this, when all, in a moment, betook themselves off: away they went to bathe, and chattered aloud; just as the way is when masters are absent.
3.5.600:
Meanwhile, sleep overtook the damsel; I slily looked askance through the fan; this way (showing how): at the same time I looked round in all directions, to see whether all was quite safe. I saw that it was. I bolted the door.
ANTIPHO
3.5.603:
What then?
CHAEREA
Eh? What then, you simpleton?
ANTIPHO
I own I am.
CHAEREA
Was I to let slip the opportunity offered me, so excellent, so short-lived, so longed for, so unexpected.
3.5.605:
In that case, i’faith, I really should have been the person I was pretending to be.
ANTIPHO
3.5.606:
Troth, you certainly are in the right; but, meantime, what has been arranged about the club-entertainment?
CHAEREA
3.5.607:
All’s ready.
ANTIPHO
You are a clever hand; but where? At your house?
CHAEREA
No, at Discus’s, our freedman.
ANTIPHO
3.5.608:
That’s a long way off.
CHAEREA
Then let’s make so much the greater haste.
ANTIPHO
Change your dress.
CHAEREA
3.5.609: Where am I to change it? I’m at a loss; for at present I’m an exile from home; I’m afraid of my brother,
3.5.610:
lest he should be in-doors: and then again of my father, lest he should have returned from the country by this.
ANTIPHO
3.5.611:
Let’s go to my house; there is the nearest place for you to change.
CHAEREA
You say right. Let’s be off; besides, I want to take counsel with you about this girl, by what means I may be able to secure the future possession of her.
ANTIPHO

4.1.614:
(Enter DORIAS, with a casket in her hand.) DORIAS
(to herself.)
So may the Gods bless me, but from what I have seen, I’m terribly afraid that
4.1.615: this mad fellow will be guilty of some disturbance to-day or of some violence to Thais. For when this young man, the brother of the damsel, arrived, she begged the Captain to order him to be admitted; he immediately began to get into a passion, and yet didn’t dare refuse; Thais still insisted that he would invite the man in. This she did for the sake of detaining him; because there was no opportunity just then of telling him what she wanted to disclose about her sister.
4.1.621: He was invited in, and took his seat. Then she entered into discourse with him. But the Captain, fancying it was a rival brought before his very eyes, wanted in his turn to mortify her: Hark you, boy, said he, go fetch Pamphila, that she may amuse us here. She exclaimed, At a banquet! Certainly not. The Captain still persisted to a downright quarrel.
4.1.626:
Meanwhile my mistress secretly took off her golden jewels, and gave them to me to take away: this is a sign, I’m sure, that she’ll betake herself from there as soon as she possibly can.
(Goes into the house.)

4.2.628:
(Enter PHAEDRIA.) PHAEDRIA
(to himself.)
While I was going into the country, I began on the road, as it mostly happens when there is any anxiety on the mind,
4.2.630: to reflect with myself upon one thing after another, and upon every thing in the worst light. What need of words? While I was musing thus, inadvertently I passed my country-house. I had already got some distance from it, when I perceived this; I returned again, really feeling quite uneasy; when I came to the very turning that leads to the house, I came to a stop,
4.2.635: and began to reason with myself; What! must I stay here alone for two days without her? Well, and what then? It’s nothing at all. What? Nothing at all? Well now, if I haven't the privilege of touching her, am I not even to have that of seeing her? If I may not do the one, at least I may the other. Surely to love at a distance
4.2.640:
even, is better than nothing at all. I purposely passed the house. But how’s this, that Pythias is suddenly hurrying out in such a fright?
(Stands apart.)

4.3.642:
(Enter PYTHIAS and DORIAS in haste from the house of THAIS.) PYTHIAS
(aloud.)
Where, wretch that I am, shall I find this wicked and impious fellow? Or where look for him? That he should dare to commit so audacious a crime as this! I’m ruined outright!
PHAEDRIA
(apart.)
4.3.643:
I dread what this may be.
PYTHIAS
4.3.644: Besides, too, the villain, after he had abused the girl,
4.3.645:
rent all the poor thing’s clothes, and tore her hair as well.
PHAEDRIA
(apart, in surprise.)
4.3.646:
Ha!
PYTHIAS
If he were just now in my reach, how eagerly would I fly at that villain’s eyes with my nails!
PHAEDRIA
(apart.)
4.3.648:
Really I can’t imagine what disturbance has happened to us at home in my absence. I’ll accost them. (Going up to them.) What’s the matter? Why in such haste? Or whom are you looking for, Pythias?
PYTHIAS
4.3.650:
Why, Phaedria, whom should I be looking for? Away with you, as you deserve, with such fine presents of yours.
PHAEDRIA
4.3.652:
What, do you ask? The Eunuch you gave us, what confusion he has caused. He has ravished the girl whom the Captain made present of to my mistress.
PHAEDRIA
4.3.653:
What is it you say?
PYTHIAS
4.3.654:
I’m ruined outright!
PHAEDRIA
You are drunk.
PYTHIAS
I wish that they were so, who wish ill to me.
DORIAS
4.3.655:
Oh, prithee, my dear Pythias, what a monstrous thing this is!
PHAEDRIA
4.3.656:
You are out of your senses. How could a Eunuch possibly do this?
PYTHIAS
I know nothing about him: as to what he has done, the thing speaks for itself. The girl is in tears; and when you ask her what’s the matter, she does not dare tell. But he, a precious fellow, is nowhere to be seen. To my sorrow I suspect too,
4.3.660:
that when he took himself off he carried something away from the house.
PHAEDRIA
I can not enough wonder, whither this varlet can possibly have betaken himself to any distance from here; unless perhaps he has returned home to our house.
PYTHIAS
4.3.662:
Pray, go and see whether he is there.
PHAEDRIA
I’ll let you know immediately.
(Goes into the house of LACHES.)
DORIAS
4.3.663:
Ruined outright! Prithee, my dear, I never did so much as hear of a deed so abominable!
PYTHIAS
4.3.664: Why, faith, I had heard that they were extremely fond of the women,
4.3.665: but were incapable; unfortunately what has happened never came into my mind; otherwise I should have shut him up somewhere, and not have intrusted the girl to him.

4.4.667:
(Enter PHAEDRIA from the house of LACHES, with DORUS in CHAEREA’s clothes.) PHAEDRIA
(dragging him out.)
Come out, you villain! What, do you lag behind, you runaway? Out with you, you sorry bargain!
DORUS
(crying out.)
4.4.668:
Mercy, I do entreat you!
PHAEDRIA
Oh, do look at that! How the villain distorts his face.
4.4.670:
What means your coming back hither? Why this change of dress? What have you to say? If I had delayed a moment, Pythias, I shouldn’t have found him at home: he had just prepared, in this fashion, for flight.
(Pointing at his dress.)
PYTHIAS
4.4.673:
Have you caught the fellow, pray?
PHAEDRIA
Caught him, why not?
PYTHIAS
O well done!
DORIAS
4.4.674:
Upon my faith that really is capital!
PYTHIAS
Where is he?
PHAEDRIA
Do you ask the question? Don’t you see him?
(Pointing to the EUNUCH.)
PYTHIAS
(staring about.)
4.4.675:
See whom, pray?
PHAEDRIA
This fellow, to be sure (pointing).
PYTHIAS
What person is this?
PHAEDRIA
4.4.676:
The same that was brought to your house to-day.
PYTHIAS
Not one of our people has ever beheld this person with her eyes, Phaedria.
PHAEDRIA
4.4.678:
Not beheld him?
PYTHIAS
Prithee, did you fancy that this was he who was brought to our house?
PHAEDRIA
4.4.679:
Why, I had no other.
PYTHIAS
O dear!
4.4.680:
this one really isn’t to be compared with the other. He was of a handsome and genteel appearance.
PHAEDRIA
4.4.681:
He seemed so, just then, because he was decked out in party-colored clothes: now he appears ugly, for this reason—because he hasn’t got them on.
PYTHIAS
4.4.684: Prithee, do hold your tongue; as though indeed the difference was so trifling.
4.4.685:
A young man was brought to our house to-day, whom, really, Phaedria, you would have liked to look upon. This is a withered, antiquated, lethargic, old fellow, with a speckled complexion.
PHAEDRIA
(starting.)
4.4.688: Hah! What tale is this? You’ll so befool me that I sha’n’t know what I bought.
4.4.690:
(To DORUS.) How now, sirrah, did I not buy you?
DORUS
You did buy me.
PYTHIAS
Bid him answer me in my turn.
PHAEDRIA
4.4.691:
Question him.
PYTHIAS
(to DORUS.)
Did you come here to-day to our house? (DORUS shakes his head.) He says, no. But it was the other one that came, about sixteen years of age; whom Parmeno brought with him.
PHAEDRIA
(to DORUS.)
4.4.693: Well now, in the first place tell me this, where did you get that dress that you have on? What, are you silent?
4.4.695:
Monster of a fellow, are you not going to speak?
(Shakes him.)
DORUS
Chaerea came.
PHAEDRIA
4.4.696:
What, my brother?
DORUS
Yes.
PHAEDRIA
When?
DORUS
To-day.
PHAEDRIA
How long since?
DORUS
Just now.
PHAEDRIA
4.4.697:
With whom?
DORUS
With Parmeno.
PHAEDRIA
Did you know him before?
DORUS
4.4.699:
How did you know he was my brother?
DORUS
Parmeno
4.4.700:
said he was. He gave me these clothes.
PHAEDRIA
I’m undone!
DORUS
4.4.701:
He himself put on mine; afterward, they both went out together.
PYTHIAS
4.4.702:
Now are you quite satisfied that I am sober, and that we have told you no falsehood? Is it now sufficiently evident that the girl has been ravished?
PHAEDRIA
4.4.703:
Avaunt, you beast, do you believe what he says?
PYTHIAS
4.4.704:
What is there to believe? The thing speaks for itself.
PHAEDRIA
(apart to DORUS.)
4.4.705:
Step aside a little this way. Do you hear? (DORUS steps aside.) A little further still. That will do. Now tell me this once more; did Chaerea take your clothes off you?
DORUS
4.4.707:
He did.
PHAEDRIA
And did he put them on?
DORUS
He did.
PHAEDRIA
And was he brought here instead of you?
DORUS
Yes.
PHAEDRIA
4.4.708:
Great Jupiter! O wicked and audacious fellow!
PYTHIAS
Woe unto me! Now at last will you believe that we have been insulted in a disgraceful manner?
PHAEDRIA
4.4.710:
It is no wonder that you believe what the fellow says. (Aside.) What I’m to do I know not. (Aside to DORUS.) Hark you, deny it all again. (Aloud.) Can I not this day extract the truth from you? Did you really see my brother Chaerea?
DORUS
4.4.712:
No.
PHAEDRIA
He can’t be brought to confess without being punished, I see: follow me this way. At one moment he affirms, at another denies. (Aside.) Ask pardon of me.
DORUS
4.4.714:
Indeed, I do entreat you, Phaedria.
PHAEDRIA
(kicking him.)
Be off in-doors.
DORUS
Oh! oh!
PHAEDRIA
(aside.)
4.4.715:
How in any other fashion to get decently out of this I don’t know; for really it’s all up with me. (Aloud, with pretended indignation.) Will you be trifling with me even here, you knave?
(Follows DORUS into the house.)
PYTHIAS
4.4.717:
I’m as certain that this is the contrivance of Parmeno as that I’m alive.
DORIAS
4.4.718:
So it is, no doubt.
PYTHIAS
I’faith, I’ll find out a method to-day to be even with him. But now, what do you think ought to be done, Dorias?
DORIAS
4.4.719: Do you mean with regard to this
4.4.720:
girl?
PYTHIAS
Yes; whether I ought to mention it or be silent?
DORIAS
4.4.721:
Upon my word, if you are prudent, you won’t know what you do know, either about the Eunuch or the girl’s misfortune. By this method you’ll both rid yourself of all perplexity, and have done a service to her. Say this only, that Dorus has run away.
PYTHIAS
4.4.723:
I’ll do so.
DORIAS
But don’t I see Chremes? Thais will be here just now.
PYTHIAS
4.4.724:
Why so?
DORIAS
Because when I came away from there, a quarrel had just commenced between them.
PYTHIAS
4.4.725:
Take in these golden trinkets; I shall learn from him what’s the matter.
(DORIAS takes the casket into the house.)

4.5.726:
(Enter CHREMES, somewhat drunk.) CHREMES
Heyday! upon my faith, I’ve been bamboozled: the wine that I’ve drunk has got the upper hand. But, so long as I was reclining, how extremely sober I did seem to myself to be; when I got up, neither feet nor senses were quite equal to their duty.
PYTHIAS
4.5.729:
Chremes!
CHREMES
(turning round.)
Who’s that? What, Pythias; dear me, how much more charming you now
4.5.730:
seem to me than a short time since!
PYTHIAS
Troth now, you are much more merry, that’s certain.
CHREMES
4.5.731:
Upon my faith, it is a true saying, that Venus grows cold without Ceres and Bacchus. But has Thais got here long before me?
PYTHIAS
4.5.732:
Has she already come away from the Captain’s?
CHREMES
4.5.733:
A long time ago; an age since. There has been a most violent quarrel between them.
PYTHIAS
4.5.734:
Did she say nothing about you following her?
CHREMES
Nothing at all; only, on going away, she gave me a nod.
PYTHIAS
4.5.735:
Well now, wasn’t that enough?
CHREMES
Why, I didn’t know that she meant that, until the Captain gave me an explanation, because I was dull of comprehension; for he bundled me out of the house. But look, here she is; I wonder how it was I got here before her.

4.6.738:
(Enter THAIS.) THAIS
(to herself.)
I really do believe that he’ll be here presently, to force her away from me. Let him come; but if he touches her with a single finger, that instant his eyes shall be torn out.
4.6.740:
I can put up with his impertinences and his high-sounding words, as long as they remain words: but if they are turned into realities, he shall get a drubbing.
CHREMES
4.6.742:
Thais, I’ve been here some time.
THAIS
O my dear Chremes, you are the very person I was wanting. Are you aware that this quarrel took place on your account, and that the whole of this affair, in fact, bore reference to yourself?
CHREMES
4.6.744:
To me? How so, pray?
THAIS
Because, while I’ve been doing my best
4.6.745:
to recover and restore your sister to you, this and a great deal more like it I’ve had to put up with.
CHREMES
4.6.746:
Where is she?
THAIS
At home, at my house.
CHREMES
(starting.)
Hah!
THAIS
4.6.747:
What’s the matter? She has been brought up in a manner worthy of yourself and of her.
CHREMES
What is it you say?
THAIS
That which is the fact. Her I present to you, nor do I ask of you any return for her.
CHREMES
4.6.749:
Thanks are both felt and shall be returned in such way, Thais, as you deserve.
THAIS
4.6.750:
