But still, take care, Chremes, that you don’t lose her, before you receive her from me; for it is she, whom the Captain is now coming to take away from me by force. Do you go, Pythias, and bring out of the house the casket with the tokens.
CHREMES
(looking down the side Scene.)
4.6.753:
Don’t you see him, Thais?
PYTHIAS
(to THAIS.)
Where is it put?
THAIS
In the clothes’ chest. Tiresome creature, why do you delay?
(PYTHIAS goes into the house.)
CHREMES
4.6.754: What a large body of troops the Captain is bringing with him against you.
4.6.755:
Bless me!
THAIS
Prithee, are you frightened, my dear sir?
CHREMES
Get out with you. What, I frightened? There’s not a man alive less so.
THAIS
4.6.757:
Then now is the time to prove it.
CHREMES
Why, I wonder what sort of a man you take me to be.
THAIS
4.6.758:
Nay, and consider this too; the person that you have to deal with is a foreigner; of less influence than you, less known, and one that has fewer friends here.
CHREMES
4.6.760:
I’m aware of that; but it’s foolish to run the risk of what you are able to avoid. I had rather we should prevent it, than, having received an injury, avenge ourselves upon him. Do you go in and fasten the door, while I run across hence to the Forum; I should like us to have the aid of some legal adviser in this disturbance.
(Moves, as if going.)
THAIS
(holding him.)
4.6.764:
Let me go, I’ll be here presently.
THAIS
There’s no occasion, Chremes.
4.6.765:
Only say that she is your sister, and that you lost her when a little girl, and have now recognized her; then show the tokens.
(Re-enter PYTHIAS from the house, with the trinkets.)
PYTHIAS
(giving them to THAIS.)
4.6.766:
Here they are.
THAIS
(giving them to CHREMES.)
Take them. If he offers any violence, summon the fellow to justice; do you understand me?
CHREMES
4.6.768:
Take care and say this with presence of mind.
CHREMES
I’ll take care.
THAIS
Gather up your cloak. (Aside.) Undone! the very person whom I’ve provided as a champion, wants one himself.
(They all go into the house.)

4.7.770:
(Enter THRASO, followed by GNATHO, SANGA, and other Attendants.) THRASO
Am I to submit, Gnatho, to such a glaring affront as this being put upon me? I’d die sooner. Simalio, Donax, Syriscus, follow me! First, I’ll storm the house.
GNATHO
4.7.772:
Quite right.
THRASO
I’ll carry off the girl.
GNATHO
Very good.
THRASO
4.7.773:
I’ll give her own self a mauling.
GNATHO
Very proper.
THRASO
(arranging the men.)
Advance hither to the main body, Donax, with your crowbar; you, Simalio, to the left wing; you, Syriscus, to the right.
4.7.775:
Bring up the rest; where’s the centurion Sanga, and his maniple of rogues?
SANGA
(coming forward.)
See, here he is.
THRASO
4.7.776:
What, you booby, do you think of fighting with a dish-clout, to be bringing that here?
SANGA
4.7.777:
What, I? I knew the valor of the general, and the prowess of the soldiers; and that this could not possibly go on without bloodshed; how was I to wipe the wounds?
THRASO
4.7.779:
Where are the others?
SANGA
Plague on you, what others? Sannio is the only one left on guard at home.
THRASO
(to GNATHO.)
4.7.780:
Do you draw up your men in battle order; I’ll be behind the second rank; from that position I’ll give the word to all.
(Takes his place behind the second rank.)
GNATHO
(aside.)
4.7.781:
That’s showing prudence; as soon as he has drawn them up, he secures a retreat for himself.
THRASO
(pointing to the arrangements.)
4.7.782:
This is just the way Pyrrhus used to proceed.
(CHREMES and THAIS appear above at a window.)
CHREMES
Do you see, Thais, what plan he is upon? Assuredly, that advice of mine about closing the door was good.
THAIS
4.7.784: He who now seems to you to be a hero, is in reality a mere vaporer;
4.7.785:
don’t be alarmed.
THRASO
(to GNATHO.)
What seems best to you?
GNATHO
I could very much like a sling to be given you just now, that you might pelt them from here on the sly at a distance; they would be taking to flight.
THRASO
(to GNATHO.)
4.7.787:
But look (pointing), I see Thais there herself.
GNATHO
How soon are we to fall to?
THRASO
Hold (holding him back); it behooves a prudent person to make trial of every thing before arms. How do you know but that she may do what I bid her without compulsion?
GNATHO
4.7.789: Ye Gods, by our trust in you,
4.7.790:
what a thing it is to be wise! I never come near you but what I go away from you the wiser.
THRASO
4.7.791:
Thais, in the first place, answer me this. When I presented you that girl, did you not say that you would give yourself up to me alone for some days to come?
THAIS
4.7.793: Do you ask the question? You, who have been and brought your lover under my very eyes?
4.7.794:
What business had you with him?
With him, too, you clandestinely betook yourself away from me.
THAIS
4.7.795:
I chose to do so.
THRASO
Then give me back Pamphila; unless you had rather she were taken away by force.
CHREMES
4.7.796:
Give her back to you, or you lay hands upon her? Of all the—
GNATHO
Ha! What are you about? Hold your tongue.
THRASO
4.7.797:
What do you mean? Am I not to touch my own?
CHREMES
Your own, indeed, you gallows-bird!
GNATHO
(to CHREMES.)
4.7.798:
Have a care, if you please. You don’t know what kind of man you are abusing now.
CHREMES
(to GNATHO.)
Won’t you be off from here? Do you know how matters stand with you? If you cause any disturbance here to-day,
4.7.800:
I’ll make you remember the place, and day, and me too, for the rest of your life.
GNATHO
4.7.801:
I pity you, who are making so great a man as this your enemy.
CHREMES
4.7.802:
I’ll break your head this instant if you are not off.
GNATHO
Do you really say so, puppy? Is it that you are at?
THRASO
(to CHREMES.)
4.7.803:
What fellow are you? What do you mean? What business have you with her?
CHREMES
4.7.804:
I’ll let you know: in the first place, I assert that she is a freeborn woman.
THRASO
(starting.)
Ha!
CHREMES
A citizen of Attica.
THRASO
Whew!
CHREMES
4.7.805:
My own sister.
THRASO
Brazen face!
CHREMES
Now, therefore, Captain, I give you warning; don’t you use any violence toward her. Thais, I’m going to Sophrona, the nurse, that I may bring her here and show her these tokens.
THRASO
4.7.807:
What! Are you to prevent me from touching what’s my own?
CHREMES
4.7.808:
I will prevent it, I tell you.
GNATHO
(to THRASO.)
Do you hear him? He is convicting himself of theft. Is not that enough for you?
THRASO
4.7.809:
Do you say the same, Thais?
THAIS
Go, find some one to answer you.
(She and CHREMES go away from the window.)
THRASO
(to GNATHO.)
4.7.810:
What are we to do now?
GNATHO
Why, go back again: she’ll soon be with you, of her own accord, to entreat forgiveness.
THRASO
4.7.811:
Do you think so?
GNATHO
Certainly, yes. I know the disposition of women: when you will, they won’t; when you won’t, they set their hearts upon you of their own inclination.
THRASO
4.7.813:
Shall I dismiss the army then?
THRASO
Whenever you like.
GNATHO
Sanga, as befits gallant soldiers, take care in your turn to remember your homes and hearths.
SANGA
4.7.815:
My thoughts have been for some time among the sauce-pans.
GNATHO
You are a worthy fellow.
THRASO
(putting himself at their head.)
You follow me this way.
(Exeunt omnes.)

5.1.816:
(Enter THAIS from her house, followed by PYTHIAS.) THAIS
What! do you persist, hussy, in talking ambiguously to me? I do know; I don’t know; he has gone off; I have heard; I wasn’t there. Don’t you mean to tell me plainly, whatever it is? The girl in tears, with her garments torn, is mute;
5.1.820:
the Eunuch is off: for what reason? What has happened? Won’t you speak?
PYTHIAS
5.1.821:
Wretch that I am, what am I to say to you? They declare that he was not a Eunuch.
THAIS
5.1.822:
What was he then?
PYTHIAS
That Chaerea.
THAIS
5.1.823:
What Chaerea?
PYTHIAS
That stripling, the brother of Phaedria.
THAIS
5.1.824:
What’s that you say, you hag?
PYTHIAS
And I am satisfied of it.
THAIS
5.1.825:
Pray, what business had he at my house? What brought him there?
PYTHIAS
I don’t know; unless, as I suppose, he was in love with Pamphila.
THAIS
5.1.826:
Alas! to my confusion, unhappy woman that I am, I’m undone, if what you tell me is true. Is it about this that the girl is crying?
PYTHIAS
5.1.828:
I believe so.
THAIS
How say you, you arch-jade? Did I not warn you about this very thing, when I was going away from here?
PYTHIAS
5.1.830:
What could I do? Just as you ordered, she was intrusted to his care only.
THAIS
5.1.831:
Hussy, I’ve been intrusting the sheep to the wolf. I’m quite ashamed to have been imposed upon in this way. What sort of man was he?
PYTHIAS
5.1.833:
Hush! hush! mistress, pray; we are all right. Here we have the very man.
THAIS
5.1.834:
Where is he?
PYTHIAS
Why there, to the left.
5.1.835:
Don’t you see?
THAIS
I see.
PYTHIAS
Order him to be seized as quickly as possible.
THAIS
5.1.836:
What can we do to him, simpleton?
PYTHIAS
What do to him, do you ask? Pray, do look at him; if his face doesn’t seem an impudent one.
THAIS
5.1.838:
Not at all.
PYTHIAS
Besides, what effrontery he has.

5.2.839:
(Enter CHAEREA, in the EUNUCH’s dress, on the other side of the stage.) CHAEREA
(to himself.)
At Antipho’s, both of them, father and mother,
5.2.840: just as if on purpose, were at home, so that I couldn’t any way get in, but that they must have seen me. In the mean time, while I was standing before the door, a certain acquaintance of mine was coming full upon me. When I espied him, I took to my heels as fast as I could down a narrow unfrequented alley; thence again
5.2.845:
to another, and thence to another; thus have I been most dreadfully harassed with running about, that no one might recognize me. But isn’t this Thais that I see? It is she. I’m at a stand. What shall I do? But what need I care? What can she do to me?
THAIS
(to PYTHIAS.)
5.2.849: Let’s accost him. (To CHAEREA.) Good Mister Dorus, welcome; tell me,
5.2.850:
have you been running away?
CHAEREA
Madam, I did so.
THAIS
Are you quite pleased with it?
CHAEREA
5.2.851:
No.
THAIS
Do you fancy that you’ll get off with impunity?
CHAEREA
Forgive this one fault; if I’m ever guilty of another, then kill me.
THAIS
5.2.853:
Were you in fear of my severity?
CHAEREA
No.
THAIS
No? What then?
CHAEREA
(pointing at PYTHIAS.)
5.2.854:
I was afraid of her, lest she might be accusing me to you.
THAIS
5.2.855:
What had you done?
CHAEREA
A mere trifle.
PYTHIAS
Come now, a trifle, you impudent fellow. Does this appear a trifle to you, to ravish a virgin, a citizen?
CHAEREA
5.2.857:
I took her for my fellow-servant.
PYTHIAS
5.2.858:
Fellow-servant? I can hardly restrain myself from flying at his hair. A miscreant! Even of his own free will he comes to make fun of us.
THAIS
(to PYTHIAS.)
5.2.860:
Won’t you begone from here, you mad woman?
PYTHIAS
Why so? Really, I do believe I should be something in this hang-dog’s debt, if I were to do so; especially as he owns that he is your servant.
THAIS
5.2.863: We’ll pass that by. Chaerea, you have behaved unworthily of yourself; for if I am deserving in the highest degree of this affront,
5.2.865: still it is unbecoming of you to be guilty of it. And, upon my faith, I do not know what method now to adopt about this girl: you have so confounded all my plans, that I can not possibly return her to her friends in such a manner as is befitting and as I had intended;
5.2.870:
in order that, by this means, I might, Chaerea, do a real service to myself.
CHAEREA
5.2.871:
But now, from henceforth, I hope, Thais, that there will be lasting good-will between us. Many a time, from some affair of this kind and from a bad beginning, great friendships have sprung up. What if some Divinity has willed this?
THAIS
5.2.875:
I’faith, for my own part I both take it in that view and wish to do so.
CHAEREA
5.2.876:
Yes, prithee, do so. Be sure of this one thing, that I did not do it for the sake of affronting you, but in consequence of passion.
THAIS
5.2.877: I understand, and, i’faith, for that reason do I now the more readily forgive you. I am not, Chaerea, of a disposition so ungentle, or so inexperienced,
5.2.880:
as not to know what is the power of love.
CHAEREA
5.2.881:
So may the Deities kindly bless me, Thais; I am now smitten with you as well.
PYTHIAS
5.2.882:
Then, i’faith, mistress, I foresee you must have a care of him.
CHAEREA
5.2.883:
I would not dare—
PYTHIAS
I won’t trust you at all in any thing.
THAIS
(to PYTHIAS.)
Do have done.
CHAEREA
5.2.884: Now I entreat you that you will be my assistant in this affair.
5.2.885:
I intrust and commit myself to your care; I take you, Thais, as my protectress; I implore you; I shall die if I don’t have her for my wife.
THAIS
5.2.888:
But if your father should say any thing—
CHAEREA
Oh, he’ll consent, I’m quite sure of that, if she is only a citizen.
THAIS
5.2.889: If you will wait a little,
5.2.890:
the brother himself of the young woman will be here presently; he has gone to fetch the nurse, who brought her up when a little child; you yourself, shall be present Chaerea, at his recognition of her.
CHAEREA
5.2.893:
I certainly will stay.
THAIS
In the mean time, until he comes, would you prefer that we should wait for him in the house, rather than here before the door?
CHAEREA
5.2.895:
Why yes, I should like it much.
PYTIH.
(to THAIS.)
Prithee, what are you going to do?
THAIS
5.2.896:
Why, what’s the matter?
PYTHIAS
Do you ask? Do you think of admitting him after this into your house?
THAIS
5.2.897:
Why not?
PYTHIAS
Trust my word for it, he’ll be creating some new disturbance.
THAIS
5.2.898:
O dear, prithee, do hold your tongue.
PYTHIAS
5.2.899:
You seem to me to be far from sensible of his assurance.
CHAEREA
5.2.900:
I’ll not do any thing, Pythias.
PYTHIAS
Upon my faith, I don’t believe you, Chaerea, except in case you are not trusted.
CHAEREA
5.2.901:
Nay but, Pythias, do you be my keeper.
PYTHIAS
5.2.902:
Upon my faith, I would neither venture to give any thing to you to keep, nor to keep you myself: away with you!
THAIS
5.2.904:
Most opportunely the brother himself is coming.
CHAEREA
I’faith, I’m undone. Prithee,
5.2.905:
let’s be gone in-doors, Thais. I don’t want him to see me in the street with this dress on.
THAIS
5.2.906:
For what reason, pray? Because you are ashamed?
CHAEREA
5.2.907:
Just so.
PYTHIAS
Just so? But the young woman—
THAIS
Go first; I’ll follow. You stay here, Pythias, that you may show Chremes in.
(THAIS and CHAEREA go into the house.)

5.3.909:
(Enter CHREMES and SOPHRONA.) PYTHIAS
(to herself.)
Well! what now can suggest itself to my mind?
5.3.910:
What, I wonder, in order that I may repay the favor to that villain who palmed this fellow off upon us?
CHREMES
5.3.911:
Really, do bestir yourself more quickly, nurse.
SOPHRONA
5.3.912:
I am bestirring.
CHREMES
So I see; but you don’t stir forward.
PYTHIAS
(to CHREMES.)
5.3.913:
Have you yet shown the tokens to the nurse?
CHREMES
All of them.
PYTHIAS
5.3.914:
Prithee, what does she say? Does she recognize them?
CHREMES
Yes, with a full recollection of them.
PYTHIAS
5.3.915: Upon my faith, you do bring good news; for I really wish well to this young woman. Go in-doors: my mistress has been for some time expecting you at home. (CHREMES and SOPHRONA go into THAIS’s house.) But look, yonder I espy that worthy fellow, Parmeno, coming: just see, for heaven’s sake, how leisurely he moves along. I hope I have it in my power to torment him after my own fashion.
5.3.920:
I’ll go in-doors, that I may know for certain about the discovery; afterward I’ll come out, and give this villain a terrible fright.
(Goes into the house.)

5.4.922:
(Enter PARMENO.) PARMENO
(to himself.)
I’ve just come back to see what Chaerea has been doing here. If he has managed the affair with dexterity, ye Gods, by our trust in you, how great and genuine applause will Parmeno obtain!
5.4.925: For not to mention that a passion, full of difficulty and expense, with which he was smitten for a virgin, belonging to an extortionate courtesan, I’ve found means of satisfying for him, without molestation, without outlay, and without cost; then, this other point—that is really a thing that I consider my crowning merit,
5.4.930: to have found out the way by which a young man may be enabled to learn the dispositions and manners of courtesans, so that by knowing them betimes, he may detest them ever after. (PYTHIAS enters from the house unperceived.) For while they are out of doors, nothing seems more cleanly, nothing more neat or more elegant;
5.4.935:
and when they dine with a gallant, they pick daintily about: to see the filth, the dirtiness, the neediness of these women; how sluttish they are when at home, and how greedy after victuals; in what a fashion they devour the black bread with yesterday’s broth:—to know all this, is salvation to a young man.
(Enter PYTHIAS from the house.)
PYTHIAS
(apart, unseen by PARMENO.)
5.4.940:
Upon my faith, you villain, I’ll take vengeance upon you for these sayings and doings; so that you sha’n’t make sport of us with impunity. (Aloud, coming forward.) O, by our trust in the Gods, what a disgraceful action! O hapless young man! O wicked Parmeno, to have brought him here!
PARMENO
5.4.944: I do pity him; and so that I mightn’t see it, wretched creature that I am, I hurried away out of doors.
5.4.945:
What a dreadful example they talk of making him!
PARMENO
O Jupiter! What is this tumult? Am I then undone? I’ll accost her. What’s all this, Pythias? What are you saying? An example made of whom?
PYTHIAS
5.4.947:
Do you ask the question, you most audacious fellow? You’ve proved the ruin of the young man whom you brought hither for the Eunuch, while you were trying to put a trick upon us.
PARMENO
5.4.949:
How so, or what has happened? Tell me.
PYTHIAS
5.4.950:
I’ll tell you: that young woman who was to-day made a present to Thais, are you aware that she is a citizen of this place, and that her brother is a person of very high rank?
PARMENO
5.4.952:
I didn’t know that.
PYTHIAS
But so she has been discovered to be; he, unfortunate youth, has ravished her. When the brother came to know of this being done, in a most towering rage, he—
PARMENO
5.4.954:
Did what, pray?
PYTHIAS
First, bound him in a shocking manner.
PARMENO
5.4.955:
Bound him?
PYTHIAS
And even though Thais entreated him that he wouldn’t do so—
PARMENO
5.4.956:
What is it you tell me?
PYTHIAS
Now he is threatening that he will also do that which is usually done to ravishers; a thing that I never saw done, nor wish to.
PARMENO
5.4.957:
With what assurance does he dare perpetrate a crime so heinous?
PYTHIAS
5.4.958:
How so heinous?
PARMENO
Is it not most heinous? Who ever saw any one taken up as a ravisher in a courtesan’s house?
PYTHIAS
5.4.960:
I don’t know.
PARMENO
But that you mayn’t be ignorant of this, Pythias, I tell you, and give you notice that he is my master’s son.
PYTHIAS
5.4.961:
How! Prithee, is it he?
PARMENO
5.4.962:
Don’t let Thais suffer any violence to be done to him. But why don’t I go in myself?
PYTHIAS
5.4.963: Take care, Parmeno, what you are about, lest you both do him no good and come to harm yourself; for it is their notion,
5.4.965:
that whatever has happened, has originated in you.
PARMENO
What then, wretch that I am, shall I do, or how resolve? But look, I see the old gentleman returning from the country; shall I tell him or shall I not? By my troth, I will tell him; although I am certain that a heavy punishment is in readiness for me; but it’s a matter of necessity, in order that he may rescue him.
PYTHIAS
5.4.968:
You are wise. I’m going in-doors; do you relate to him every thing exactly as it happened.
(Goes into the house.)

5.5.970:
(Enter LACHES.) LACHES
(to himself.)
I have this advantage from my country-house being so near at hand; no weariness, either of country or of town, ever takes possession of me; when satiety begins to come on, I change my locality. But is not that our Parmeno? Surely it is he. Whom are you waiting for, Parmeno, before the door here?
PARMENO
(pretends not to see him.)
5.5.975:
Who is it (Turning round.) Oh, I’m glad that you have returned safe.
LACHES
5.5.976:
Whom are you waiting for?
PARMENO
(aside.)
I’m undone: my tongue cleaves to my mouth through fright.
LACHES
5.5.977:
Why, what is it you are trembling about? Is all quite right? Tell me.
PARMENO
5.5.978:
Master, in the first place, I would have you persuaded of what is the fact; whatever has happened in this affair has happened through no fault of mine.
LACHES
5.5.980:
What is it?
PARMENO
Really you have reason to ask. I ought first to have told you the circumstances. Phaedria purchased a certain Eunuch, to make a present of to this woman here.
LACHES
5.5.982:
To what woman?
PARMENO
To Thais.
LACHES
5.5.983:
Bought? Good heavens, I’m undone! For how much?
PARMENO
Twenty minae.
LACHES
5.5.984:
Done for, quite.
PARMENO
Then, Chaerea is in love with a certain music-girl here.
(Pointing to THAIS’s house.)
LACHES
5.5.985:
How! What? In love? Does he know already what a courtesan means? Is he come to town? One misfortune close upon another.
PARMENO
5.5.987:
Master, don’t look so at me; he didn’t do these things by my encouragement.
LACHES
5.5.988:
Leave off talking about yourself. If I live, you hang-dog, I’ll— But first give me an account of it, whatever it is.
PARMENO
5.5.990:
He was taken to the house of Thais in place of the Eunuch.
LACHES
5.5.991:
In place of the Eunuch?
PARMENO
Such is the fact. They have since apprehended him in the house as a ravisher, and bound him.
LACHES
5.5.993:
Mark the assurance of courtesans.
LACHES
Is there any other calamity or misfortune besides, that you have not told me of?
PARMENO
5.5.995:
That’s all.
LACHES
Do I delay rushing in here?
(Runs into the house of THAIS.)
PARMENO
(to himself.)
5.5.996: There’s no doubt but that I shall have a heavy punishment for this affair, only that I was obliged to act thus. I’m glad of this, that some mischief will befall these women here through my agency, for the old man has, for a long time, been on the look-out for some occasion
5.5.1000: to do them a bad turn; at last he has found it.

5.6.1001:
(Enter PYTHIAS from the house of THAIS, laughing.) PYTHIAS
(to herself, on entering.)
Never, upon my faith, for a long time past, has any thing happened to me that I could have better liked to happen, than the old gentleman just now, full of his mistake, coming into our house. I had the joke all to myself, as I knew what it was he feared.
PARMENO
(apart.)
5.6.1004:
Why, what’s all this?
PYTHIAS
Now I’m come out to meet with Parmeno.
5.6.1005:
But, prithee, where is he?
(Looking around.)
PARMENO
(apart.)
She’s looking for me.
PYTHIAS
And there he is, I see; I’ll go up to him.
PARMENO
5.6.1006:
What’s the matter, simpleton? What do you mean? What are you laughing about? Still going on?
PYTHIAS
(laughing.)
I’m dying; I’m wretchedly tired with laughing at you.
PARMENO
5.6.1007:
Why so?
PYTHIAS
Do you ask? Upon my faith, I never did see, nor shall see, a more silly fellow. Oh dear, I can not well express what amusement you’ve afforded in-doors.
5.6.1010: And still I formerly took you to be a clever and shrewd person. Why, was there any need for you instantly to believe what I told you? Or were you not content with the crime, which by your advice the young man had been guilty of, without betraying the poor fellow to his father as well?
5.6.1014:
Why, what do you suppose his feelings must have been at the moment when his father saw him clothed in that dress? Well, do you now understand that you are done for?
(Laughing.)
PARMENO
5.6.1016:
Hah! what is it you say, you hussy? Have you been telling me lies? What, laughing still? Does it appear so delightful to you, you jade, to be making fools of us?
PYTHIAS
(laughing.)
5.6.1018:
Yes, indeed, if you can do it with impunity.
PYTHIAS
Exactly so.
PARMENO
By heavens, I’ll repay you!
PYTHIAS
I believe you; but, perhaps, that which you are threatening, Parmeno, will need a future day;
5.6.1020:
you’ll be trussed up directly, for rendering a silly young man remarkable for disgraceful conduct, and then betraying him to his father; they’ll both be making an example of you.
(Laughing.)
PARMENO
5.6.1022:
I’m done for!
PYTHIAS
This reward has been found you in return for that present of yours; I’m off.
(Goes into the house.)
PARMENO
(to himself.)
5.6.1023: Wretch that I am; just like a rat, this day I’ve come to destruction through betrayal of myself.

5.7.1024:
(Enter THRASO and GNATHO.) GNATHO
(to THRASO.)
Well now? With what hope, or what design, are we come hither? What do you intend to do, Thraso?
THRASO
5.7.1025:
What, I? To surrender myself to Thais, and do what she bids me.
GNATHO
What is it you say?
THRASO
5.7.1026:
Why any the less so, than Hercules served Omphale.
GNATHO
The precedent pleases me. (Aside.) I only wish I may see your head stroked down with a slipper; but her door makes a noise.
THRASO
5.7.1028:
Confusion! Why, what mischiefsthis? I never saw this person before; why, I wonder, is he rushing out in such a hurry?
(They stand aside.)

5.8.1030:
(Enter CHAEREA from the house of THAIS, on the other side of the stage.) CHAEREA
(to himself, aloud.)
O fellow-townsmen, is there any one alive more fortunate than me this day? Not any one, upon my faith: for clearly in me have the Gods manifested all their power, on whom, thus suddenly, so many blessings are bestowed.
PARMENO
(apart.)
5.8.1033:
Why is he thus overjoyed?
CHAEREA
(seeing PARMENO, and running up to him.)
O my dear Parmeno, the contriver, the beginner, the perfecter of all my delights, do you know what are my transports?
5.8.1035:
Are you aware that my Pamphila has been discovered to be a citizen?
PARMENO
I have heard so.
CHAEREA
Do you know that she is betrothed to me?
PARMENO
5.8.1036:
So may the Gods bless me, happily done.
GNATHO
(apart to THRASO.)
Do you hear what he says?
CHAEREA
And then, besides, I am delighted that my brother’s mistress is secured to him; the family is united. Thais has committed herself to the patronage of my father; she has put herself under our care and protection.
PARMENO
5.8.1039:
Thais, then, is wholly your brother’s.
CHAEREA
Of course.
PARMENO
5.8.1040:
Then this is another reason for us to rejoice, that the Captain will be beaten out of doors.
CHAEREA
5.8.1041:
Wherever my brother is, do you take care that he hears this as soon as possible.
PARMENO
I’ll go look for him at home.
(Goes into the house of LACHES.)
THRASO
(apart to GNATHO.)
5.8.1042:
Do you at all doubt, Gnatho, but that I am now ruined everlastingly?
GNATHO
(to THRASO.)
5.8.1043:
Without doubt, I do think so.
CHAEREA
(to himself.)
What am I to make mention of first, or commend in especial? Him who gave me the advice to do so, or myself, who ventured
5.8.1045:
to undertake it? Or ought I to extol fortune, who has been my guide, and has so opportunely crowded into a single day events so numerous, so important; or my father’s kindness and indulgence Oh Jupiter, I entreat you, do preserve these blessings unto us!
(Enter PHAEDRIA from the house of LACHES.)
PHAEDRIA
(to himself.)
5.8.1048:
Ye Gods, by our trust in you, what incredible things has Parmeno just related to me! But where is my brother?
CHAEREA
(stepping forward.)
5.8.1050:
I’m overjoyed.
CHAEREA
I quite believe you. There is no one, brother, more worthy to be loved than this Thais of yours: so much is she a benefactress to all our family.
PHAEDRIA
5.8.1052:
Whew! are you commending her too to me?
THRASO
(apart.)
I’m undone; the less the hope I have, the more I am in love. Prithee, Gnatho, my hope is in you.
GNATHO
(apart.)
5.8.1053:
What do you wish me to do?
THRASO
(apart.)
Bring this about, by entreaties or with money, that I may at least share Thais’s favors in some degree.
GNATHO
(apart.)
5.8.1055:
It’s a hard task.
THRASO
(apart.)
If you set your mind on any thing, I know you well. If you manage this, ask me for any present you like as your reward; you shall have what you ask.
GNATHO
(apart.)
5.8.1057:
Is it so?
THRASO
(apart.)
It shall be so.
GNATHO
(apart.)
If I manage this, I ask that your house, whether you are present or absent, may be open to me; that, without invitation, there may always be a place for me.
THRASO
(apart.)
5.8.1059:
I pledge my honor that it shall be so.
GNATHO
(apart.)
I’ll set about it then.
PHAEDRIA
Who is it I hear so close at hand? (Turning round.) O Thraso—
THRASO
(coming forward.)
5.8.1060:
Save you both—
PHAEDRIA
Perhaps you are not aware what has taken place here.
THRASO
5.8.1061:
I am quite aware.
PHAEDRIA
Why, then, do I see you in this neighborhood?
THRASO
5.8.1062:
Depending on your kindness.
PHAEDRIA
Do you know what sort of dependence you have? Captain, I give you notice, if ever I catch you in this street again, even if you should say to me, I was looking for another person, I was on my road this way, you are undone.
GNATHO
5.8.1064:
Come, come, that’s not handsome.
PHAEDRIA
5.8.1065:
I’ve said it.
GNATHO
I didn’t know you gave yourself such airs.
PHAEDRIA
So it shall be.
GNATHO
5.8.1066:
First hear a few words from me; and when I have said the thing, if you approve of it, do it.
PHAEDRIA
5.8.1070:
but if the same thing is of advantage to yourselves, it would be folly for you not to do it.
PHAEDRIA
5.8.1071:
What is it?
GNATHO
I’m of opinion that the Captain, your rival, should be received among you.
PHAEDRIA
(starting.)
5.8.1072:
Be received?
GNATHO
(to PHAEDRIA.)
Only consider. I’faith, Phaedria, at the free rate you are living with her, and indeed very freely you are living, you have but little to give; and it’s necessary for Thais to receive a good deal.
5.8.1075:
That all this may be supplied for your amour and not at your own expense, there is not an individual better suited or more fitted for your purpose than the Captain. In the first place, he both.has got enough to give, and no one does give more profusely. He is a fool, a dolt, a blockhead; night and day he snores away; and you need not fear that the lady will fall in love with him; you may easily have him discarded whenever you please.
CHAEREA
(to PHAEDRIA.)
5.8.1080:
What shall we do?
GNATHO
And this besides, which I deem to be of even greater importance,—not a single person entertains in better style or more bountifully.
CHAEREA
5.8.1082:
It’s a wonder if this sort of man can not be made use of in some way or other.
PHAEDRIA
I think so too.
GNATHO
5.8.1083:
You act properly. One thing I have still to beg of you,—that you’ll receive me into your fraternity; I’ve been rolling that stone for a considerable time past.
PHAEDRIA
5.8.1085:
And with all my heart.
GNATHO
Then I, in return for this, Phaedria, and you, Chaerea, make him over to you to be eaten and drunk to the dregs.
CHAEREA
5.8.1087:
He quite deserves it.
GNATHO
(calling to THRASO.)
Thraso, whenever you please, step this way.
THRASO
Prithee, how goes it?
GNATHO
5.8.1088: How? Why, these people didn’t know you; after I had discovered to them your qualities, and had praised you as your actions and your virtues deserved,
5.8.1090:
I prevailed upon them.
THRASO
You have managed well; I give you my best thanks. Besides, I never was any where but what all were extremely fond of me.
GNATHO
(to PHAEDRIA and CHAEREA.)
5.8.1092:
Didn’t I tell you that he was a master of the Attic elegance?
PHAEDRIA
5.8.1093:
He is no other than you mentioned. (Pointing to his FATHER’s house.) Walk this way.
(To the AUDIENCE.) Fare you well, and grant us your applause.

0.0.1:
THE PROLOGUE.
SINCE the old Poet can not withdraw our bard from his pursuits and reduce him to indolence, he endeavors, by invectives, to deter him from writing: for he is wont to say to this effect,—that the Plays which he has hitherto composed
0.0.5: are poor in their language, and of meagre style; because he has nowhere described a frantic youth as seeing a hind in flight, and the hounds pursuing; while he implores and entreated that he would give her aid. But if he had been aware that his Play, when formerly first represented,
0.0.10: stood its ground more through the merits of the performers than its own, he would attack with much less boldness than he does. Now, if there is any one who says or thinks to this effect, that if the old Poet had not assailed him first, the young one could have devised no Prologue
0.0.15: for him to repeat, without having some one to abuse, let him receive this for an answer: that the prize is proposed in common to all who apply to the Dramatic art. He has aimed at driving our Poet from his studies to absolute want; he then has in-tended this for an answer, not an attack.
0.0.20: If he had opposed him with fair words, he would have heard himself civilly addressed; what has been given by him, let him consider as now returned. I will make an end of speaking about him, when, of his own accord, he himself makes an end of offending.
0.0.25: Now give your attention to what I request. I present you a new Play, which they call Epidicazomenos, in Greek: in the Latin, he calls it Phormio; because the person that acts the principal part is Phormio, a Parasite, through whom, principally, the plot will be’ carried on, if your favor attends the Poet.
0.0.30: Lend your attention; in silence give an ear with impartial feelings, that we may not experience a like fortune to what we did, when, through a tumult, our Company was driven from the place; which place, the merit of the actor, and your good-will and candor seconding it, has since restored unto us.

1.1.35:
(Enter DAVUS, with a bag of money in his hand.) DAVUS
Geta, my very good friend and fellow-townsman, came to me yesterday. There had been for some time a trifling balance of money of his in my hands upon a small account; he asked me to make it up. I have done so, and am carrying it to him. But I hear that his master’s son has taken
1.1.40: a wife; this, I suppose, is scraped together as a present for her. How unfair a custom!—that those who have the least should always be giving something to the more wealthy! That which the poor wretch has with difficulty spared, ounce by ounce, out of his allowance, defrauding himself of every indulgence,
1.1.45: the whole of it will she carry of, without thinking with how much labor it has been acquired. And then besides, Geta will be struck for another present when his mistress is brought to bed; and then again for another present, when the child’s birthday comes; when they initiate him, too: all this the mother will carry off;
1.1.50: the child will only be the pretext for the present. But don’t I see Geta there?

1.2.51:
(Enter GETA, from the house of DEMIPHO.) GETA
(at the door, to those within.)
If any red-haired man should inquire for me—
DAVUS
(stepping forward.)
Here he is, say no more.
GETA
(starting.)
Oh! Why I was trying to come and meet you, Davus.
DAVUS
(giving the money to GETA.)
1.2.52:
Here, take it; it’s all ready counted out; the number just amounts to the sum I owed you.
GETA
1.2.54:
I am obliged to you; and I return you thanks for not having forgotten me.
DAVUS
1.2.55:
Especially as people’s ways are nowadays; things are come to such a pass, if a person repays you any thing, you must be greatly obliged to him. But why are you out of spirits?
GETA
1.2.57:
What, I? You little know what terror and peril I am in.
DAVUS
1.2.58:
What’s the matter?
GETA.
You shall know, if you can only keep it secret.
DAVUS
1.2.60:
the man, whose trustworthiness you have experienced as to money, are you afraid to intrust with words? In what way have I any interest in deceiving you?
GETA
1.2.62:
Well then, listen.
DAVUS
I give you my best attention.
GETA
1.2.63:
Davus, do you know Chremes, the elder brother of our old gentleman?
DAVUS
1.2.64:
Why should I not?
GETA
Well, and his son Phaedria?
DAVUS
1.2.65:
As well as your own self.
GETA
It so happened to both the old gentlemen, just at the same period, that the one had to take a journey to Lemnos, and our old man to Cilicia, to see an old acquaintance; he tempted over the old man by letters, promising him all but mountains of gold.
DAVUS
1.2.70:
that is his way.
DAVUS
Oh, as for that, I really ought to have been a man of fortune.
GETA
1.2.71:
When departing hence, both the old gentlemen left ne as a sort of tutor to their sons.
DAVUS
1.2.72:
Ah, Geta, you undertook a hard task there.
GETA
1.2.73: I came to experience it, I know that. I’m quite sure that I was forsaken by my good Genius, who must have been angry with me.
1.2.75: I began to oppose them at first; but what need of talking? As long as I was trusty to the old men, I was paid for it in my shoulder-blades.
1.2.77:
This, then, occurred to my mind: why, this is folly to kick against the spur. I began to do every thing for them that they wished to be humored in.
DAVUS
1.2.79:
You knew how to make your market.
GETA
1.2.80: Our young fellow did no mischief whatever at first; that Phaedria at once picked up a certain damsel, a Music-girl, and fell in love with her to distraction. She belonged to a most abominable Procurer; and their fathers had taken good care that they should have nothing to give him.
1.2.85: There remained nothing for him then but to feed his eyes, to follow her about, to escort her to the school, and to escort her back again. We, having nothing to do, lent our aid to Phaedria. Near the school at which she was taught, right opposite the place, there was a certain barber’s shop: here we were generally in the habit
1.2.90: of waiting for her, until she was coming home again. In the mean time, while one day we were sitting there, there came in a young man in tears; we were surprised at this. We inquired what was the matter? Never, said he, has poverty appeared to me a burden so grievous and so insupportable as just now.
1.2.95: I have just seen a certain poor young woman in this neighborhood lamenting her dead mother. She was laid out before her, and not a single friend, acquaintance, or relation was there with her, except one poor old woman, to assist her in the funeral: I pitied her.
1.2.100: The girl herself was of surpassing beauty. What need of a long story? She moved us all. At once Antipho exclaims, Would you like us to go and visit her? The other said, I think we ought—let us go—show us the way, please. We went, and arrived there; we saw her; the girl was beautiful, and that you might say so the more,
1.2.105: there was no heightening to her beauty; her hair disheveled, her feet bare, herself neglected, and in tears; her dress: mean, so ’that, had there not been an excess of beauty in her very charms, these circumstances must have extinguished those charms. The one who had lately fallen in love with the Music-girl
1.2.110:
said: She is well enough; but our youth—
DAVUS
I know it already—fell in love with her.
GETA
1.2.111: Can you imagine to what an extent? Observe the consequence. The day after, he goes straight to the old woman; entreats her to let him have her: she, on the other hand, refuses him, and says that he is not acting properly; that, she is a citizen of Athens,
1.2.115:
virtuous, and born of honest parents: that if he wishes to make her his wife, he is at liberty to do so according to law; but if otherwise, she gives him a refusal. Our youth was at a loss what to. do. He was both eager to marry her, and he dreaded his absent father.
DAVUS
1.2.119:
Would not his father, if he had returned, have given him leave?
GETA
1.2.120:
He let him marry a girl with no fortune, and of obscure birth! He would never do so.
DAVUS
1.2.121:
What came of it at last?
GETA
1.2.122:
What came of it? There is one Phormio here, a Parasite, a fellow of great assurance; may all the Gods confound him!
DAVUS
1.2.124:
What has he done?
GETA
He has given this piece of advice, which I will tell you of.
1.2.125: There is a law, that orphan girls are to marry those who are their next-of-kin; and the same law commands such persons to marry them. I’ll say you are the next-of-kin, and take out a summons against you; I’ll pretend that I am a friend of the girl’s father; we will come before the judges: who her father was,
1.2.130:
who her mother, how she is related to you—all this I’ll trump up, just as will be advantageous and suited to my purpose; on your disproving none of these things, I shall prevail, of course. Your father will return; a quarrel will be the consequence; what care I? She will still be ours.
DAVUS
1.2.134:
An amusing piece of assurance!
GETA
1.2.135:
He was, persuaded to this. It was carried out; they came into court: we were beaten. He has married her.
DAVUS
1.2.136:
What is it you tell me?
GETA
Just what you have heard.
DAVUS
O Geta, what will become of you?
GETA
1.2.137:
Upon my faith, I don’t know; this one thing I do know, whatever fortune may bring, I’ll bear it with firmness.
DAVUS
1.2.138:
You please me; well, that is the duty of a man.
GETA
1.2.139:
All my hope is in myself.
DAVUS
1.2.140:
I commend you.
GETA
Suppose I have recourse to some one to intercede for me, who will plead for me in these terms: Pray, do forgive him this time; but if after this he does any thing, I make no entreaty: if only he doesn’t add, When I’ve gone, e’en kill him for my part.
DAVUS
1.2.144:
What of the one who was usher to the Music-girl?
GETA
(shrugging his shoulders.)
1.2.145:
So so, but poorly.
DAVUS
Perhaps he hasn’t much to give.
GETA
1.2.146:
Why, really, nothing at all, except mere hopes.
DAVUS
1.2.147:
Is his father come back or not?
GETA
Not yet.
DAVUS
Well, when do you expect your old man?
GETA
1.2.148: I don’t know for certain; but I just now heard that a letter has been brought from him,
1.2.150:
and has been left with the officers of the customs: I’m going to fetch it.
DAVUS
1.2.151:
Is there any thing else that you want with me, Geta?
GETA
Nothing, but that I wish you well. (Exit DAVUS.) Hark you, boy (calling at the door). Is nobody coming out here? (A LAD comes out.) Take this, and give it to Dorcium.
(He gives the purse to the LAD, who carries it into DEMIPHO’S house and exit GETA.)

1.3.153:
(Enter ANTIPHO and PHAEDRIA.) ANTIPHO
That things should have come to such a pass, Phaedria, that I should be in utter dread,of my father, who wishes me so well, whenever his return comes into my thoughts!
1.3.155:
Had I not been inconsiderate, I might have waited for him, as I ought to have done.
PHAEDRIA
1.3.160:
but still, this perpetual anxiety would not have been tormenting my mind (touching PHAEDRIA).
PHAEDRIA
I hear you.
ANTIPHO
1.3.161:
While I am every moment expecting his return, who is to sever from me this connection.
PHAEDRIA
1.3.162: Other men feel uneasiness because they can not gain what they love; you complain because you have too much. You are surfeited with love, Antipho. Why, really, upon my faith, this situation of yours is surely one to be coveted and desired.
1.3.165: So may the Gods kindly bless me, could I be at liberty to be so long in possession of the object of my love, I could contentedly die. Do you, then, form a judgment as to the rest, what I am now suffering from this privation, and what pleasure you enjoy from the possession of your desires; not to mention how, without any expense, you have obtained a well-born and genteel woman, and have got a wife of unblemished reputation:
1.3.170:
happy you, were not this one thing wanting, a mind capable of bearing all this with moderation. If you had to deal with that Procurer with whom I have to deal, then you would soon be sensible of it. We are mostly all of us inclined by nature to be dissatisfied with our lot.
ANTIPHO
1.3.173: Still, on the other hand, Phaedria, you now seem to me the fortunate man, who still have the liberty, without restraint, of resolving on what pleases you best:
1.3.175: whether to keep, to love on, or to give her up. I, unfortunately, have got my-self into that position, that I have neither right to give her up, nor liberty to retain her. But how’s this? Is it our Geta I see running this way? ’Tis he himself. Alas! I’m dreadfully afraid what news it is he’s now bringing me.

1.4.180:
so suddenly do such mighty evils now threaten me thus unprepared, which I neither know how to shun, nor how to extricate myself therefrom; for this daring step of:ours can not now any longer be kept a secret. If such a result is not adroitly guarded against, these matters will cause the ruin of myself, or of my master.
ANTIPHO
(to PHAEDRIA.)
1.4.183:
Why, I wonder, is he coming in such fright?:
GETA
(to himself.)
1.4.184:
Besides, I’ve but a moment left for this matter—my master’s close at hand.
ANTIPHO
(to PHAEDRIA.)
What mischief is this?
GETA
(to himself.)
1.4.185: When he comes to hear of it, what remedy shall I discover for his anger Am I to speak? I shall irritate him: be silent? I shall provoke him: excuse myself? I should be washing a brickbat. Alas! unfortunate me! While I am trembling for myself, this Antipho distracts my mind. I am concerned for him; I’m in dread for him: ’tis he that now keeps me here; for had it not been for him, I should have made due provision for my safety, and have taken vengeance on the old man for his crabbedness;
1.4.190:
I should have scraped up something, and straightway taken to my heels away from here.
ANTIPHO
(to PHAEDRIA.)
1.4.191:
I wonder What running away or theft it is that he’s planning.
GETA
(to himself.)
1.4.192:
But where shall I find Antipho, or which way go look for him?
PHAEDRIA
(to ANTIPHO.)
1.4.193:
He’s mentioning your name.
ANTIPHO
(to PHADRIA.)
I know not what great misfortune I expect to hear from this messenger.
PHAEDRIA
(to ANTIPHO.)
1.4.194:
Why, are you in your senses?
GETA
(to himself.)
I’ll make my way homeward; he’s generally there.
PHAEDRIA
(to ANTIPHO.)
1.4.195:
Let’s call the fellow back.
ANTIPHO
(calling out.)
Stop, this instant.
GETA
(turning round.)
Heyday—with authority enough, whoever you are.
ANTIPHO
1.4.196:
Geta!
GETA
The very person I wanted to find.
ANTIPHO
1.4.197:
Pray, tell me what news you bring, and dispatch it in one word, if you can.
GETA
1.4.198:
I’ll do so.
ANTIPHO
Out with it.
GETA
Just now, at the harbor—
ANTIPHO
What, my father?—
GETA
You’ve hit it.
ANTIPHO
Ruined outright!
PHAEDRIA
Pshaw!
ANTIPHO
1.4.199:
What am I to do?
PHAEDRIA
(to GETA.)
What is it you say?
GETA
That I have seen his father, your uncle.
ANTIPHO
1.4.200:
How am I, wretch that I am, now to find a remedy for this sudden misfortune? But if it should be my fortune, Phanium, to be torn away from you, life would cease to be desirable.
GETA
1.4.202:
Therefore, Antipho, since matters are thus, the more need have you to be on your guard; fortune helps the brave.
ANTIPHO
1.4.205:
for if your father perceives that you are alarmed, he will think that you have been guilty of some fault.
PHAEDRIA
1.4.206:
That’s true.
ANTIPHO
I can not change.
GETA
1.4.207:
What would you do, if now something else still more difficult had to be done by you?
ANTIPHO
1.4.208:
As I am not equal to this, I should be still less so to the other.
GETA
This is doing nothing at all, Phaedria, let’s be gone; why do we waste our time here to no purpose. I shall be off.
PHAEDRIA
1.4.209:
And I too.
(They move as if going.)
ANTIPHO
Pray, now,
1.4.210:
if I assume an air, will that do? (He endeavors to assume another air.)
GETA
You are trifling.
ANTIPHO
Look at my countenance—there’s for you. (Assuming a different air.) Will that do?
GETA
1.4.211:
No.
ANTIPHO
Well, will this? (Assuming another air.)
GETA
Pretty well.
ANTIPHO
Well then, this? (Assuming a still bolder air.)
GETA
That’s just the thing. There now, keep to that, and answer him word for word, like for like; don’t let him, in his anger, disconcert you with his blustering words.
ANTIPHO
1.4.214: Say that you were forced against your will by law, by sentence of the court; do you take me?
1.4.215:
(Looking earnestly in one direction.) But who is the old man that I see at the end of the street?
ANTIPHO
’Tis he himself. I can not stand it. (Going.)
GETA
1.4.216:
Oh! What are you about? Whither are you going, Antipho? Stop, I tell you.
ANTIPHO
1.4.217:
I know my own self and my offense; to your management I trust Phanium and my own existence. (Exit hastily.)
PHAEDRIA
1.4.219:
Geta, what’s to be done now?
GETA
You will just hear some harsh language:
1.4.220:
I shall be trussed up and trounced, if I am not somewhat mistaken. But what we were just now advising Antipho to do, the same we must do ourselves, Phaedria.
PHAEDRIA
1.4.223:
Away with your musts; rather do you command me what I am to do.
GETA
1.4.224: Do you remember what were your words formerly
1.4.225:
on our entering upon this project, with the view of protecting yourselves from ill consequences—that their cause was just, clear, unanswerable, and most righteous?
PHAEDRIA
1.4.227:
I remember it.
GETA
Well then, now there’s need of that plea, or of one still better and more plausible, if such there can be.
PHAEDRIA
1.4.228:
I’ll use my best endeavors.
GETA
1.4.229: Do you then accost him first; I’ll be here
1.4.230:
in re-serve, by way of reinforcement, if you give ground at all.
PHAEDRIA
Very well.
(They retire to a distance.)

2.1.231:
(Enter DEMIPHO, at the other side of the stage.) DEMIPHO
(to himself.)
And is it possible that Antipho has taken a wife without my consent? and that no authority of mine—but let alone authority—no displeasure of mine, at all events, has he been in dread of? To have no sense of shame! O audacious conduct! O Geta, rare adviser!
GETA
(apart to PHAEDRIA.)
2.1.234:
Just brought in at last.
DEMIPHO
What will they say to me, or what excuse will they find?
2.1.235:
I wonder much.
GETA
(apart.)
Why, I’ve found that out already; do think of something else.
DEMIPHO
Will he be saying this to me: I did it against my will; the law compelled me? I hear you, and admit it.
GETA
(apart.)
2.1.237:
But knowingly, in silence, to give up the cause to his adversaries—did the law oblige him to do that as well?
GETA
(apart.)
2.1.238:
That is a hard blow.
PHAEDRIA
I’ll clear that up; let me alone for that.
DEMIPHO
2.1.239: It is a matter of doubt what I am to do; for beyond expectation, and quite past all belief, has this befallen me.
2.1.240: So enraged am I, that I can not compose my mind to think upon it. Wherefore it is the duty of all persons, when affairs are the most prosperous, then in especial to reflect within themselves in what way they are to endure adversity. Returning from abroad, let him always picture to himself dangers and losses, either offenses committed by a son, or the death of his wife, or the sickness of a daughter,—
2.1.245:
that these things are the common lot, so that no one of them may ever come as a surprise upon his feelings. Whatever falls out beyond his hopes, all that he must look upon as so much gain.
GETA
(apart.)
2.1.247: O Phaedria, it is incredible how much I surpass my master in wisdom. All my misfortunes have been already calculated upon by me, upon my master coming home. I must grind at the mill, be beaten, wear fetters,
2.1.250:
be set to work in the fields; not one individual thing of these will happen unexpected by my mind. Whatever falls out beyond my expectations, all that I shall look upon as so much gain. But why do you hesitate to accost him, and soften him at the outset with fair words?
(PHAEDRIA goes forward to accost DEMIPHO.)
DEMIPHO
(to himself.)
2.1.253:
I see Phaedria, my brother’s son, coming toward me.
PHAEDRIA
2.1.254:
My uncle, welcome!
DEMIPHO
Greetings to you; but where is Antipho?
PHAEDRIA
2.1.255:
That you have arrived in safety—
DEMIPHO
I believe it; answer my question.
PHAEDRIA
2.1.256:
He is well; he’s close at hand; but is every thing quite to your wishes?
DEMIPHO
2.1.257:
I wish it was so, indeed.
PHAEDRIA
What’s the matter?
DEMIPHO
Do you ask me, Phaedria? You people have cooked up a fine marriage in my absence.
PHAEDRIA
2.1.259:
What now, are you angry with him for that?
GETA
(apart.)
What a clever contriver!
DEMIPHO
2.1.260:
Have I not reason to be angry with him? I long for him to come into my sight, that he may know that through his faultiness, from being a mild father, I am become a most severe one.
PHAEDRIA
2.1.263:
But he has done nothing, uncle, for which you should blame him.
DEMIPHO
2.1.264: Now, do look at that; all alike; all hanging together;
2.1.265:
when you know one, you know all.
PHAEDRIA
That is not the case.
DEMIPHO
2.1.266:
When the one is in fault, the other is at hand to defend him; when it is the other, then he is ready; they just help one another by turns.
GETA
(apart.)
2.1.268:
The old man, without. knowing it, has exactly described their proceedings.
DEMIPHO
2.1.269:
For if it had not been so, you would not, Phaedria, have stood up for him.
PHAEDRIA
2.1.270: If, uncle; it is the fact, that Antipho has been guilty of any fault, in consequence of which he has been too regardless of his interest or his reputation, I would not allege any reason why he should not suffer what he deserves. But if some one by chance, relying upon his own artfulness, has laid a snare for our youthful age,
2.1.275:
and has succeeded, is it our fault or that of the judges, who often, through envy, take away from the rich, or, through compassion, award to the poor?
GETA
(apart.)
2.1.278:
Unless I knew the case, I could fancy he was saying the truth.
DEMIPHO
2.1.279: Is there any judge who can possibly know
2.1.280:
your rights, when you yourself don’t answer a word—as he has done?
PHAEDRIA
2.1.281:
He acted the part of an ingenuous young man; after they had come before the judges, he was not able to say what he had intended, so much did his modesty confuse him there through his bashfulness.
GETA
(apart.)
2.1.285:
I commend him: but why do I hesitate at once to accost the old man? (Going forward to DEMIPHO.) Master, welcome to you! I’m glad to see you safe returned.
DEMIPHO
(ironically.)
2.1.286:
Ah, excellent guardian! save you, stay of my family, no doubt, to whom, at my departure, I intrusted my son.
GETA
2.1.289: For some minutes past I’ve heard you accusing all of us
2.1.290:
undeservedly; and me the most undeservedly of them all; for what would you have had me do for you in this affair? The laws do not allow a person who is a slave to plead; nor is there any giving evidence on his part.
DEMIPHO
2.1.293: I grant all that: I admit this too—the young man, unused to courts, was bashful; I allow it:
2.1.295:
you, too, are a slave: still, if she was ever so near a relative, it was not necessary for him to marry her, but as the law enjoins, you might have given her a portion; she could have looked out for another husband. Why, then, in preference, did he bring a pauper home?
GETA
2.1.299:
No particular reason; but he hadn’t the money.
DEMIPHO
He might have borrowed it
2.1.300:
from some person or other.
GETA
From some person or other? Nothing more easily said.
DEMIPHO
2.1.301:
After all, if on no other terms, on interest.
GETA
2.1.302:
Aye, aye, fine talking; as if any one would have trusted him, while you were living.
DEMIPHO
2.1.303: No, it shall not be so; it must not be. Ought I to allow her to remain with him as his wife a single day?
2.1.305:
She merits no indulgence. I should like this fellow to be pointed out to me, or to be shown where he lives.
GETA
2.1.307:
Phormio, do you mean?
DEMIPHO
That fellow, the woman’s next friend?
GETA
2.1.308:
I’ll have him here immediately.
DEMIPHO
Where is Antipho at present?
GETA
Away from home.
DEMIPHO
2.1.309:
Go, Phedria, look for him, and bring him here.
PHAEDRIA
I’Il go straightway to the place.
GETA
(aside.)
2.1.310:
To Pamphila, you mean.
(Exeunt PHAEDRIA and GETA.)
DEMIPHO
(to himself.)
2.1.311:
I’ll just step home to salute the house-hold Gods. From there, I’ll go to the Forum, and summon some of my friends to give me their assistance in this affair; so that I may not be unprepared, when Phormio comes.
(Goes into his house.)

2.2.315:
(Enter PHORMIO and GETA.) PHORMIO
And so you say that, dreading his father’s presence, he has taken himself off?
GETA
Exactly so.
PHORMIO
2.2.316:
That Phanium is left alone?
GETA
Just so.
PHORMIO
And that the old man is in a rage?
GETA
2.2.317:
Extremely so.
PHORMIO
The whole business, Phormio, rests on yourself alone; you yourself have hashed it up; it must all be swallowed by yourself, so set about it.
GETA
2.2.319:
I entreat you—
PHORMIO
(to himself.)
If he inquires.
GETA
In you is all our hope.
PHORMIO
(to himself.)
Look at this, now:—
2.2.320:
What if he sends her back?
GETA
It was you that urged us.
PHORMIO
(to himself.)
I think that will do.
GETA
Do help us.
PHORMIO
(with alacrity.)
2.2.321:
Let the old gentleman come; all my plans are now ready prepared in my mind.
GETA
2.2.322:
What will you do?
PHORMIO
What would you have me? But that Phanium may continue with him, and that I may clear Antipho from this charge, and turn upon myself all the wrath of the old gentleman?
GETA
2.2.324: O brave and kind man! But, Phormio, I often
2.2.325:
dread lest this courage may end in the stocks at last.
PHORMIO
Oh, by no means; I’ve made trial, and have already pondered on the paths for my feet. How many men before to-day do you suppose I have beaten, even to death, strangers as well as citizens: the better I understand it, the oftener I try it. Just tell me, look you, did you ever hear of an action of damages being brought against me?
GETA
2.2.335:
they have no wish to maintain a devouring fellow; and, in my opinion, they are wise, if for an injury they are unwilling to return the highest benefits.
GETA
2.2.337:
It’s impossible that sufficient thanks can be returned you by him for your kindness.
PHORMIO
2.2.338: Why no; no person can return thanks sufficient to his patron for his kindness. For you to take your place at table at free cost, anointed and just washed at the bath,
2.2.340:
with your mind at ease, whereas he is devoured with the care and expense: while every thing is being done to give you delight, he is being vexed at heart; you are laughing away, first to drink, take the higher place; a banquet full of doubts is placed before you—
GETA
2.2.343:
What is the meaning of that expression?
PHORMIO
When you are in doubt which in especial to par-take of. When you enter upon a consideration how delicious these things are, and how costly they are,
2.2.345:
the person who provides them, must you not account him a very God—neither more nor less?
GETA
2.2.346:
The old man is coming; take care what you are about; the first onset is the fiercest; if you stand that, then, afterward, you may play just as you please.
(They retire to a distance.)

2.3.348:
(Enter, at a distance, DEMIPHO, HEGIO, CRATINUS, and CRITO, following him.) DEMIPHO
Well now—did you ever hear of an injury being done to any person in a more affronting manner than this has to me?
2.3.350:
Assist me, I do beg of you.
GETA
(apart.)
He’s in a passion.
PHORMIO
(apart.)
Do you mind your cue; I’ll rouse him just now. (Stepping forward and crying aloud.) Oh immortal Gods! does Demipho deny that Phanium here is related to him?
GETA
2.3.353:
He does deny it.
DEMIPHO
(to his friends.)
2.3.354:
I believe it is the very man I was speaking about. Follow me. (They all come forward.)
PHORMIO
(to GETA.)
And that he knows who her father was?
GETA
2.3.356:
And that he knows who Stilpho was?
GETA
He does deny it.
PHORMIO
2.3.357:
Because the poor thing was left destitute, her father is disowned; she herself is slighted: see what avarice does.
GETA
(in a loud voice.)
2.3.359:
If you are going to accuse my: master of avarice, you shall hear what you won’t like.
DEMIPHO
2.3.360:
Oh, the impudence of the fellow! Does he come on purpose to accuse me?
PHORMIO
2.3.361: For really, I have no reason why I should be offended at the young man, if he did not know him; since that person, when growing aged and poor, and supporting himself by his labor, generally confined himself to the country; there he had a piece of land from my father
2.3.365:
to cultivate; full oft, in the mean time, did the old. man tell me that this kinsman of his neglected him: but what a man? The very best I ever saw in all my life.
GETA
(in a loud voice.)
2.3.368:
Look to yourself as well as to him, how you speak.
PHORMIO
(with affected indignation.)
Away, to utter perdition, with you. For if I had not formed such an opinion of him, I should never
2.3.370:
have incurred such enmity with your family on her account, whom he now slights in such an ungenerous manner.
GETA
(aloud.)
2.3.372:
What, do you persist in speaking abusively of my master in his absence, you most abominable fellow?
PHORMIO
2.3.373:
Why, it’s just what he deserves.
GETA
(aloud.)
Say you so, you jail-bird?
DEMIPHO
(calling aloud.)
Geta!
GETA
(aloud.)
2.3.374:
A plunderer of people’s property—a perverter of the laws!
DEMIPHO
(calling aloud.)
Geta!
PHORMIO
(apart, in a low voice.)
2.3.375:
Answer him.
GETA
Who is it? (Looking round.) Oh!—
DEMIPHO
Hold your peace.
GETA
He has never left off uttering abuse against you behind your back, unworthy of you, and just befitting himself.
DEMIPHO
2.3.377: Well now, have done. (Addressing PHORMIO.) Young man, in the first place, with your good leave, I ask you this, if you may possibly be pleased to give me an answer:
2.3.380:
explain to me who this friend of yours was, that you speak of, and how he said that he was related to me.
PHORMIO
(sneeringly.)
2.3.382:
You are fishing it out, just as if you didn’t know.
DEMIPHO
I, know?
PHORMIO
Yes.
DEMIPHO
2.3.383:
I say I do not; you, Who affirm it, recall it to my recollection.
PHORMIO
2.3.385:
tell me his name.
PHORMIO
His name?
DEMIPHO
Of course. (PHORMIO hesitates.) Why are you silent now?
PHORMIO
(aside.)
2.3.386:
Heavens, I’m undone; I’ve forgot the name.
DEMIPHO
Well, what do you say?
PHORMIO
(aside, to GETA.)
Geta, if you recollect the name I told you a short time since, prompt me. (Aloud, to DEMIPHO.) Well then, I sha’n’t tell you; as if you didn’t know, you come to pump me.
DEMIPHO
2.3.389:
I, come to pump you, indeed?
GETA
(whispering to PHORMIO.)
Stilpho.
PHORMIO
But, after all, what matters that to me?
2.3.390:
It is Stilpho.
DEMIPHO
Whom did you say?
PHORMIO
Stilpho, I tell you; you knew him.
DEMIPHO
2.3.391:
I neither know him, nor had I ever any relation of that name.
PHORMIO
2.3.392:
Say you so? Are you not ashamed of this? But if he had left you ten talents—
DEMIPHO
2.3.394:
May the Gods confound you!
PHORMIO
You’d have been the first, from memory,
2.3.395:
to trace your line of kindred, even as far back as from grandfather and great-grandfather.
DEMIPHO
2.3.396:
Very likely what you say. In that case, when I had undertaken it, I should have shown how she was related to me; do you do the same: tell me, how is she related to me?
GETA
2.3.398:
Well done, my master, that’s right! (Threateningly to PHORMIO.) Hark you, take you care.
PHORMIO
2.3.399: I’ve already made the matter quite plain where I ought,
2.3.400:
before the judges; besides, if it was untrue, why didn’t your son disprove it?
DEMIPHO
2.3.401:
Do you talk about my son to me? Of whose folly there is no speaking in the language it deserves.
PHORMIO
2.3.403: Then do you, who are so wise, go to the magistrates, that for you they may give a second decision in the same cause,
2.3.405:
since you reign alone here, and are the only man allowed to get a second trial in the same cause.
DEMIPHO
2.3.407: Although wrong has been done me, still, however, rather than engage in litigation, or listen to you, just as though she had been my relation, as the law orders
2.3.410:
one to find her a portion, rid me of her, and take five minae.
PHORMIO
2.3.411:
laughing.) Ha, ha, ha! a pleasant individual!
DEMIPHO
Well! am I asking any thing unfair? Or am I not to obtain even this, which is my right at common law?
PHORMIO
2.3.413: Pray, really is it so, that when you have abused-her like a courtesan, the law orders you to pay her hire and pack her off? Or
2.3.415:
is it the fact, that in order that a citizen may bring no disgrace upon herself through poverty, she has been ordered to be given to her nearest relative, to pass her life with him alone? A thing which you mean to prevent.
DEMIPHO
2.3.418:
Yes, to her nearest.relative, indeed; but why to us, or on what ground?
PHORMIO
Well, well, a thing tried, they say, you can’t try over again.
DEMIPHO
2.3.419: Not try it? On the contrary, I shall not desist
2.3.420:
until I have gone through with it.
PHORMIO
You are trifling.
DEMIPHO
Only let me alone for that.
PHORMIO
2.3.421:
In short, Demipho, I have nothing to do with you; your son has been cast, and not you; for your time of life for marrying has now gone by.
DEMIPHO
2.3.423: Consider that it is he that says to you all I now say,
2.3.425:
or else assuredly, together with this wife of his, I’ll be forbidding him the house.
GETA
(aside.)
2.3.426:
He’s in a passion.
PHORMIO
You’ll be acting more considerately.
DEMIPHO
2.3.427:
Are you so resolved, you unlucky fellow, to do me all the mischief you can?
PHORMIO
(aside, to GETA.)
2.3.428:
He’s afraid of us, although he’s so careful to conceal it.
GETA
(aside, to PHORMIO.)
2.3.429:
Your beginning has turned out well.
PHORMIO
But if, on the contrary,
2.3.430:
you endure what must be endured, you’ll be doing what’s worthy of you, so that we may be on friendly terms.
DEMIPHO
(indignantly.)
2.3.431:
What, I seek your friendship, or have any wish to see or hear you?
PHORMIO
2.3.433:
If you can agree with her, you will have some one to cheer up your old age; just consider your time of life.
DEMIPHO
2.3.435:
Let her cheer up yourself; keep her to yourself.
PHORMIO
Really, do moderate your passion.
DEMIPHO
Mark what I say. There have been words enough already; if you don’t make haste to fetch away the woman, I shall turn her out: I have said it, Phormio.
PHORMIO
2.3.438: If you use her in any other manner than is befitting a free-born woman, I shall be bringing a swinging action against you: I have said it, Demipho.
2.3.440:
(To GETA.) Hark you, if there should be any occasion for me, I shall be at home.
GETA
(apart.)
I understand you.
(Exit PHORMIO.)

2.4.441:
(DEMIPHO, HEGIO, CRATINUS, CRITO, and GETA.) DEMIPHO
What care and anxiety my son does bring upon me, by entangling himself and me in this same marriage! And he doesn’t so much as come into my sight, that at least I might know what he says about this matter. or what his sentiments are.
2.4.445:
(To GETA.) Be off, go see whether he has returned home or not by this.
GETA
2.4.446:
I will. (Goes into the house.)
DEMIPHO
(to the ASSISTANTS.)
You see how the case stands. What am I to do? Tell me, Hegio.
HEGIO
2.4.447:
What, I? I think Cratinus ought, if it seems good to you.
DEMIPHO
2.4.448:
Tell me, Cratinus.
CRATINUS
What, do you wish me to speak?
2.4.449: I should like you to do what is most for your advantage;
2.4.450:
it is my opinion, that what this son of yours has done in your absence, in law and justice ought to be annulled; and that you’ll obtain redress. That’s my opinion.
DEMIPHO
2.4.453: I believe that he has spoken with due deliberation; but it is the fact, as many men, so many minds; every, one his own way.
2.4.455:
It doesn’t appear to me that what has been done by law can be revoked; and it is wrong to attempt it.
DEMIPHO
2.4.457:
I am of opinion that we must deliberate further; it is a, matter of importance.
HEGIO
2.4.458:
Do you want any thing further with us?
DEMIPHO
You have done very well. (Exeunt ASSISTANTS.) I am much more at a loss than before.
(Re-enter GETA, from the house.)
GETA
2.4.459:
They say that he has not come back.
DEMIPHO
2.4.460:
I must wait for my brother. The advice that he gives me about this matter, I shall follow. I’ll go make inquiry at the harbor, when he is to come back.
(Exit.)
GETA
2.4.463: And I’ll go look for Antipho, that he may learn what has passed here. But look, I see him coming this way, just in the very nick of time.

3.1.465:
(Enter ANTIPHO, at a distance.) ANTIPHO
(to himself.)
Indeed, Antipho, in many ways you are to be blamed for these feelings; to have thus run away, and intrusted your existence to the protection of other people. Did you suppose that others would give more attention to your interests than your own self? For, however other matters stood, certainly you should have thought of her whom you have now at home, that she might not suffer any harm in consequence of her confiding in you,
3.1.470:
whose hopes and resources, poor thing, are all now centred in yourself alone.
GETA
(coming forward.)
3.1.471:
Why really, master, we have for some time been censuring you here in your absence, for having thus gone away.
ANTIPHO
3.1.472:
You are the very person I was looking for.
GETA
But still, we were not a bit the more remiss on that account.
ANTIPHO
3.1.473:
Tell me, I beg of you, in what posture are my interests and fortunes. Has my father any suspicion?
GETA
3.1.474:
Not any at present.
ANTIPHO
Is there still any hope?
GETA
I don’t know.
ANTIPHO
Alas!
GETA
3.1.475:
But Phaedria has not neglected to use his endeavors in your behalf.
ANTIPHO
He did nothing new.
GETA
3.1.476:
Then Phormio, too; in this matter, just as in every thing else, showed himself a man of energy.
ANTIPHO
3.1.477:
What did he do?
GETA
With his words he silenced the old man, who was very angry.
ANTIPHO
3.1.478:
Well done, Phormio!
GETA
I, too, did all I could.
ANTIPHO
My dear Geta, I love you all.
GETA
3.1.479: The commencement is just in this position, as I tell you: matters, at present are going on smoothly,
3.1.480:
and your father intends to wait for your uncle till he arrives.
ANTIPHO
Why him?
GETA
He said he was wishful to act by his advice, in all that relates to this business.
ANTIPHO
3.1.482:
How greatly now, Geta, I do dread my uncle’s safe arrival! For, according to his single sentence, from what I hear, I am to live or die.
GETA
3.1.484:
Here comes Phaedria.
ANTIPHO
Where is he, pray?
GETA
See, he’s coming from his place of exercise.

3.2.485:
(Enter from DORIO’S house, DORIO, followed by PHAEDRIA.) PHAEDRIA
Prithee, hear me, Dorio.
DORIO
3.2.486:
I’ll not hear you.
PHAEDRIA
Only a moment.
DORIO
Let me alone.
PHAEDRIA
3.2.487:
Do hear what I have to say.
DORIO
Why really I am tired of hearing the same thing a thousand times over.
PHAEDRIA
3.2.488:
But now, I have something to tell you that you’ll hear with pleasure.
DORIO
Speak then; I’m listening.
PHAEDRIA
3.2.489:
Can I not prevail on you to wait for only three days? Whither are you going now?
DORIO
3.2.490:
I was wondering if you had any thing new to offer.
ANTIPHO
(apart, to GETA.)
3.2.491:
I’m afraid for this Procurer, lest—
GETA
(apart, to ANTIPHO.)
Something may befall his own safety.
PHAEDRIA
3.2.492:
You don’t believe me?
DORIO
You guess right.
PHAEDRIA
But if I pledge my word.
DORIO
Nonsense!
PHAEDRIA
3.2.493:
You will have reason to say that this kindness was well laid out by you on interest.
DORIO
Stuff!
PHAEDRIA
3.2.494:
Believe me, you will be glad you did so; upon my faith, it is the truth.
DORIO
Mere dreams!
PHAEDRIA
3.2.495:
Do but try; the time is not long.
DORIO
The same story over again.
PHAEDRIA
3.2.496:
You will be my kinsman, my father, my friend; you—
DORIO
Now, do prate on.
PHAEDRIA
3.2.497:
For you to be of a disposition so harsh and inexorable, that neither by pity nor by entreaties can you be softened!
DORIO
3.2.499: For you to be of a disposition so unreasonable and so unconscionable, Phaedria,
3.2.500:
that you can be talking me over with fine words, and be for amusing yourself with what’s my property for nothing!
ANTIPHO
(apart, to GETA.)
3.2.501:
I am sorry for him.
PHAEDRIA
(aside.)
Alas! I feel it to be too true.
GETA
(apart, to ANTIPHO.)
How well each keeps up to his character!
PHAEDRIA
(to himself.)
3.2.502:
And would that this misfortune had not befallen me at a time when Antipho was occupied with other cares as well.
ANTIPHO
(coming forward.)
3.2.503:
Ah Phaedria, why, what is the matter?
PHAEDRIA
3.2.504:
O most fortunate Antipho!
ANTIPHO
What, I?
PHAEDRIA
To have in your possession the object of your love,
3.2.505:
and have no occasion to encounter such a nuisance as this.
ANTIPHO
3.2.506:
What I, in my possession? Why yes, as the saying is, I’ve got a wolf by the ears; for I neither know how to get rid of her, nor yet how to keep her.
DORIO
3.2.508:
That’s just my case with regard to him (pointing to PHAEDRIA).
ANTIPHO
(to DORIO.)
Aye, aye, don’t you show too little of the Procurer. (To PHAEDRIA.) What has he been doing?
PHAEDRIA
3.2.509: What, he? Acting the part of a most inhuman fellow;
3.2.510:
been and sold my Pamphila.
GETA
What! Sold her?
ANTIPHO
Sold her, say you?
PHAEDRIA
3.2.511:
Sold her.
DORIO
(ironically.)
What a shocking crime—a wench bought with one’s own money!
PHAEDRIA
3.2.512:
I can not prevail upon him to wait for me the next three days, and so far break off the bargain with the person, while I get the money from my friends, which has been promised me; if I don’t give it him then, let him not wait a single hour longer.
DORIO
3.2.515:
Very good.
ANTIPHO
It’s not a long time that he asks, Dorio; do let him prevail upon you; he’ll pay you two-fold for having acted to him thus obligingly.
DORIO
3.2.517:
Mere words!
ANTIPHO
Will you allow Pamphila to be carried away from this place? And then, besides, can you possibly allow their love to be severed asunder?
DORIO
3.2.519:
Neither I nor you cause that.
GETA
May all the Gods grant you what you are deserving of!
DORIO
3.2.520:
I have borne with you for several months quite against my inclination; promising and whimpering, and yet bringing nothing; now, on the other hand, I have found one to pay, and not be sniveling; give place to your betters.
ANTIPHO
3.2.523:
I’ faith, there surely was a day named, if I remember right, for you to pay him.
PHAEDRIA
3.2.524:
It is the fact.
DORIO
Do I deny it?
ANTIPHO
3.2.525:
Is that day past, then?
DORIO
No; but this one has come before it.
ANTIPHO
Are you not ashamed of your perfidy?
DORIO
3.2.526:
Not at all, so long as it is for my interest.
GETA
Dunghill!
PHAEDRIA
Dorio, is it right, pray, for you to act thus?
DORIO
3.2.527:
It is my way; if I suit you, make use of me.
ANTIPHO
3.2.530: he has deceived me; I’m not a bit different to him from what I was before. But however that may be, I’ll yet do this; the captain has said, that to-morrow morning he will pay me the money; if you bring it me before that, Phaedria, I’ll follow my rule, that he is the first served who is the first to pay. Farewell! (Goes into his house.)

3.3.534:
(PHAEDRIA, ANTIPHO, and GETA.) PHAEDRIA
What am I to do? Wretch that I am! where am I now in this emergency to raise the money for him,
3.3.535:
I, who am worse than nothing? If it had been possible for these three days to be obtained of him, it was promised me by then.
ANTIPHO
3.3.536:
Geta, shall we suffer him to continue thus wretched, when he so lately assisted me in the kind way you were mentioning? On the contrary, why not, as there’s need of it try to do him a kindness in return?
GETA
3.3.539:
For my part, I’m sure it is but fair.
ANTIPHO
Come then, you are the only man able to serve him.
GETA
3.3.540:
What can I do?
ANTIPHO
Procure the money.
GETA
I wish I could; but where it is to come from—tell me that.
ANTIPHO
3.3.541:
My father has come home.
GETA
I know; but what of that?
ANTIPHO
Oh, a word to the wise is quite enough.
GETA
3.3.542:
Is that it, then?
ANTIPHO
Just so.
GETA
Upon my faith, you really do give me fine advice; out upon you! Ought I not to be heartily glad, if I meet with no mishap through your marriage, but what, in addition to that, you must now bid me, for his sake, to be seeking risk upon risk?
ANTIPHO
3.3.545:
’Tis true what he says.
PHAEDRIA
What! am I a stranger to you, Geta?
GETA
I don’t consider you so. But is it so trifling a matter that the old gentleman is now vexed with us all, that we must provoke him still more, and leave no room for entreaty?
PHAEDRIA
3.3.548: Is another man to take her away from before my eyes to some unknown spot? Alas!
3.3.549:
speak to me then, Antipho, and look upon me while you have the opportunity, and while I’m present.
ANTIPHO
3.3.550:
Why so, or what are you going to do? Pray, tell me.
PHAEDRIA
3.3.551:
To whatever part of the world she is borne away, I’m determined to follow her or to perish.
GETA
3.3.552:
May the Gods prosper your design! Cautiously’s the word, however.
ANTIPHO
(to GETA.)
3.3.553:
Do see if you can give him any assistance at all.
GETA
Any at all—how?
ANTIPHO
Pray, do try, that he mayn’t be doing something that we may afterward be more or less sorry for, Geta.
GETA
3.3.555:
I’m considering, (He pauses.) He’s all safe, so far as I can guess: but still, I’m afraid of mischief.
ANTIPHO
3.3.556:
Don’t be afraid: together with you, we’ll share good and bad.
GETA
(to PHAEDRIA.)
3.3.557:
How much money do you want? Tell me.
PHAEDRIA
Only thirty minae.
GETA
3.3.558:
Thirty? Heyday! she’s monstrous dear, Phaedria.
PHAEDRIA
Indeed, she’s very cheap.
GETA
3.3.559:
Well, well, I’ll get them for you.
PHAEDRIA
Oh the dear man! (They both fall to hugging GETA.)
GETA
Take yourselves off. (Shakes them of.)
PHAEDRIA
There’s need for them directly.
GETA
You shall have them directly;
3.3.560:
but I must have Phormio for my assistant in this business.
ANTIPHO
3.3.561:
He’s quite ready; right boldly lay on him any load you like, he’ll bear it: he, in especial, is a friend to his friend.
GETA
3.3.562:
Let’s go to him at once then.
ANTIPHO
3.3.563:
Will you have any occasion for my assistance?
GETA
None; but be off home, and comfort that poor thing, who I am sure is now in-doors almost dead with fear. Do you linger?
ANTIPHO
3.3.565:
There’s nothing I could do with so much pleasure.
(Goes into the house of DEMIPHO.)
PHAEDRIA
3.3.566:
What way will you manage this?
GETA
I’ll tell you on the road; first thing, betake yourself off. (Exeunt.)

4.1.567:
(Enter DEMIPHO and CHREMES.) DEMIPHO
Well, have you brought your daughter with you, Chremes, for whom you went to Lemnos?
CHREMES
4.1.569: When her mother found that I staid here longer than usual,
4.1.570:
and at the same time the age of the girl did not suit with my delays, they told me that she, with all her family, set out in search of me.
DEMIPHO
4.1.572:
Pray, then, why did you stay there so long, when you had heard of this?
CHREMES
4.1.574:
Why, faith, a malady detained me.
DEMIPHO
From what cause? Or what was it?
CHREMES
Do you ask me?
4.1.575:
Old age itself is a malady. However, I heard that they had arrived safe, from the caps tain who brought them.
DEMIPHO
4.1.577:
Have you heard, Chremes, what has happened to my son in my absence?
CHREMES
4.1.578: ’Tis that, in fact, that has embarrassed me in my plans. For if I offer my daughter in marriage to any person that’s a stranger,
4.1.580: it must all be told how and by whom I had her. You I knew to be fully as faithful to me as I am to myself; if a stranger shall think fit to be connected with me by marriage, he will hold his tongue, just as long as good terms exist between us: but if he takes a dislike to me, he’ll be knowing more than it’s proper he should know.
4.1.585:
I am afraid, too, lest my wife should, by some means, come to know of it; if that is the case, it only remains for me to shake myself and leave the house; for I’m the only one I can rely on at home.
DEMIPHO
4.1.588: I know it is so, and that circumstance is a cause of anxiety to me; and I shall never cease trying,
4.1.590: until I’ve made good what I promised you.

4.2.595: he was quite delighted; complimented me; asked where the old man was; gave thanks to the Gods that an opportunity was afforded him for showing himself no less a friend to Phaedria than to Antipho: I bade the fellow wait for me at the Forum; whither I would bring the old gentleman.
4.2.600: But see, here’s the very man (catching sight of the Old Man). Who is the further one? Heyday, Phaedria’s father has got back! still, brute beast that I am, what was I afraid of? Is it because two are presented instead of one for me to dupe? I deem it preferable to enjoy a two-fold hope.
